#5558. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5557. Alwaleed Philanthropies and The Research, Development and Innovation Authority Sign Strategic Partnership valued at SAR 10 million to Advance Innovation and Technology Solutions

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Alwaleed Philanthropies, chaired by HRH Prince Alwaleed bin talal Al Saud and the Research, Development and Innovation Authority (RDIA) have signed a strategic partnership agreement in the presence of HRH Princess Lamia bint Majed Al Saud, Secretary General of Alwaleed Philanthropies, and HE Dr. Munir bin Mahmoud Eldesouki, Acting Governor of RDIA, to strengthen Saudi Arabia's research, development and innovation ecosystem, empower researchers and innovators, and advance technology solutions with meaningful impact.

The partnership will also promote a culture of research and innovation, build national capabilities, and enable the development of programs and initiatives aligned with the Kingdom's priorities in key technology fields.

As part of the partnership, Alwaleed Philanthropies will play a role in enabling the Open RAN Technology Challenge and contributing to the ongoing oversight of the participating startup. Four startups were selected as winners after presenting innovative and deployable technology solutions. The partnership will enable the winning startups to further develop their solutions, accelerate their transition to deployment, launch their products, and measure their impact.

Alwaleed Philanthropies will also contribute to promoting a culture of research, development and innovation and strengthening its presence within the local community. The Research, Development and Innovation Authority will coordinate with relevant stakeholders across the RDI ecosystem, monitor the startups' performance and periodic reports, share updates with Alwaleed Philanthropies, and assess the initiative's outputs and impact.

The partnership includes the formation of a joint working group to oversee implementation, fulfil shared commitments, monitor the participating startups, and facilitate the launch of products developed through the initiative. The two organizations will also explore and develop joint programs and initiatives in research and innovation, strengthening collaboration between the public and nonprofit sectors and creating sustainable impact in Saudi Arabia and internationally, in line with applicable laws and regulations.

The strategic partnership builds on the successful collaboration between Alwaleed Philanthropies and the Research, Development and Innovation Authority. Their first joint initiative enabled 96 women to pursue postgraduate studies in fields of the future, including artificial intelligence and renewable energy, at universities ranked among the world's top 30, contributing to the development of highly qualified national capabilities.

The partnership represents a sustainable model for empowering national talent, advancing innovation, and developing technology solutions with tangible impact. It will help address national challenges and transform ideas and research into products and solutions that create lasting knowledge and economic value, supporting the Kingdom's transition toward an economy powered by knowledge and innovation.

#5556. Canopy Realtor® Association Names Rob Nanfelt Next CEO

Canopy Realtor® Association has announced the appointment of Rob Nanfelt as its next Chief Executive Officer, effective Jan. 4, 2027. Nanfelt succeeds current CEO Anne Marie DeCatsye, who is retiring from the position at the end of 2026 following 26 years of leadership. Nanfelt will also serve as CEO of Canopy Housing Foundation.

As CEO, Canopy noted that Nanfelt will provide strategic and executive leadership to Canopy Realtor® Association and Canopy Housing Foundation, working with their respective Boards to advance their missions, strengthen member value, expand community partnerships, and identify opportunities for innovation and organizational growth. The Canopy Housing Foundation will continue to have a dedicated Executive Director responsible for its programs and activities.

“Our region is strategically poised to grow our economic health within all real estate disciplines,” said Nanfelt. “By reinforcing the vital role government advocacy plays in supporting our industry, we can find solutions to critical issues and advance the real estate profession with a shared purpose. I look forward to galvanizing those strategic goals across the entire breadth of leadership here at Canopy.”

Nanfelt’s 25 years of experience spans the disciplines of executive leadership, association management, strategic planning, government affairs, and public policy, as noted in a release.

In his previous position as Executive Director of the Real Estate & Building Industry Coalition (REBIC), Nanfelt worked with business executives, elected officials, and community leaders to address issues central to the Charlotte region’s economic vitality and long-term growth. Prior to this, he served as Executive Vice President and Government Affairs Director of the Colorado Association of Home Builders, forging new strategic initiatives and becoming a leader in innovation and policy advancement for the industry. Earlier in his career, Nanfelt held several positions on Capitol Hill, including Chief of Staff to U.S. Congressman Bob Schaffer of Colorado.

“My hope was that the search committee would not simply find a successor, but secure someone with the vision, and experience needed to take Canopy to the next level.” said DeCatsye. “I have tremendous confidence in his leadership, fresh perspective, established relationships, and his deep understanding of what it takes to leverage the opportunities ahead. I could not be more excited about Canopy’s future, and I’m thrilled with the selection of Rob Nanfelt as our next CEO.”

Joan Goode, 2026 President of Canopy Realtor® Association, echoed DeCatsye’s sentiment, adding that Nanfelt’s appointment “reflects the Search Committee’s commitment to identifying a proven executive with the experience, relationships, and vision to lead Canopy into the future.”

“He is exceptionally well positioned to strengthen Canopy’s influence, advance its mission, support the success of our members, and build upon its respected legacy,” she continued.

Canopy noted that Nanfelt’s appointment represents an important milestone in its planned leadership transition. Beginning in 2027, Canopy Realtor® Association and Canopy MLS will operate under separate executive leadership and governance structures, allowing each organization to focus on its distinct mission while maintaining collaboration through shared leadership and administrative services. Steve Byrd, who became CEO of Canopy MLS in August 2026, will continue in that role.

For DeCatsye, the transition carries a personal connection.

“Before joining Canopy 26 years ago, I spent six years as Deputy Executive Director of REBIC, an experience that gave me a deep appreciation for advocacy and how it moves our industry forward,” she shared. “There is something wonderfully fitting about Rob following a similar path and I am delighted that he will lead with those ideals fully embedded in his mission for Canopy.”

For more information, visit https://www.canopyrealtors.com/.

#5555. Five thoughts from Cisco’s first quarter of fiscal 2027

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Cisco Systems Inc. opened fiscal 2027 with a quarter that should put any question about whether artificial intelligence will act as a massive tailwind for it to rest. Revenue and earnings hit records, growth rates were the best Cisco has posted in more than 15 years, and management raised its full-year outlook and AI infrastructure revenue target.

While Cisco has delivered a string of solid quarters, some investors are concerned about the durability of the growth. After listening to the analyst call, I maintain that accelerated growth is what Cisco watchers should expect, as AI will act as a catalyst for several years. Here are my five thoughts, plus the one metric I think investors should care about most:

Asked why this isn’t simply the top of a hyperscaler spending cycle, Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) cited five growth drivers: hyperscale AI, the campus refresh, the “post-Mythos” security upgrade cycle, sovereign infrastructure and enterprise hybrid data centers. “All five of these are multiyear, multibillion,” he said. “And they’re all in relatively early stages.” In particular, the enterprise opportunity is in its infancy. Using the baseball analogy for “what inning” we’re in, the pitchers are still warming up, and enterprise is what Cisco does best.

Though hyperscalers have been driving AI growth across the industry, only one of the five trends Robbins highlighted was related to that group of companies. Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson reinforced the point by breaking down the guidance raise, noting that a large share came from Cisco’s core, non-hyperscale business. “It’s not just campus,” he said. “It’s broad-based, and the core continues to do quite well.”

The market still views the enterprise as a slow-refresh business. The call made a strong case that it’s about to become the bigger part of Cisco’s AI story.

During the investor Q&A, a data point was worth highlighting. Robbins said that of the campus switching Cisco sold this quarter, “only 9% was really coming from the new portfolio.” Despite multiple quarters of strong campus growth, the installed base has barely moved to the next generation.

Two forces will push this base to accelerate an upgrade. One is agentic AI, which Robbins said is driving “modernization for bandwidth reasons” because agents generate traffic that campus networks were never designed to handle. The other is the security fallout from frontier models such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos — the Mythos moment. “We’re beginning to hear from customers who are attributing orders to early Mythos implications,” Robbins said, noting that European service providers are upgrading managed customer premises equipment.

Robbins added that customers “got to get the architecture exactly right.” That suggests a long, deliberate redesign rather than a buying spree, which is characteristic of a multiyear cycle.

Cisco has long been criticized for building its own silicon as the industry shifted to merchant silicon. Robbins said that outside of optics, the hyperscale AI business is “100% Silicon One-based platforms.” The P200 continues to win scale-across deals, and the G300 is now in customer labs.

Asked why Cisco keeps winning those deals, Robbins kept it simple: “It’s really about performance and power. And there’s just this whole focus on diversity of silicon in the space.” The second point is the more strategic one. No hyperscaler wants a single supplier for any critical layer of its AI fabric, and Cisco is the credible second source.

The bigger long-term play is the enterprise. Silicon One is already shipping across parts of the enterprise portfolio, and Robbins said the target to convert all of it by fiscal 2029 “is still on track.” That gives Cisco a single silicon architecture from the hyperscale data center to the branch, with cost and roadmap control competitors can’t match.

The reality is that at Cisco’s volumes, it makes no sense to buy merchant silicon. Not only can it build it cheaper, but it can also optimize it specifically for its own features and capabilities.

A theme running through the call is that AI is decentralizing. “Our enterprise customers will be running AI applications in the cloud, but they’re also investing heavily in private data centers,” Robbins said. “They want to run open-weight and open-source models in their own data centers. They want to train on their own data in their own data centers.”

Sovereignty is driving in the same direction, with Cisco extending its Sovereign Critical Infrastructure portfolio from Europe to Canada and preannouncing India. Robbins noted that Cisco is “one of the few companies that has maintained a robust on-premises portfolio.” For years, analysts treated that on-premises focus as a liability. In a world where countries and regulated industries want operational control, it has become an advantage.

Equally important is what Cisco isn’t chasing. Robbins called neocloud exposure “relatively immaterial,” adding that “we’ve been very conservative relative to the credit situations.” That’s a disciplined choice. Cisco is growing into the safest parts of the AI build-out rather than financing its riskiest buyers.

Given the number of neoclouds, one could look at them as a massive pot of gold, but they often required vendor financing. If the neocloud isn’t successful, it’s the financing organization left holding the bag. This was the case with CLECs in the Internet days. Cisco was conservative then and will continue to be.

Security has been the weak spot in Cisco’s story, so this quarter’s progress matters. Robbins said core security orders, excluding Splunk, were “the best it’s been in three years,” with firewalls, Zero Trust secure access, and AI Defense all gaining customers. Patterson said Cisco is “a little bit above the expectations that we set out” and feels “good about turning the corner.”

The refresh cycle drives near-term numbers, but the strategic prize is trust for AI agents. Robbins said enterprise conversations now center on “agentic security, agentic identity, agentic observability, as well as the new security architecture needed for the AI era.” The network is where agent traffic flows, making it the natural enforcement point. Cisco owns more of that network than anyone.

Investor concerns received clear answers. On margins, Patterson said, “gross margins are pretty much right on target,” and on supply, “we’re seeing not a lot of issues at all.” Robbins added that Cisco is growing revenue “with less headcount than we had at the beginning” two years ago.

The number I’d watch most closely isn’t AI revenue, campus orders, or gross margin. It’s the growth of Cisco Cloud Control. Robbins mentioned it almost in passing, noting thousands of sign-ups and integrations with AI Canvas, Cisco IQ and Cisco Model Foundry. Most people will think of Cloud Control as a network management tool, but that badly understates its potential.

Cloud Control is now Cisco’s core product. The best analogy is VMware vCenter, the data center’s control point that turned a collection of products into a sticky platform. Cheaper, sometimes free hypervisors never made a dent in VMware’s share because the operational control gained from vCenter far outweighed the few bucks saved on hypervisor licenses. Cloud Control is broader and potentially more impactful because Cisco is positioning it as the control point for enterprise AI, not just the network through the following capabilities.

Cisco’s numerous network and security competitors have their own agentic operations platforms, and many beat Cisco to market. However, Cisco played the long game. In my conversations with Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel, he has been emphatic about how important Cloud Control is to Cisco’s vision of shifting to a platform company. It enables customers to manage the underlying infrastructure, including third parties, through a single dashboard.

If Cloud Control becomes the enterprise IT console for managing AI-era infrastructure, Cisco stops competing on boxes and starts competing on control. Hardware cycles always ebb and flow, so always being best of breed is impossible. Whether this one becomes a transformation for Cisco depends on whether customers run their environments on Cloud Control. My advice to Cisco is to start disclosing active usage, partner integrations, and attach rates for the platform.

My advice to investors is to start asking for them. That number will tell you what Cisco is worth five years from now.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5554. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5553. IRS raises 401(k) limit for 2027 to $25,500

The IRS increased the 2027 401(k) deferral limit to $25,500 and raised catch-up limits to $8,500, or $11,750 for ages 60 to 63. IRA limits remain at $7,500, while multiple IRA and Saver’s Credit income thresholds increased.  AI Summary

The IRS has increased the annual contribution limit for 401(k) plans in 2027 to $25,500, up $1,000 from the 2026 limit of $24,500, the agency announced on Thursday.

The higher limit also applies to employees participating in 403(b) plans, governmental 457 plans and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan, according to guidance issued by the IRS in Notice 2026-66. The notice outlines cost-of-living adjustments for retirement plans and other retirement-related tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

The catch-up contribution limit for employees ages 50 and older increased to $8,500, up from $8,000 in 2026. That brings the total annual contribution limit for most eligible participants ages 50 and older to $34,000.

Employees ages 60 through 63 are eligible for a higher catch-up contribution limit under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022. For 2027, that limit increased to $11,750, allowing eligible participants to contribute up to $37,250.

The annual contribution limit for individual retirement accounts remains unchanged at $7,500. The IRA catch-up contribution limit for individuals ages 50 and older also remains at $1,100.

“Along with the Working Families Tax Cuts, this increase in the pension limitations will help American families keep more of their hard-earned income,” IRS CEO Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.

The IRS also increased several income thresholds used to determine eligibility for tax deductions and retirement account contributions.

For traditional IRAs, the income phase-out range for single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan increased to $83,000 to $93,000, up from $81,000 to $91,000 in 2026.

For married couples filing jointly, the range increased to $133,000 to $153,000, up from $129,000 to $149,000, when the spouse making the contribution is covered by a workplace retirement plan.

For IRA contributors who are not covered by a workplace retirement plan but are married to someone who is, the phase-out range increased to $250,000 to $260,000, up from $242,000 to $252,000.

The income phase-out range for Roth IRA contributions also increased. For single taxpayers and heads of household, the range is now $158,000 to $173,000, compared with $153,000 to $168,000 in 2026. For married couples filing jointly, it increased to $250,000 to $260,000, up from $242,000 to $252,000.

The IRS also raised the annual contribution limit for SIMPLE retirement accounts to $17,500, up from $17,000. Certain eligible SIMPLE plans have a higher limit of $19,100, compared with $18,100 in 2026.

Catch-up contribution limits for most SIMPLE plans remain unchanged at $4,000 for employees ages 50 and older. The limit is $3,850 for certain applicable SIMPLE plans and $5,250 for employees ages 60 through 63.

The income limits for the Saver’s Credit, which benefits low- and moderate-income workers who save for retirement, also increased. For 2027, the limits are $83,000 for married couples filing jointly, $62,250 for heads of household, and $41,500 for single taxpayers and married individuals filing separately.

The IRS said the adjustments are intended to account for cost-of-living changes and help taxpayers and employers plan for the coming year.

#5552. Freightos Receives Nasdaq Notice Regarding Minimum Bid Price Requirement

BARCELONA, Spain, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Freightos Limited (NASDAQ: CRGO) ("Freightos" or the "Company"), the leading vendor-neutral global freight pricing, booking and procurement platform, today announced that on November 10, 2026, it received a written notification letter (the "Notification Letter") from the Listing Qualifications Department of The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC ("Nasdaq") notifying the Company that it is not in compliance with the minimum bid price requirement set forth in Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2) for continued listing on the Nasdaq Capital Market.

Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2) requires listed securities to maintain a minimum bid price of $1.00 per share, and Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A) provides that a failure to meet this requirement exists if the deficiency continues for a period of 30 consecutive business days. The Notification Letter indicated that the closing bid price of the Company's ordinary shares had been below $1.00 per share for 30 consecutive business days, from September 29, 2026 through November 9, 2026.

In accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A), the Company has been provided an initial period of 180 calendar days from the date of the Notification Letter, or until May 10, 2027, to regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement. The Company will regain compliance if, at any time during this compliance period, the closing bid price of its ordinary shares is at least $1.00 per share for a minimum of 10 consecutive business days, unless Nasdaq exercises its discretion to extend this period under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(H). If the Company regains compliance, Nasdaq will provide the Company with written confirmation and the matter will be closed.

If the Company does not regain compliance by May 10, 2027, the Company may be eligible for an additional 180-calendar-day compliance period.

The Notification Letter has no immediate effect on the listing of the Company's ordinary shares. The Company's ordinary shares will continue to be listed and to trade on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the symbol "CRGO" during the compliance period. The Notification Letter does not affect the Company's business operations.

The Company intends to monitor the closing bid price of its ordinary shares and is evaluating available options to regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement within the applicable compliance period, which may include, if necessary, effecting a reverse share split, subject to any required shareholder approval. There can be no assurance that the Company will regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement or maintain compliance with any other Nasdaq continued listing requirement.

#5551. Mortgage industry expects CFPB servicing rule to narrow

The CFPB has sent a revised version of its 2024 “Streamlining Mortgage Servicing for Borrowers Experiencing Payment Difficulties” rule to the Office of Management and Budget, moving closer to finalizing new loss-mitigation standards under Regulation X. Industry attorneys expect a significantly narrower rule than the original proposal, shaped by President Trump’s directive to modernize Dodd-Frank-era rules and broad stakeholder pushback against open-ended requirements.  AI Summary

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) last week took another step toward finalizing new loss-mitigation standards, sending a revised version of its 2024 mortgage servicing proposal to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review.

The final rule, “Streamlining Mortgage Servicing for Borrowers Experiencing Payment Difficulties” under Regulation X, is expected to be narrower than the 2024 proposal advanced when the CFPB was led by Rohit Chopra, according to industry attorneys. The CFPB did not immediately reply to HousingWire‘s request for comments.

The move comes in the wake of President Donald Trump’s March 13 executive order, “Promoting Access to Mortgage Credit,” which directs the CFPB to modernize Dodd-Frank-era rules that lenders and servicers say increase compliance costs. The current standards were finalized in 2013.

“We won’t know the final rule’s content until it is published. But the comment record and the current Bureau’s priorities point toward a significantly narrower rule,”Joseph M. DeFazio and Joe Reilly, partners at Troutman Pepper Locke, wrote in a blog post. “Since President Trump’s second term began, the Bureau has also rescinded prior guidance and signaled that it prefers clear, fixed rules to open-ended frameworks like the one in the 2024 proposal.”

The CFPB received more than 80 comments on the proposal, with what the attorneys described as an “unusual degree of convergence” among groups that rarely agree.

The American Bankers Association (ABA) has urged the CFPB to finalize only a limited portion of the 2024 proposal, pressing the bureau to focus on targeted changes rather than a full rewrite.

“The Bureau’s 2024 proposal was founded on the misconception that servicers prioritize foreclosure over helping borrowers find a successful solution to resolve their payment disruptions,” Teshale Smith, the ABA’s senior counsel for regulatory compliance and policy, said in a letter to the CFPB in June. “In fact, sustained low foreclosure rates and high customer satisfaction rates demonstrate that servicers remain committed to helping struggling borrowers.”

The 2024 proposed rule aimed to make permanent several pandemic-era practices used when large numbers of borrowers needed fast assistance. Industry estimates showed that 8.8 million families were helped, with the re-default rate for loans exiting COVID-19 loss-mitigation programs at about 10%, ABA said in its letter.The proposal allows servicers to evaluate loss-mitigation options before borrowers complete an application, prohibits late fees and other charges while a loss-mitigation review is underway, and makes assistance possible in multiple languages.As it relates to foreclosure, the draft allows a loss-mitigation review cycle to start when the borrower asks for help, not only after a completed application, lasting until the loan is current or all options are ruled out. During that time, servicers could not begin or advance foreclosure, a protection that currently applies only after a complete application is on file. Foreclosure could resume only after options were exhausted or the borrower stopped communicating.

Attorneys at Troutman Pepper Locke expect the final rule to permit sequential review of loss-mitigation options instead of requiring servicers to evaluate all options at once; dropping the proposed ban on fee accrual during loss-mitigation reviews; and removal of the language access provisions that were part of the 2024 draft.

Isaac Boltansky, head of public policy at Pennymac, said the company “supports clear, consistent standards that give servicers the certainty they need to deliver the best possible outcomes for homeowners, particularly those facing financial hardship.”

#5549. CNFinance Announces Change of Auditor

GUANGZHOU, China, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CNFinance Holdings Limited (NYSE: CNF) ("CNFinance" or the "Company"), a leading home equity loan service provider in China, today announced the change of auditor, effective November 13, 2026. HTL International, LLC ("HTL") has served as the Company's independent registered public accounting firm since December 2024. HTL declined to stand for re-election to serve as the independent registered public accounting firm for the audits of the Company's financial statements for the financial year ending December 31, 2026. The decision was not a result of any disagreement between the Company and HTL on any matter of accounting principles or practices, financial statement disclosure, or auditing scope or procedure. The audit committee of the Company's Board of Directors has approved the change of auditor and appointed Guangdong Prouden CPAs GP ("Prouden") as the Company's independent registered public accounting firm for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2026.

The appointment of Prouden was made after a careful and thorough evaluation process and has been approved by the audit committee of the Company's board of directors.

Prouden succeeds HTL, the Company's previous independent registered public accounting firm. The reports of HTL on the Company's consolidated financial statements for each of the fiscal years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025 did not contain an adverse opinion or a disclaimer of opinion and were not qualified or modified as to uncertainty, audit scope or accounting principle.

During each of the fiscal years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025 and the subsequent period through November 13, 2026, there have been no disagreements between the Company and HTL on any matter of accounting principles or practices, financial statement disclosure, or auditing scope or procedure, which disagreements, if not resolved to the satisfaction of HTL, would have caused HTL to make reference to the subject matter of the disagreements in its report on the consolidated financial statements, and there have been no "reportable events" as the term is described in Item 16F(a)(1)(v) of Form 20-F.

The Company is working closely with HTL and Prouden to ensure a seamless transition.

The audit committee would like to express its sincere gratitude to HTL for its quality of services rendered to the Company over the past years.

CNFinance Holdings Limited (NYSE: CNF) ("CNFinance" or the "Company") is a leading home equity loan service provider in China. CNFinance, through its operating subsidiaries in China, conducts business by connecting demands and supplies through collaborating with sales partners and trust companies under the trust lending model, and sales partners, local channel partners and commercial banks under the commercial bank partnership model. Sales partners and local channel partners are responsible for recommending micro- and small-enterprise ("MSE") owners with financing needs to the Company and the Company introduces eligible borrowers to licensed financial institutions with sufficient funding sources including trust companies and commercial banks who will then conduct their own risk assessments and make credit decisions. The Company's primary target borrower segment is MSE owners who own real properties in Tier 1 and Tier 2 cities and other major cities in China. The Company's risk mitigation mechanism is embedded in the design of its loan products, supported by an integrated online and offline process focusing on risks of both borrowers and collateral and further enhanced by effective post-loan management procedures.

#5548. Google Cloud takes aim at the cost of keeping idle AI agents running on Kubernetes

Kubernetes has become the go-to platform for distributed training and inference, but what happens to the compute bill when it runs AI agents that spend most of their time waiting?

When an agent’s container or virtual machine stays provisioned, customers pay for the wait as well as the work. To help customers control those costs and make agent workloads more predictable, Google LLC has donated three projects to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, according to Allan Naim (pictured, left), director of product management, AI infrastructure, at Google Cloud. For Kubernetes itself, the new challenge is freeing up compute between bursts of activity while letting each agent pick up where it left off.

“Act 2 is a few years back; Kubernetes became the de facto for inference and training,” Naim said. “What’s really interesting right now is we’re embarking on this Act 3 … where the typical patterns are very, very different from how Kubernetes was designed.”

Naim and Gari Singh (right), product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google Cloud is using open-source tools to cut compute costs when AI agents sit idle. (* Disclosure below.)

Cost presents a serious problem in agentic workloads, with agents sitting idle 90% to 95% of the time waiting on models, test runs or human approvals, Naim explained. Google developed Agent Substrate, an open-source runtime that hosts AI agents in isolated environments on Kubernetes. When an agent is suspended, the runtime saves a snapshot of its memory and local files and frees up its compute for other agents. When work resumes, it restores the agent from that snapshot in an available sandbox.

“It helps from an economic standpoint,” Naim said. “We’ve seen 10x reduction in cost in terms of running Agent Substrate on Kubernetes versus running these agents directly on dedicated virtual machines and containers.”

Security is another concern. In response, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018, which sits on top of the host kernel to block or audit every system call an agent makes, according to Singh.

“Agents and agent harnesses are designed to solve a problem — and to try to solve a problem — until they can’t solve the problem,” Singh said. “They will find all kinds of clever workarounds. They know everything that’s around. You want to make sure that it didn’t go make some low-level change to [your] low-level security, didn’t make an outbound network call, didn’t try to open a file that it shouldn’t.”

Google is also working with Anyscale Inc. on KubeRay, which runs Anyscale’s Ray platform natively on Kubernetes so platform teams can offer distributed training and inference to many research groups, Singh noted. OpenRL brings that approach to reinforcement learning, which teaches post-trained models guardrails, Naim added.

“In the past, to do reinforcement learning, you needed to hire a dozen research scientists with PhDs,” Naim said. “Our goal was, ‘How can we bring reinforcement learning into the world of platform engineering so that you can run reinforcement learning on your Kubernetes environment and take advantage of it to actually do continuous improvement for your agentic workload?'”

#5547. Builder credit conditions tighten for 19th straight quarter

NAHB’s Q3 2026 AD&C Financing survey shows credit for land acquisition, development and construction tightened for the 19th consecutive quarter, mirroring Federal Reserve loan officer data. Contract rates moved only modestly and were offset by lower points, keeping effective borrowing costs elevated across most AD&C categories. Builders are increasingly using construction-to-permanent loans tied to end buyers, with 32% of respondents using them and, for those, 58% of homes financed this way. Persistent tight AD&C lending threatens to slow lot development and new-home supply, reinforcing structural housing shortages even as the mortgage market shows its own signs of stress.  AI Summary

Credit conditions for residential land acquisition, development and construction (AD&C) loans tightened again in the third quarter of 2026, extending a nearly five-year stretch of more restrictive lending for homebuilders, according to a National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) survey.

NAHB’s quarterly AD&C Financing survey showed a net easing index of -15.3 in Q3, meaning more builders and developers reported tighter credit than easier credit. It marks the 19th consecutive quarter of net tightening for AD&C borrowers, NAHB economist Paul Emrath wrote in an analysis published Nov. 13.

The findings closely track the Federal Reserve’s October survey of senior loan officers. NAHB reported that the Fed’s net easing index for residential AD&C loans came in at -15.5 in the third quarter. Aside from modest lender-reported easing in the second quarter of 2026, both lenders and builders have indicated that AD&C credit has been tightening steadily since early 2022. The Fed’s index has been in negative territory in 18 of the past 19 quarters.

For homebuilders and land developers, those readings underscore that bank appetite for risk in residential construction remains weak even as broader housing demand depends on new supply.

While credit availability continued to contract, AD&C financing costs showed only modest quarter-to-quarter movement in the third quarter, with no clear trend toward either higher or lower overall borrowing costs.

NAHB reported the following changes in average contract interest rates between the second and third quarters of 2026:

At the same time, initial points on AD&C loans declined across all four categories, NAHB found:

Those offsetting moves left effective borrowing costs — which combine contract rates and points — little changed for most types of AD&C credit:

For builders, the message is that even where nominal rates tick lower, the all-in cost of capital for lots and vertical construction remains high by historical standards. Combined with tighter underwriting, that environment can slow lot pipeline development, constrain spec building and push more risk and cost back onto builders’ balance sheets.

NAHB’s third-quarter survey also highlighted increased use of construction-to-permanent, or one-time-close, loans tied directly to the end buyer.

Among survey respondents who built single-family homes in the third quarter, 32% said they financed at least some production with construction-to-permanent loans to the ultimate homebuyer. On average, 58% of the homes those respondents built were financed this way, NAHB reported.

Those structures can help builders reduce their direct exposure to AD&C credit by shifting some financing to retail mortgage channels earlier in the process. They can also appeal to buyers looking to lock both construction and permanent financing terms in a single transaction, an important hedge in a volatile rate environment.

NAHB noted that market stress in residential mortgages – including a recent drop in applications and rising delinquencies – has drawn significant attention. But the group argued that constrained AD&C financing is an underappreciated bottleneck for adding new supply, especially in affordable and entry-level segments.

Because AD&C loans finance land pipelines, infrastructure and vertical construction, persistently tight lending standards can limit lot development, delay projects and reduce the number of homes that reach the for-sale market. That dynamic can amplify the impact of low existing-home inventory and keep upward pressure on home prices and rents.

For builders, developers and their lenders, the survey results suggest that planning assumptions for 2027 should continue to factor in restricted credit availability, elevated effective borrowing costs and a need for diversified capital sources, including joint ventures, private capital and greater use of buyer-based construction-to-perm structures.

More detail on credit conditions for residential builders and developers, including cross-tabs on lender behavior and loan terms, is available on NAHB’s AD&C Financing Survey web page.

#5545. FiEE, Inc. Announces Third Quarter 2026 Unaudited Financial Results

Revenue for the First Nine Months of 2026 Surged 382.1% Year-on-Year to Approximately $9.6 Million

Profit Turnaround for the First Nine Months of 2026 with Net Income of $3.6 Million

OSAKA, Japan, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FiEE, Inc. (NASDAQ:FIEE) ("FiEE," the "Company," "we," "our," or similar terms), a technology company that leverages IoT, connectivity, and AI to deliver SaaS solutions for content creation and brand management, along with phygital art advisory services that connect artists, collectors, and brands, today announced its unaudited financial results for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026.

Operational and Financial Highlights for the Nine Months Ended September 30, 2026

Operational and Financial Highlights for the Three Months Ended September 30, 2026

Rafael Li, Chief Executive Officer and President of FiEE, commented, "We delivered solid financial results during the period and made meaningful progress in building a more diversified, scalable digital services platform. By expanding our AI-driven content offerings, phygital art advisory services, and software services, we continued to strengthen our market position and open up new avenues for growth. We were also pleased with the success of our recent art exhibition and collector engagement, which highlighted the increasing value of connecting creators, audiences, and collectors through our ecosystem."

Mr. Li added, " Building on this foundation, including our recently completed art exhibition, we have begun generating revenue across art advisory, acquisition assistance, exhibition services, post-transaction support, and MCN brokerage services, and expect this momentum to continue. We are excited about what this means for our creator ecosystem, as these services have given creators a platform to showcase their work and a direct line to collectors who value their work. By broadening our services and deepening engagement with our community of creators and collectors, we believe we can further expand our market reach, scale our platform, and deliver sustainable, long-term value to our stockholders."

Financial Results for the Nine Months Ended September 30, 2026

Revenue was approximately $9.6 million, compared to $2.0 million in the same period of 2025.

Gross profit was approximately $7.3 million, compared to $1.6 million in the same period of 2025.

Gross margin was 76.3%, compared to 83.0% in the same period of 2025. The decrease primarily reflected higher amortization costs included in cost of revenues.

Operating expenses were approximately $3.5 million, representing an increase of 26.0% from $2.8 million in the same period of 2025.

Operating income was approximately $3.8 million, marking a turnaround from a loss of $1.1 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2025.

Net income was approximately $3.6 million, representing a turnaround from the $1.3 million loss for the nine months ended September 30, 2025.

Diluted earnings per common share was $0.24, compared to a diluted loss per common share of $0.25 for the nine months ended September 30, 2025.

FiEE, Inc. (NASDAQ:FIEE), formerly Minim, Inc., was founded in 1977. The Company has a historical track record of delivering a comprehensive WiFi/Software as a Service platform in the market. After years of development, FiEE made the strategic decision to transition to a Software First Model, rebranding itself as a technology company leveraging its expertise in IoT, connectivity, and AI to improve artwork circulation, as well as engagement with artists and collectors.

Notably, FiEE has introduced its innovative Software as a Service solutions, which integrate its AI and data analytics capabilities into content creation and brand management. Building on its established pool of KOLs and artist network, FiEE further extended its offerings to phygital art advisory services, providing a platform for artists, collectors, and brands to connect through exhibitions and other value-added services.

#5544. Why Midwest buyer demand is holding up in the face of higher mortgage rates

Midwest metros, including Columbus and Cincinnati, are keeping pending sales near or above new listings as mortgage activity stays mixed. Lower list prices and smaller loan amounts appear to support demand, even with rates above 7% pressuring affordability.  AI Summary

Several Midwest housing markets are showing signs of resilient buyer demand compared to other parts of the country, with pending home sales keeping pace with new listings even as purchase mortgage activity remains largely flat or declines.

Columbus, Ohio, had 127 pending sales for every 100 new listings as of Nov. 6, according to HousingWire Data. Cincinnati followed at 125. These markets were well above the national average of 95 pending sales per 100 new listings, while Cleveland (91) and St. Louis (90) were running slightly below the U.S. average.

The same markets also had median list prices that were considerably lower than the national average of $429,000. Cleveland led the way at $174,000, followed by St. Louis ($225,000), Columbus ($255,000) and Cincinnati ($300,000).

In St. Louis, buyers remain active despite elevated mortgage rates, although they are being more deliberate about their decisions, said Greg Iverson, a divisional sales manager for Neighborhood Loans.

“I wouldn’t say it’s necessarily a buyer’s market, but it’s starting to become that way in certain areas,” Iverson said in an interview with HousingWire.

Like most buyers nationwide, affordability remains the biggest obstacle for his clients, Iverson said. Mortgage rates above 7% have added to the rising costs of property taxes, homeowners insurance, building materials and home repairs. Inventory has also increased in some price ranges, he said, but not across the board.

But Iverson said St. Louis continues to see activity from first-time and move-up buyers alike since the market’s lower home prices have helped keep these buyers from being priced out entirely.

A similar pattern is playing out in smaller Ohio markets. Scott Snapp, a Findlay, Ohio-based branch manager at loanDepot, said his business has remained steady, with loan applications coming in at about the same pace as last year.

When comparing his October 2026 production with the same point a year earlier, Snapp said he had closed 57 loans totaling $12 million last year, versus 51 loans totaling $11 million at the time of the interview. Snapp said his average loan size is about $215,000.

“I’m not seeing a drop, realistically,” he said. “Applications coming in are still at the same pace as they were last year around here.”

Mortgage data platform Modex shows that purchase lending has been relatively steady in several Midwest markets, but it has not uniformly increased.

Cleveland was the only one of four Midwest metros in HousingWire’s comparison to record year-over-year growth in purchase loans from January through July, with 11,809 loans, up 0.9%. Cincinnati recorded 14,048 loans, down 2.2%, while Columbus had 12,820, down 2.7%. St. Louis recorded 9,811 loans, a 6.8% decline. The St. Louis figure excludes St. Louis County since 2026 county records were still being updated.

Modex data indicated that median purchase loan amounts in these Midwest markets ranged from $217,075 in Cleveland to $294,566 in Columbus. Lower loan amounts and home prices could attest to some of the Midwest’s relative resilience. More than 20% of purchase loans in Cleveland and St. Louis were for less than $150,000.

But the resilience is still being tested. Jason Harris, a Columbus-based branch manager at Rate, described September as a slow month for contracts that would have closed in October. And he expected October to be one of the slower months the market had seen in years due to higher mortgage rates.

But he added that contract activity improved over the course of October as mortgage rates eased.

“I feel blessed to be in Columbus because it’s still an area where you can purchase an affordable home,” Harris said. “Affordability is something that is so desperately needed by buyers right now. … Even three-eighths of a percent is having a meaningful impact on demand.”

Harris said first-time buyers, as well as borrowers using down payment assistance and state bond programs, typically make up a larger share of his business late in the year. These buyers, coupled with lower-priced homes, typically bring down his average loan size in the fourth quarter, while also driving more Federal Housing Administration loans and government-backed adjustable-rate mortgages, he said.

Back in St. Louis, Iverson said the metro area has continued to attract interest from real estate investors, including those who are becoming more selective about where they purchase as costs rise in other markets.

Snapp also pointed to local employment as a source of housing demand in his part of Ohio, citing new distribution centers and business activity, including facilities opened by Amazon and planned by Sheetz.

“We’re seeing a lot of businesses coming into this area and opening up, and that’s helped us,” he said.

The market has also benefited from buyers relocating from other states, Snapp said. Some have moved for work, while others are returning to the area to be near family.

St. Louis and smaller Ohio markets contrast with areas where mortgage professionals have reported weaker activity. Iverson said he has heard of homes sitting longer in markets such as San Diego, while Snapp said colleagues in Las Vegas and Seattle had described slower conditions.

Harris said he expects demand in central Ohio to pick up again as the market moves into 2027, even if some buyers are postponing purchases until the spring. He said the region’s underlying need for housing remains strong.

“The number of people that need homes and want homes in central Ohio over the next five years is going to be good,” he said.

#5543. Greenland Technologies Holding Corporation Receives Nasdaq Notification Regarding Minimum Bid Price Deficiency

HANGZHOU, China, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Greenland Technologies Holding Corporation (Nasdaq: GTEC) ("Greenland" or the "Company"), a technology developer and manufacturer of electric industrial vehicles and drivetrain systems for material handling machineries and vehicles, today announced that the Company received a written notification (the "Notification Letter") from the Nasdaq Stock Market LLC ("Nasdaq") on November 10, 2026, notifying the Company that it is not in compliance with the minimum bid price requirement set forth in the Nasdaq Listing Rules for continued listing on the Nasdaq.

Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2) requires listed securities to maintain a minimum bid price of US$1.00 per share, and Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A) provides that a failure to meet the minimum bid price requirement exists if the deficiency continues for a period of 30 consecutive business days. Based on the closing bid price of the Company's Class A ordinary shares for the 30 consecutive business days from September 29, 2026 to November 9, 2026, the Company no longer meets the minimum bid price requirement.

The Notification Letter does not impact the Company's listing on the Nasdaq Capital Market at this time. In accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A), the Company has been provided 180 calendar days, or until May 10, 2027, to regain compliance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2). To regain compliance, the Company's Class A ordinary shares must have a closing bid price of at least US$1.00 for a minimum of 10 consecutive business days. In the event the Company does not regain compliance by May 10, 2027, the Company may be eligible for additional time to regain compliance or may face delisting.

The Company's business operations are not affected by the receipt of the Notification Letter. The Company intends to monitor the closing bid price of its Class A ordinary shares and may, if appropriate, consider implementing available options, including, but not limited to, implementing a share consolidation, to regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement under the Nasdaq Listing Rules.

#5542. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

#5541. Will the Fifth Circuit keep FinCEN anti-money laundering rule off the books?

ALTA and TLTA urged the Fifth Circuit to uphold a March ruling that vacated FinCEN’s residential real estate AML reporting rule. The groups argue FinCEN underestimated compliance costs and exceeded its authority under the Bank Secrecy Act.  AI Summary

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network’s (FinCEN) Residential Real Estate Rule is not currently in effect and the American Land Title Association (ALTA) and the Texas Land Title Association (TLTA) would like it to stay that way.

In late October, ALTA and TLTA filed amicus briefs asking the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit to uphold a ruling that vacated FinCEN’s nationwide anti-money laundering (AML) rule.

The AML rule mandated reporting for any non-financed residential real estate transfer where ownership was held by an entity or trust — with no geographic or price threshold.

The rule was overturned in late March by a federal judge in the Eastern District of Texas after the law had been in effect for less than three weeks. In early May, FinCEN appealed the ruling.

This ruling and subsequent appeal are part of a lawsuit filed by Flowers Title Companies, LLC, which argued that FinCEN lacked authority under the Bank Secrecy Act to impose such sweeping reporting requirements.

In their briefs ALTA and TLTA argued that the rule “imposes significant costs and operational burdens on title and settlement professionals without adequately demonstrating that its benefits justify those requirements.”

According to ALTA, FinCEN’s cost estimate of implementing the policy of $559.4 million was too low, as the association felt FinCEN did not fully account for the cost to title companies for employee training, technology changes, record keeping and the time it takes to get information from buyers and sellers. Additionally, ALTA argues that title professionals have no authority to force buyers or sellers to provide them with beneficial ownership information and that financial institutions already collect beneficial ownership information from their business customers when accounts are opened.

In its filing, TLTA adds that the transactions FinCEN’s rule targets are routine and legal, noting that FinCEN’s legal authority only applies to “suspicious” transactions, not an entire class of transaction.

It remains to be seen how the appeals court will rule on this issue. However, FinCEN has also said it will not require retroactive reporting for transactions that would have been reportable during these legal proceedings.

FinCEN had argued the rule was necessary to close loopholes that allowed money launderers, drug traffickers and other illicit actors to use shell companies and trusts to purchase property with anonymity.

Fidelity National Financial (FNF) has also challenged FinCEN’s AML rule in court, but this resulted in the rule being upheld. That decision has since been appealed by FNF in the Eleventh Circuit.
