#5521. Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here’s why

Despite a carve-out in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, BTR and SFR operators say Treasury implementation and legislative risk is still suppressing capital. NAA Q3 2026 data shows units under construction down 18.5% YoY, completions down 40.2%, and sales volume down 51.5%.  AI Summary

Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act‘s institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels.

According to the National Apartment Association’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse, released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction, the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out.

The industry’s legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects.

Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry.

“I would say it hasn’t normalized. In other words, it wasn’t where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences, said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

“I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.”

Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position.

“Capital’s coming in, but it’s not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it’s really hard for them to write checks.

According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets.

Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere.

“When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn’t have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview.

Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29.

“Capital’s just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market’s still trying to find itself,” Tanner said.

In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern.

“Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury, which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said.

Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy.

Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued.

The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects.

Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban.

For The Amherst Group, uncertainty continues to obscure how Treasury will define the exception for homes requiring substantial repairs under the ROAD institutional investor ban. Many of Amherst’s acquisitions are older homes, typically 25 to 40 years old, that require substantial renovations. While the renovate-to-rent exception could allow Amherst to continue acquiring and renovating these properties for rent, the lack of finalized parameters has left investors uncertain.

“There’s no money to be raised right now,” Dobson said, of capital for financing renovate-to-rent acquisitions.

What’s more, the possibility of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill raises even more concerns among many BTR operators and developers. They fear they face continued uncertainty and risk over whether future federal or state legislation could restrict the BTR business model.

However, it’s not yet clear whether any such legislation will gain traction in the next Congress. While many successful candidates for the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives ran on a platform of opposing institutional ownership of single-family homes, campaign rhetoric and slogans don’t necessarily translate full-stop into policy.

“I worked campaigns for a number of years throughout the country, and the first thing they kind of teach you in campaigning out there is everyone needs a boogeyman. I think you campaign in slogans, and you govern in prose,” Owen Caine, Assistant Vice President of Federal Legislative Affairs at the National Apartment Association (NAA), said in an interview.

Despite the expectation that some members of Congress may push for more aggressive institutional ownership restrictions, Cain was encouraged by the widespread bipartisan pushback against previous provisions that would have undermined BTR. Caine hopes this bipartisan support will keep Congress from passing such far-reaching legislation in the future.

“The fact that we got to where we were with such bipartisan support, and with basically complete industry and nonprofit support, [means] messing around with that at this point, before it’s been fully implemented and before we’ve seen any benefits of the bill whatsoever, doesn’t make a lot of sense from a policy perspective,” he explained.

However, the new Congress comes with another challenge — the sheer size of the incoming freshman class. In the House of Representatives, for example, about 110 new representatives are expected, along with new staff members.

“Those are each offices we have to hit individually to educate about build-to-rent because the odds that the average person has any idea what a build-to-rent development is, is pretty low,” Caine explained.

Ross noted that lawmakers are usually receptive once they learn more about BTR and the legislative challenges facing the industry. A recent meeting with Senator-elect Roy Cooper (D-N.C.) was one example, with Cooper responding positively to those concerns.

“I spent 30 minutes with him personally, explaining what build-to-rent was. He said, ‘Oh, I understand. That makes sense.’ So that’s just something that everyone in this business will have to do again,” Ross explained.

While much of the attention has focused on federal legislation, state-level policy, particularly proposals to restrict institutional investors, may be just as critical an area to watch.

While it’s not clear what the newly elected state legislatures and governors may prioritize, several states have already considered bills limiting the influence of institutional ownership of housing.

In Virginia, for example, state lawmakers from both parties introduced legislation to restrict institutional home purchases. SB 693 and SB 1424 would have prohibited entities with more than $50 million in assets under management from buying single-family homes, but neither bill passed.

In Michigan, however, a similar measure, HB 6074, was signed into law on July 21, 2026. The bill prohibits corporations with a net worth of $375 million or more from owning more than 100 single-family homes in the state, while explicitly exempting build-to-rent (BTR) properties.

As more states consider restrictions on institutional ownership of single-family homes, will BTR secure the exemptions achieved in Michigan, or could operators face a tougher legislative environment in Congress and in other state legislatures?

That’s a key question to watch in 2027 and beyond.

#5520. Binance said North Korean hackers used fake job interviews in $6.3 billion heist

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Binance's incident report traces the Oct. 29 theft to a tampered coding tool, a fraudulent recruitment process and an internal AI tool

Binance said Tuesday that hackers it attributes to North Korea used fake job interviews and malicious software to steal $6.3 billion from the exchange, according to Bloomberg. The company called the breach a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" in an incident report published Tuesday, Bloomberg reported.

The attack began in June, when a staffer who builds Binance's wallets installed a doctored AI tool, according to Reuters. Binance spotted the problem, swapped out the device and reset credentials, though the hacker still learned the employee's role and those of teammates on the wallet team, Reuters reported.

In September, someone posing as a project director approached a second software engineer through a job hunting platform, according to Bloomberg. That engineer then took part in an interview on a social messaging app with someone posing as the CEO of an invented company, and was told to download an assignment that held a "malicious code repository."

On Oct. 20, the attackers leveraged an internal AI tool along with the second engineer's infected computer to seize command of the devices belonging to two other engineers, according to The Block $SQ. Then on Oct. 29, the attackers logged in with stolen credentials, set up a container and ran a malicious script that kicked off the theft from the wallet, The Block reported.

“This was not a single mistake or a single breach. It was a campaign built over many months,” Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said, according to Bloomberg. Teng said the attackers blended sham hiring interviews, malware posing as genuine developer tools, hijacked devices and AI-driven methods.

About $2.85 billion in assets has been frozen or intercepted by Binance, which has also restored 98% of the affected assets, according to The Block. Binance has said it is reimbursing every customer who lost money, according to Reuters.

The exchange paused withdrawals after the incident and began letting users take out funds again on Sunday, according to Bloomberg. By Tuesday, deposits per hour had begun to outpace withdrawals per hour, Bloomberg reported.

Binance said it has shut the entry points the attackers exploited, replaced or rebuilt the systems that were hit, tightened controls on devices and broadened its AI-based anomaly detection, according to The Block. It also said it caught and stopped 57 attacks in 2026 that it suspects were tied to North Korea, many of which relied on comparable methods.

The FBI has attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, according to Bloomberg. North Korea has denied the claim. On Monday, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un called the FBI's claims a "grave political provocation," according to The Block.

#5519. Fly-E Group, Inc. Announces Second Quarter and First Half of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results

NEW YORK, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly-E Group, Inc. (Nasdaq: FLYE) ("Fly-E" or the "Company"), an electric vehicle company engaged in designing, installing, selling, and renting smart electric motorcycles, electric bikes, and electric scooters, today announced its unaudited financial results for the second quarter and first half of fiscal year 2027 ended September 30, 2026.

Second quarter of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Summary

Mr. Zhou (Andy) Ou, Chief Executive Officer of Fly-E, commented, "During the second quarter, our operational network stabilized following the retail restructuring, with our top-line revenue holding steady sequentially. Our wholesale revenues grew 21.4% year-over-year and accounted for a significantly higher proportion of our total revenue. This evolving revenue mix, combined with promotional pricing in our retail business, naturally influenced our overall margin profile for the period. Meanwhile, we continued to control store-level costs and address corporate matters carefully to strengthen the Company's foundation for the future. By maintaining our operational network and disciplined cost management, we are dedicated to preserving business stability while positioning Fly-E to explore strategic opportunities for long-term growth."

Second quarter of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results

Net revenues were $2.6 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 33.7% from $3.9 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily driven by a lower sales volume of 7,392 units in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to 18,564 in the same period last year, resulting from the reduction in our direct retail store count to four stores as of September 30, 2026, compared to 11 stores as of September 30, 2025.

Cost of revenues was $2.4 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 18.8% from $2.9 million in the same period last year, primarily aligning with lower sales volume driven by the downsizing of our retail store network.

Gross profit was $0.2 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $1.0 million in the same period last year. Gross margin was 8.1% in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to 25.0% in the same period last year. The decrease in gross margin was primarily attributable to a structural mix shift from direct retail toward lower-priced wholesale channels, further impacted by competitive retail pricing and inventory clearance discounts.

Total operating expenses were $1.8 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 9.8% compared to $2.0 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily attributable to store-level operational savings, which were partially offset by increases in expected credit losses and professional fees.

Net loss was $1.7 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $1.8 million in the same period last year.

Basic and Diluted Earnings (Losses) per Share

Basic and diluted losses per share were $1.07 in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $2.18 in the same period last year.

EBITDA was negative $1.3 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to negative EBITDA of $1.0 million in the same period last year.

First Half of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results

Net revenues were $5.3 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 42.2% from $9.2 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily driven by a significant reduction in direct retail store counts, resulting in a lower sales volume of 14,950 units in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to 29,012 in the same period last year.

Cost of revenues was $4.8 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 19.5% from $6.0 million in the same period last year, primarily reflecting lower sales volume following the downsizing of our retail store network.

Gross profit was $0.5 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $3.2 million in the same period last year. Gross margin was 9.5% in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to 35.1% in the same period last year. The decrease in gross margin was primarily attributable to the greater revenue percentage of wholesale channels at lower-priced wholesale pricing, as well as promotional retail pricing adjustment and inventory clearance discounts.

Total operating expenses were $5.7 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 2.2% compared to $5.8 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily attributable to operational cost savings from retail store reductions, which were offset by increases in expected credit losses and software development fees.

Net loss was $5.6 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $3.8 million in the same period last year.

Basic and Diluted Earnings (Losses) per Share

Basic and diluted losses per share were $3.48 in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $6.58 in the same period last year.

EBITDA was negative $4.7 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to negative EBITDA of $2.2 million in the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, the Company had cash of $0.5 million, compared to $0.3 million as of March 31, 2026.

Fly-E Group, Inc. is an electric vehicle company that is principally engaged in designing, installing, selling, and renting smart electric motorcycles, electric bikes, and electric scooters under the brand "Fly E-Bike." The Company's commitment is to encourage people to incorporate eco-friendly transportation into their active lifestyles, ultimately contributing towards building a more environmentally friendly future. For more information, please visit the Company's website: https://investors.flyebike.com.

To supplement our financial information presented in accordance with the generally accepted accounting principles in the United States (the "U.S. GAAP"), management periodically uses certain "non-GAAP financial measures," as such term is defined under the rules of the SEC, to clarify and enhance understanding of past performance and prospects for the future. Generally, a non-GAAP financial measure is a numerical measure of a company's operating performance, financial position or cash flows that excludes or includes amounts that are included in or excluded from the most directly comparable measure calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. For example, non-GAAP measures may exclude the impact of certain items such as acquisitions, divestitures, gains, losses and impairments, or items outside of management's control. Management believes that the following non-GAAP financial measure provides investors and analysts useful insight into our financial position and operating performance. Any non-GAAP measure provided should be viewed in addition to, and not as an alternative to, the most directly comparable measure determined in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Further, the calculation of these non-GAAP financial measures may differ from the calculation of similarly titled financial measures presented by other companies and therefore may not be comparable among companies.

We use EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) to evaluate our operating performance. We believe EBITDA provides additional insight into our underlying, ongoing operating performance and facilitates year-to-year comparisons by excluding the earnings impact of interest, tax, depreciation and amortization and that presenting EBITDA is more representative of our operational performance and may be more useful for investors.

We reconcile our non-GAAP financial measure to our net income, which is our most directly comparable financial measure calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. EBITDA includes adjustments for provision for income taxes, as applicable, interest income and expense, depreciation, and amortization. EBITDA does not represent and should not be considered an alternative to net income as determined by U.S. GAAP, and our calculations thereof may not be comparable to those reported by other companies. We believe EBITDA is an important measure of operating performance and provides useful information to investors because it highlights trends in our business that may not otherwise be apparent when relying solely on U.S. GAAP measures and because it eliminates items that have less bearing on our operating performance. EBITDA, as presented herein, is a supplemental measure of our performance that is not required by, or presented in accordance with, U.S. GAAP. We use non-GAAP financial measures as supplements to our U.S. GAAP results in order to provide a more complete understanding of the factors and trends affecting our business. EBITDA is a measure of operating performance that is not defined by U.S. GAAP and should not be considered a substitute for net (loss) income as determined in accordance with U.S. GAAP.

#5518. U.S. crude falls over 2% as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia rattle traders

Free daily briefing on global business news.

WTI fell 2.19% to $101 and Brent fell 1.89% to $114.51 as traders weighed supply risks against demand worries

U.S. crude oil futures dropped by more than 2% on Monday, with traders balancing the possibility of additional Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia against worries that steep prices could dent demand.

West Texas Intermediate futures lost 2.19% and changed hands at $101 per barrel. Brent crude futures gave up 1.89%, leaving them at $114.51. The pullback followed a rally on Friday, when prices settled close to $3 higher after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Over the course of last week, Brent gained 6% while WTI rose 2.3%.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday strikes on the principal airport in Riyadh and on Saudi oil installations. Saudi Arabia stated Sunday that it had shot down further missiles and drones. The kingdom brought part of the airport's operations back online Sunday even though earlier attacks had left it damaged, according to CNBC. The Houthis threatened more strikes.

Hopes of easing tensions between the U.S. and Iran also weighed on prices. Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran on Sunday to help calm tensions across the region, working in concert with the U.S., according to Reuters.

“Concerns over renewed military hostilities in the Middle East, which drove much of last week’s crude rally, have eased this morning, but the reprieve may prove temporary,” said Vandana Hari, founder of Vanda Insights, according to Reuters.

Michael Alfaro, chief investment officer at Gallo Partners, told CNBC that geopolitical uncertainty has inflated oil prices by about $20 per barrel. He said a serious hit to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, or to additional refineries, could push prices up, though any further rise might eat into consumption.

"What we would likely see if oil pushed above 120, 130, 140 dollars a barrel for Brent, that is, you're going to see more demand destruction," Alfaro said, according to CNBC. He added that harm to refining capacity could grow into a structural problem that lingers through 2027 and later years.

Saudi Arabia shut down its East-West Pipeline after drone attacks from Iraq in September. The pipeline can move up to 7 million barrels per day and had served as an export route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Brent climbed above $108 a barrel at the time as traders worried about when the pipeline would reopen.

Domestically, the Energy Department on Friday approved the release of as many as 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, aimed at easing a supply disruption at a Louisiana refinery, according to CNBC.

Energy ministers from Saudi Arabia and Singapore announced on Monday that state-owned Saudi Aramco will begin holding crude in Singapore storage during the latter half of 2027.

#5516. Leaving VMware starts as a cost decision, but day-two operations decide whether it works

Enterprises leaving legacy hypervisors are finding that moving virtual machines is only half the job, and that a portable data management layer often decides whether a Kubernetes migration succeeds. Rising license costs are pushing teams to run containers and VMs on one platform.

That shift is playing out at Mouser Electronics Inc., one of the world’s largest electronic components distributors. After running Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift for containers for five to six years, the company is now building a production OpenShift Virtualization cluster to move workloads off Broadcom Inc.’s VMware, according to Ronald Waller (pictured, left), systems engineer at Mouser.

“It doesn’t matter if we’re running containers or VMs, we’re running it on the same foundation, which really works well,” Waller said. “Because we can manage those things with the same tool sets and same skill sets.”

Waller and Jon Owings (right), assistant vice president of global technical presales, cloud and data services, at Portworx by Everpure, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the data management layer helps run VMs and containers on OpenShift. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes already serves as a common control plane for containerized AI workloads, and pulling VMs onto it extends that standard to older applications. Everpure Inc., which rebranded from Pure Storage Inc. this year as part of a data-centric pivot, positions Portworx as the matching abstraction for storage.

“Kubernetes provides that ubiquitous control plane for all of them, and that’s what customers are asking us for,” Owings said. “The one thing that was missing was the same thing but for data.”

The learning curve for VMware administrators moving to Kubernetes is steep, and Waller has climbed it over the last year. Storage turned out to be the easy part when he built Mouser’s proof-of-concept cluster, he explained.

“I asked the storage guy what I needed from him, and he handed me a user ID and an API key. I went to Portworx Central. I configured my spec for the operator and the storage cluster, created my secret, and boom, Portworx Enterprise did everything else on the backend,” Waller said. “I didn’t even have to think about it.”

Portworx keeps building for that use case. It made data management native to OpenShift in May and unveiled new AI and VM capabilities at KubeCon. For teams following Mouser’s path, Owings sees the exit from a legacy hypervisor as a chance to rethink day-two operations on a data management layer that travels across clouds and Kubernetes distributions.

“What can we change that we didn’t like about the last 15 years? … Were we dependent on a vendor? Were we dependent on shell scripts or PowerShell?” Owings said. “We have this great opportunity to do something new, and Kubernetes has that open API that allows you to be creative.”

#5515. Saudi Arabia told OPEC its oil output hit a wartime high in October

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Production rose from 8.372 million barrels a day in September as Brent futures fell about 21% so far in November to $93

Andrey Rudakov / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Saudi Arabia told OPEC it pumped 10.563 million barrels a day of crude in October, a rise from September's 8.372 million.

That was a 26% increase and the highest level since before the war began, according to Bloomberg. Saudi Arabia told OPEC it produced 10.882 million barrels a day in February, the final month before the Iran war upended Middle East supply, according to Reuters.

The Saudi rebound is spearheading a wider pickup in production across the region, which is easing prices, according to Bloomberg. Brent futures have dropped about 18% since the start of the month, leaving them at $93 a barrel.

Saudi Arabia's reported figure sits above its OPEC quota, according to Bloomberg. OPEC measures compliance with figures drawn from third-party estimates instead of the numbers members submit themselves. Those secondary sources put Saudi output at 9.194 million barrels a day in October, OPEC said.

OPEC+ producers pumped 41.23 million barrels a day in October, up 2.04 million from September, according to secondary sources cited by OPEC. Iraq told OPEC it produced 4.888 million barrels a day, which Bloomberg described as a new wartime high for the country.

Saudi Arabia has run covert shuttle voyages with its tankers via the Strait of Hormuz, copying an approach the United Arab Emirates first used earlier in the war, according to Bloomberg. The kingdom has additionally leaned on a second pipeline to the Red Sea, which has been attacked.

Speaking at an Abu Dhabi industry event last week, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said the company intends to "maximize production going forward in the fourth quarter," according to Bloomberg.

The output increase comes as OPEC and its allies examine the volumes each member can technically produce as groundwork for 2027 output targets. The review is expected to wrap up within the next few days, according to Bloomberg. When the full OPEC+ group convenes online on Nov. 29 to talk over 2027 targets, it will draw on that assessment.

The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran has held Gulf OPEC+ producers far below their output ceilings in recent months. Brent traded around $73 a barrel before the conflict began in late February.

#5514. RYAN KAVANAUGH TO RECEIVE OUTSTANDING VIRTUAL PRODUCTION AWARD AT INFINITY FESTIVAL'S 2026 MONOLITH AWARDS FOR ACME STUDIOS WORK

Two-Day Showcase Expands Lineup with ACME's Ryan Kavanaugh alongside George R.R. Martin, Brad Bird, Seth Rogen, Mel Brooks, Pola Maneli and Leading Animation Studios

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Infinity Festival announced today that Ryan Kavanaugh's studio, ACME Media, is being honored for pioneering the Grey Boxâ¢, an AI-driven production methodology that integrates live-action performance, virtual environments and generative visual effects. ACME AI is taking virtual production beyond the stage and into the whole of filmmaking.

They were selected for this honor as the company to make the biggest paradigm shift utilizing technology in film and entertainment today. Specifically, they were able to create a totally photoreal movie, preserve all actor performance and pioneer the use of the Grey Boxâ¢ methodology for actor capture, while utilizing their tech to create over 213 locations in 21 total days.

The Grey Boxâ¢ is a stage and actor performance capture system built around the filmmaker. A Grey Boxâ¢ production makes films the way films have always been made â it shoots with the same cameras, the same crew and the same process as any other film, just with extra technology and a precise design to allow for a more cohesive and cost effective process. #5513. Kalshi and Polymarket claim 98% accuracy in calling midterm races

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A New York Times analysis found prediction markets did no better than election forecasts for most of the race

Kalshi said the candidates its traders favored won 98% of resolved races in Tuesday's midterm elections. The company announced the figure on Wednesday.

The tally covers 479 of 487 races resolved as of 6 a.m. ET on Nov. 4, Kalshi said. Favorites won 356 of 360 House races, 32 of 33 Senate races and 33 of 34 governor races.

Polymarket said that, judged against the day before the election, 98.4% of its settled contests had pointed to the correct winner, according to The Associated Press. Polymarket put its hit rate at roughly 97% for the Senate and gubernatorial contests and at 98.6% for those in the House.

Kalshi said its markets for House control passed 99% likelihood at 8:10 p.m. ET and its Senate control markets passed 99% at 9 p.m. ET, hours ahead of the networks. Trading volume on its 2026 midterm markets topped $2.5 billion, compared with $1.3 billion for the 2024 cycle, the company said.

In a separate analysis, Kalshi said directional accuracy for races called by 6:26 a.m. ET on Nov. 4 rose from 93.8% three months out to 98.2% when polls closed. Brier scores, on which lower is better, fell from 0.040 to 0.016, the company said.

Outside experts urged caution. Ross Dahlke, a University of Wisconsin-Madison professor, said the figures include only resolved markets, which may be easier to predict, and that many races were fairly certain going into Election Day, according to The Associated Press.

An analysis by The New York Times found that prediction markets fared about the same as election forecasts through most of the midterm campaign. Markets gained an edge in the closing days, the Times said, once polls and forecasts had gone out of date. Kalshi told the Times that its ability to post odds on par with seasoned forecasters well ahead of voting demonstrated the markets’ forecasting strength.

Polymarket did not respond to a request for comment from The New York Times.

Koleman Strumpf, an economics professor at Wake Forest University who studies prediction markets, gave the markets a B, according to Bloomberg. He said the markets pointed the right way but underestimated how large the Democratic wave would be.

Kalshi said on X $TWTR that its markets outperformed forecasting models including those of Silver Bulletin, FiftyPlusOne and The Economist, according to Bloomberg. Nate Silver, who runs Silver Bulletin, said his model and others showed the Democratic wave sooner and more aggressively.

#5511. Ripple's XRP Ledger Lending to Receive Repayment Fix

The XRP Ledger's lending protocol is in for a tidy-up of how loan repayments get rounded. In plain terms, the balance after each payment would match the schedule, the update has been discribed in the official Github pull request.

After an overpayment, TotalValueOutstanding is reset to the scheduled value of the new PeriodicPayment.

Under the LendingProtocolV1_2 amendment, each on-time LoanPay would bring TotalValueOutstanding down to the scheduled value with one payment fewer, capped at the rounded PeriodicPayment.

The first commit moves the scheduled-value calculation out of computeLoanProperties into a separate scheduledValue function, with no behavior change.

That way, LoanSet and LoanPay round it the same way. Zero-interest loans also need a floor on the principal part, because their value is rounded to nearest while the principal is rounded up. Tests run on Legacy, CashBasis and FixedPrecision vaults, with and without the amendment.

Today, each payment's value part is calculated on its own, so rounding can build up across payments. The last payment can then need one unit more than the rounded PeriodicPayment, and the value parts can alternate between payments.

With the change, a method called telescoping makes the value part of every on-time payment either the floor or the ceiling of PeriodicPayment, and at least one unit. The last payment becomes exactly the rounded PeriodicPayment.

There's little to no effect for users and investors today. The extra unit on the final payment changes little. Older loans that already carried one unit above their schedule simply keep it, so the last payment still needs the PeriodicPayment and a single unit, unless the borrower overpays first.

Small overpayments are mostly ignored; the transaction goes through successfully and charges no extra XRP whatsoever.

Activation date is yet to be determined: 80% of validators agreement is needed for two weeks in a row for the amendment to go through. No public vote for LendingProtocolV1_2 has been announced yet, so the timeline remains uncertain.

#5510. Sovereign or not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin

Sovereignty is everywhere right now, and most people still can’t agree on what it means and, just as importantly, what it all means to them.

This week theCUBE Research releases its new market report, Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide. In this Breaking Analysis, we’re joined by its author, Amit Eyal Govrin, lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, to talk about why he wrote it, what sovereignty is and what it isn’t, and what surprised him most in the findings.

The full scores are in the report. Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide https://siliconangle.com/sovereign-or-not

Dave: As someone who’s been leading the thought leadership in this domain, how did you come up with the inspiration to research this topic and write the report?

Amit: To understand the how, it helps to understand the why. I’ve been thinking about this subject for a while now. It hasn’t always been called “sovereignty,” but the tenets have always been the same.

It all started around four years ago, as I’ve been a builder in this space for that long. First with Kubiya, one of the industry’s first agentic implementations, deploying agents in enterprise production environments as early as September 2023, before agents were even an industry term.

We were deploying as a software-as-a-service company, and many of those concerns were legitimate. As a software company, we got to keep our intellectual property and license it out. If we were successful, we would create dependency, which effectively meant customers lost control of their crown jewels.

When we started Agentcy Labs earlier this year, customers familiar with our work approached us, and many of these points crystallized for us. What they told us: We’re relieved you are no longer at Kubiya. It’s not that we ever doubted your technology or the value it brings. Quite the opposite. That was what they were afraid of. Kubiya creates a dependency, adoption balloons, and they lose control of their costs. Or a vendor changes the meter on them because of shareholder pressure or regulatory controls.

What clicked for us is that their resistance was never about Kubiya or our technology. It was about the loss of control of their alpha. Namely, the Agentic Operating System, the key driver of their artificial intelligence transformation, which falls under our technological pillar.

It doesn’t matter if the vendor is a startup, an AI lab or a hyperscaler. No enterprise can afford to mortgage its entire business on an external dependency on such a key issue. It’s far too strategic not to own outright.

That finding forced us to rethink the model behind software, dig deeper into sovereignty as an issue of control, and help the industry define it in a more standardized way.

Dave: So control is the heart of it. But when most people hear sovereignty, they think about where the data sits. Is that the wrong way to look at it?

Amit: Sovereignty goes well beyond territory, which is often the most misunderstood aspect. People hear sovereignty and immediately revert to the sovereign state: government initiatives, national security, on-premises air-gapped environments. That can be true in some cases. But by and large, our sovereignty discussions involve enterprises and regulated industries that have sovereignty as a core tenet of their AI initiatives.

It goes beyond buzzwords and sovereign-washing claims. Think back to the explosive Alex Karp interview on CNBC claiming enterprises are losing their alpha to frontier labs. I largely agree with that claim, by the way. Only he finished his pitch by offering customers to move it over to Palantir. In other words: Stop mortgaging your alpha to Anthropic and OpenAI, come rent it from us.

That interview was my trigger point to take up arms and educate the industry on sovereignty: what it is, what it isn’t, and most importantly, what you, as a buyer of AI, can do about it.

Dave: And you’ve been out in the field with buyers ever since. What did those conversations teach you, and how did that shape the framework?

Amit: Since then, we’ve been included in dozens of engagements with enterprises, governments and policymakers around the world, from Washington to Brussels, New Delhi, Sydney and even Riyadh. We are in the room when sovereignty discussions happen. That helped us shape our view, tease out the concerns, and focus on what really matters and why. From those discussions came the 5 Pillars of Sovereignty framework. We use it today to assess all vendor relationships, policy and regulation, and geopolitical events.

Dave: Which brings us to the report. You started with the hyperscalers. Walk us through how you approached it.

Amit: In our first edition, Sovereign or Not? The Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide, we take the buyer’s lens and assess each hyperscaler by its sovereignty posture.

Hint: By definition, working with any hyperscaler means ceding a good portion of control over your Operational, Technological, Legal and Financial pillars. Oftentimes that’s the reality in the real world.

My view: Sovereignty is not a purity test. It’s perfectly acceptable to go with a hyperscaler, as long as it’s a known dependency you priced in as an acceptable risk. If that’s the case, let us guide you through these considerations to the best path forward for your organization.

Dave: OK, let’s get to the part everyone wants to know. Who scored what, and why?

Amit: We looked at seven hyperscalers and 40 of their offerings, from the point of view of buyers in five regions: the U.S., Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the rest, including the Middle East and Africa. Everything is scored out of 5.

The short version: The most sovereign product a hyperscaler sells is the one the hyperscaler itself can’t reach.

On these tests, sovereignty often runs inverse to how a hyperscaler is built. A shared global control plane and services the vendor runs for the customer make a cloud easy to adopt, but every layer the vendor runs is a layer the buyer does not control. Amazon Web Services and Google built their platforms around that abstraction, which becomes a hindrance once a buyer needs to run the stack without them. The grades measure how much control a buyer can take back, not the quality of the cloud.

Who came out on top, who came in last, and by how much, is in the report. And every score is backed by a source. Don’t like your grade? Publish the document and we’ll re-score it.

Dave: What surprised you most when you went through the findings?

Amit: None of the hyperscalers has a practical solution for the U.S. CLOUD Act, and that alone has created a real legal clawback on non-U.S. companies.

In plain English: The U.S. government can ask an American cloud company for data it controls, no matter which country the data sits in. A sovereign cloud in Brandenburg, run by a German subsidiary, doesn’t change the answer. It’s still owned by an American company.

The vendors aren’t hiding it. AWS told us as much on the record. Microsoft’s own lawyer in France told the French Senate he couldn’t guarantee French data would never reach U.S. authorities. That’s honesty, and we don’t penalize honesty. It’s the law, and it applies to every American cloud the same way.

The fixes buyers are being sold, like keeping data local, holding your own encryption keys, or a contract promise to fight requests, don’t change who the government can go to.

Dave: So what’s a non-U.S. buyer supposed to do about that?

Amit: There’s no perfect answer today, only partial ones.

Going with a hyperscaler is fine, as long as you know the risk and priced it in. What’s not fine is believing a data center in Brandenburg, on its own merits, solved your sovereignty problem.

Dave: And this is just the first of several. Where do you go from here?

Amit: This is the first of a series: neoclouds, OEMs, telcos and specialized sovereign initiatives, wherever you happen to be, whether you’re a U.S., EU, Latin American, APAC or Middle Eastern buyer. Every edition covers the 5 Pillars, plus security, regulation and exit costs. Readers will be surprised by how deep we got, including quotes from the hyperscalers themselves and surveys of actual buyers. I truly think this will be valuable to everyone listening and reading.

Dave: That’s phenomenal, Amit. This is a cutting-edge report on a truly important and timely subject. If previously you were building on the frontier, you’re now squarely on the frontier of research. The scores, the vendor answers and the buyer data are all in the full report.

Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

Amit Eyal Govrin is lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, which designs and builds sovereign AI platforms for enterprises and governments. #5509. Suspected cyberattack hit supermarket freezers across Europe in second wave

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Retailers in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Estonia and Ireland reported temperature spikes; no one has claimed responsibility

Ahold Delhaize said an IT incident caused temperatures to climb in refrigeration systems across dozens of supermarkets it runs in Belgium and Luxembourg on Monday, according to The Guardian. Grocers in Sweden, Estonia and Ireland reported similar problems, making this the second suspected cyberattack on European store cooling systems after one in France.

Ahold Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester said the company is investigating the temperature increases, according to The Guardian. Stephan Moelans, CEO of refrigeration firm Sabcobel, said the attack switched the units' evaporators to defrost mode, according to Al Jazeera. Moelans said technicians were called out starting at 1 a.m. to cut the compromised installations off from the grid, according to The Guardian.

A Colruyt Group spokesperson said the refrigeration equipment in five Spar shops was targeted, according to Reuters. Colruyt franchises out the Spar outlets it oversees across Belgium.

In Sweden, Coop said six stores were affected, and ICA said a small number of its outlets had their cooling and freezing equipment knocked offline by an incident, according to The Guardian. Axfood said hackers broke into freezers at a Gothenburg-area hub that handles home-delivery orders, according to Al Jazeera.

John Billow, head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity center, said the agency is handling several incidents tied to cooling equipment in stores, according to Al Jazeera. He said Sweden has many exposed operational technology devices that need updates or patches.

Jann Mutso, CEO of technology supplier Kitman Coldtech, said at least one Estonian grocery chain was hit and that its temperatures had been pushed up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), according to Al Jazeera. Ireland’s SuperValu said a “cyber incident” compromised one particular type of refrigeration unit in 13 of the chain’s 223 stores, according to Al Jazeera.

No one has claimed responsibility for Monday's incidents or the French attack, according to Al Jazeera.

The incidents follow an October attack in France that disabled refrigeration at Intermarché, Coopérative U and Leclerc stores and drove temperatures in refrigerators and freezers up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) through a continuous defrost cycle. French police said hackers took over the cooling equipment of as many as 700 supermarkets, according to The Guardian. The hackers took over control units that came largely from Danfoss, a Danish company.

Ahold Delhaize notified Dutch police last month of a cybersecurity incident, according to The Guardian.

#5508. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

An anonymous Tornado Cash whale sent $7 million to Hyperliquid to open a large long on Bitcoin this morning. According to Lookonchain and Onchain Lens, the wallet went in with aggressive 20x leverage with the plan to profit from Bitcoin crushing Ether.

Large holders usually run funds through mixers to move capital privately or to get ready to cash out. This case is unusual as the movement of these funds had just previously been tracked to a chain of addresses belonging to the hackers who drained the derivatives platform Drift Protocol of $290 million in April 2026.

Some blockchain researchers warn against jumping to conclusions about where the funds came from. There's still no direct evidence: Tornado Cash covers its tracks well, and the link between the wallet and specific hacks rests only on circumstantial matches in volume.

After starting as a brand-new address that withdrew 3,100 ETH from Tornado Cash, the unknown later swapped all of the Ether through CoW Swap on the spot, locking in $6.92 million in USDC. From there, the money went to the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid as collateral for future trades.

On the exchange, the whale didn't try to guess where the market was headed and just split the collateral in half, turned on 20x cross leverage and built a position worth about $26 million in total. The position consisted of $12.84 million at an entry price of $75,762.2 and an Ethereum short of 5,740 ETH worth $12.83 million.

So far, the bet is working. Bitcoin is holding near local highs, and the gain on the BTC long fully covers the drawdown from altcoin short. Add to this the earnings on funding, collecting a regular premium from other traders for holding the ETH short.

This is a textbook dominance pair trade, where the investor couldn't care less whether the industry as a whole goes up or down and the only thing that matters is the spread - the price gap between the two largest coins.

If Bitcoin rises faster than Ether, or if Ether falls harder than Bitcoin in a broad market crash, the trade profits.

The math is elegant, but 20x leverage is always a high risk. Should Ethereum rip higher while Bitcoin stays stuck in a range, the margin will be wiped out in seconds as Hyperliquid's cross-margin system will force-close the orders, and the investor will lose the entire $6.92 million. The liquidation price is set at $37,014.09 for BTC and $3,343.60 for ETH.

#5506. Oil prices fall more than 4% as Iran peace talks ease supply fears

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Brent crude for January delivery fell 4.2% to $108.68 a barrel, reversing some of last week's gains ahead of Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections

Oil prices tumbled by upwards of 4% Monday, with negotiations to bring the U.S.-Iran conflict to a close soothing worries about Middle East supply.

Brent crude futures expiring in January slid 4.2% to $108.68 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate contracts due in December declined 4.3% to $99.61, while the January contracts shed 4.2% to reach $97.90.

The declines wiped out part of the previous week's rally. Brent had closed out October at a six-month peak.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that negotiations with mediators from Qatar about reopening the Strait of Hormuz were still under way, though no deal had been reached. He added that Iran had sent a delegation headed by a deputy foreign minister to Qatar, while no face-to-face meeting with U.S. officials was on the schedule.

Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, described the move as a technical pullback after last week’s strong gains, according to Reuters. He cited continued optimism about a diplomatic breakthrough, along with a weekend that passed without significant fighting escalating.

The risk of renewed fighting remains. According to The Wall Street Journal, the U.S. has instructed a number of Gulf Arab states to get ready for a possible brief but intense military operation against Iran once Tuesday's midterm elections are over. President Donald Trump has yet to reach a conclusive decision about resuming strikes.

Seven OPEC+ producers decided Sunday to leave their targets for December output as they were. The group, whose members include Saudi Arabia and Russia, will next convene on Nov. 29 to assess output for January.

Regional attacks also continued over the weekend. The Saudi-led coalition announced Sunday an operation against assets that the Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen depend on for their drone and missile efforts.

Vice President JD Vance wrote last week to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, to try to revive peace talks. Trump said he had approved the outreach, which was meant to outline a possible structure for talks rather than present a full peace plan.

Qatari mediators also offered a new plan to end the fighting among Iran, the U.S. and Israel. A high-ranking Iranian official dismissed the offer as unacceptable. The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17, but the agreement collapsed.

#5505. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5503. JetBlue creditors are hiring restructuring advisers as bonds crash to 42 cents

Free daily briefing on global business news.

JetBlue's $2 billion of notes due 2031 traded near 80 cents on the dollar this month; its stock has fallen more than half since August

JetBlue Airways has a group of senior creditors engaged with PJT Partners, a restructuring adviser, and the law firm Akin, as the airline deals with heavy cash outflows and high oil prices, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The airline's $2 billion of notes due 2031 sank to 42 cents on the dollar on Thursday and traded in the mid-40s on Friday, according to The Wall Street Journal, which cited market participants and Finra data. The decline followed a recent bondholder call. Finra data shows the notes changed hands at roughly 80 cents per dollar of face value earlier in October.

JetBlue stock closed at $2.62 on Friday, down 0.94%, and has fallen 42% this year. It has lost more than half its value since the start of August.

"JetBlue remains confident in its JetForward strategy and the progress being made toward returning to sustained profitability," the company said in an emailed statement, according to Reuters. A JetBlue representative told The Wall Street Journal that management's focus is on boosting revenue and developing a business that earns more. JetBlue plans to give an account of how it is progressing and where its finances are headed when it hosts its call on third-quarter results on Tuesday.

Creditors bring in advisers once they fear a borrower may not return their money in full or on time, according to The Wall Street Journal. Spirit Airlines shut down operations this year after repeated bankruptcy filings, and investors holding airline debt have been wary ever since, the Journal said.

JetBlue held $1.66 billion of cash, plus cash equivalents, as of June 30, set against $8.5 billion of borrowings and finance lease commitments, according to its filings. Much of that debt is secured by JetBlue's aircraft fleet and its TrueBlue loyalty program, according to The Wall Street Journal. Close to two-thirds of the company's assets, spanning property, equipment and intangibles, have been put up as security for lenders, according to its quarterly filings.

Some market participants fear that piling on more debt could leave JetBlue little room to maneuver if a turnaround fails, according to The Wall Street Journal. The airline also faces possible pressure from credit-card processors, which may demand that carriers hold back collateral should conditions deteriorate, the Journal said. JetBlue said it was under no such obligation when June ended.

Higher jet fuel costs tied to the Iran war have squeezed margins at U.S. airlines even as fares rose and travelers kept flying at a consistent pace, according to Reuters.

JetBlue reported a first-quarter net loss of $319 million in April, wider than the $208 million loss a year earlier. Jet fuel cost 15.2% more per gallon than in the same period a year before, and the company ended the quarter with $2.4 billion in liquidity. JetBlue arranged $500 million of financing secured by aircraft in April, and the full amount had been tapped by June 30, according to The Wall Street Journal.

#5501. Hyperliquid Recovery: Binance Reopens HYPE Withdrawals After $6.4 Billion Hack

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Binance, world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, officially reopened Hyperliquid and Aptos withdrawals, giving users a freeway to operate with HYPE and APT tokens. Confirmed by Yi He, platform's co-founder and president, the resurrection of operation came after finalization of the audit. What lies behind the announcement is the conclusion of week-long retaliation with the HYPE community as holders of native Hyperliquid token needed to wait longer than others to be able to withdraw from Binance.

💁🏻‍♀️ Withdrawals have now been re-enabled for the following networks and assets: New: ✅ HYPE ✅ APT

The predecessor of this story is the biggest cyberattack in history when, according to the FBI and Chainalysis, the North Korean hacking group TraderTraitor emptied Binance's hot wallets for about $6.3 billion in a matter of 20 minutes. What happened next is the exchange blocking $3 billion with the help of Tether, Circle; its pledge to cover 100% of users' money from the SAFU fund; and thorough audits across Solana and Ethereum chains. Then, starting November 1, Binance started reopening tokens for withdrawal.

HYPE was the last to become eligible and the community behind DeFi giant met such a measure with discontent, crying about sabotage and unfair competition tactics. It's not that deep: Hyperliquid, being the headliner of decentralized finance, amasses a big share of the pie in on-chain derivatives trading, and of course this affects Binance's business.

The retaliation between the two has continued since 2025 when Hyperliquid founder Jeff Yan publicly accused Binance of lowering liquidations data after the October 10, 2025 event, when positions worth around $40 billion were marginally closed across the crypto market. Binance then delayed the spot listing of HYPE token until September 24, 2026 and gave it 'Seed Tag', which is usually applied to high-risk cryptocurrencies. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao diplomatically refused the accusations and said that strong decentralized exchanges on the contrary increase 'the pie' for the whole industry.

The delay indeed has a technical aspect. HYPE operates within its own Layer-1, HyperEVM. Auditing a custom blockchain architecture — not standard EVM or Solana-based — in the aftermath of such a hack requires more time and attention to be carried out properly.

In the wake of the cybersecurity crisis the pause was still interpreted as corporate vengeance. This makes Yi He's words and the demonstrative relaunch of withdrawals a sign that obligations for clients take priority over market rivalry.

#5500. NeuralSat raises $3.2M to bring high-speed data connectivity and compute to space

German startup NeuralSat GmbH announced Thursday that it has raised €2.9 million, about $3.2 million, in pre-seed funding to develop a 72-satellite data-relay processing network aimed at speeding up the flow of data from space.

Capnamic and Bayern Kapital co-led the round. Other investors participating in the round included ZOHO.VC, Robin Capital, BAB – Die Förderbank für Bremen und Bremerhaven, Mission E and KIEMIS Holding.

Founded in early 2026, NeuralSat’s satellite constellation will allow operators to offload computing and communications. According to the company, its network will deliver up to 50 gigabits per second via optical and high-frequency radio links.

The network will support real-time edge processing, hosted workloads for commercial and defense clients and provide for time-critical missions like Earth observation and signals intelligence.

“We believe the next major evolution in space will… come from connecting satellites to shared infrastructure that enables them to communicate, access computing resources, and operate together,” Chief Executive Mohd Bilal said in a statement. “Just as the internet transformed how computers interact on Earth, we intend to transform how intelligence is connected and delivered in space.”

The company said the funding will help it accelerate plans to launch its first in-orbit demonstration node, planned for October 2027. After that, NeuralSat plans to begin rolling out commercial operational satellites.

The race to develop and build better connectivity and compute capabilities in space is on. Canadian startup Kepler Communications Inc. launched its first commercial space data relay service in January, allowing resilient data transfer and onboard computing, with a next-gen optical relay network announced in August. Skyloom, acquired by quantum computing firm IonQ Inc. in early 2026, deployed 84 optical terminals and a relay architecture in low Earth orbit.

Space is not the optimal place to run processors because heat dissipation becomes a major issue with no air to carry it away. But space technology firms have developed solutions to radiate it from giant sails and other surfaces. Space-based compute may not replace terrestrial data centers, but it can enable edge compute given payload weight restrictions for orbital launch.

Starcloud Inc., formerly known as Lumen Orbit, raised $250 million in August at a $2.3 billion valuation. The company has already tested an Nvidia H100 graphics processing unit in orbit in late 2025, proving that it can scale to multi-satellite AI “data centers.” The company is now collaborating with Nvidia Corp. on upcoming space-grade chips.

Currently, data relay and compute processing in space reduce the need for other satellites to send data to Earth to complete workloads. Talking to a nearby satellite for edge compute can shave significant time off data transfers. Sending data down to Earth can take a round trip of four to more than 30 milliseconds; satellite-to-satellite is slightly faster, at three to 30 milliseconds.

The real boost comes from relaying between satellites rather than routing long distances on the ground to a data center and back, often via optical cable ground networks, which add additional lag. Over long distances across the globe, inter-satellite links are around 30% to 50% faster than sending signals down to Earth for processing.

Companies such as NeuralSat hope to use the advantage of being right there, near the data production, to provide processing capabilities, or swift relay to a satellite closer geographically to terrestrial data center processing to reduce delays.

#5499. Christine Lagarde is resigning as head of the European Central Bank months early

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The departure gives European leaders time to settle on a replacement before France holds its presidential vote in 2027

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7, 2027, ahead of the scheduled end of her term.

Lagarde informed the ECB's Governing Council and European Council President António Costa of the decision on Thursday, the ECB said. The European Council will appoint her successor following the nomination process outlined in Article 283 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the ECB said. The Governing Council gave her a long standing ovation, the ECB said.

Her eight-year term had been set to expire on Oct. 31, 2027, according to The Associated Press.

In a clip she shared on X $TWTR, Lagarde called it "a great pride and a huge privilege to serve this institution."

Costa said the selection process "will be initiated today and will proceed without delay."

The departure gives European leaders time to settle on a replacement before France holds its presidential vote in 2027. Two other top ECB posts are also changing hands. Chief economist Philip Lane's term ends May 31, and executive board member Isabel Schnabel is leaving Jan. 3 to join the International Monetary Fund, according to The Associated Press.

Leaders are expected to strike a package deal that spreads the three open jobs across E.U. member states, according to The Associated Press.

Klaas Knot, who used to head the Netherlands' central bank, and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, a onetime Spanish central bank governor, are regarded as the leading contenders to take over from Lagarde, according to Reuters.

Lagarde’s announcement landed on the same day the ECB is scheduled to publish its interest rate decision at 1:15 p.m. GMT (9:15 a.m. ET), with her regular press conference set for 1:45 p.m. GMT, according to Reuters. The bank is broadly predicted to leave borrowing costs unchanged, with the deposit rate staying at 2.5%, according to Reuters.
