#5482. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:49 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

#5481. How GTA Online makes money: free updates, Shark Cards and 10 moments

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How GTA Online makes money comes down to Shark Cards, free updates and console and PC re-releases, traced here through 10 moments from 2013 to 2022

GTA Online gives away its new content and sells the currency players spend inside it. New missions, vehicles, properties and game modes arrive as free updates. Many of the biggest items in those updates carry steep prices. Players pay those prices in GTA$, an in-game currency they can either earn through play or buy with real money.

That arrangement explains how GTA Online makes money. It turned a multiplayer mode into a business built on content that players never pay for directly. Each new update gives players something else to spend on. Each purchase helps fund the next round of free updates.

The mode came from Rockstar Games, the studio that developed Grand Theft Auto V, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, its publisher and parent company. GTA V went on sale Sept. 17, 2013. Take-Two reported that the game passed $1 billion in sales within its first three days. That figure covers GTA V as a whole, not GTA Online on its own. The online mode opened on Oct. 1, two weeks later, inside a game that had already reached a large audience.

The start was rough. Connection failures and characters that would not save marked the first weeks. Rockstar gave affected players GTA$500,000 as an apology. From there the model took shape one piece at a time. Shark Cards, added in the weeks after launch, gave players a direct way to buy GTA$. Heists, businesses and a casino added new things to do and new things to buy. Releases on newer consoles and PC kept bringing fresh players into the same online world.

The 10 slides that follow are a selection of those moments and mechanisms, arranged in chronological order. They run from the October 2013 launch to the March 2022 release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR|S. That release arrived alongside a new subscription called GTA+. These slides are not a ranking, and they are not the complete story. Each one covers a specific update, release or business decision in the mode's history.

GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013, two weeks after Grand Theft Auto V went on sale on Sept. 17. The online mode was not sold separately. It arrived as part of a game that players had already bought.

Rockstar Games developed both the story campaign and the online mode. Rockstar North, the studio's team in Edinburgh, Scotland, led the work. Take-Two Interactive $TTWO published GTA V and is Rockstar's parent company.

GTA V first went on sale for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. GTA Online opened on those same two consoles. On those consoles, a single session held up to 16 players.

The story campaign follows three playable leads: Michael, Franklin and Trevor. Their story plays out in Los Santos, a fictional city modeled on Los Angeles, and in the countryside of Blaine County. GTA Online uses the same map. Players build their own character instead of controlling the three story leads.

That shared setting tied the two halves of the package together. Players who spent the first two weeks in the campaign already knew the streets, the vehicles and the layout of the city. The multiplayer side did not have to introduce a new world.

Some faces carried over as well. Characters from the campaign, including Lamar Davis and Lester Crest, hand out jobs to online players. Those jobs sit alongside races, deathmatches and other modes that pit players against each other or put them on the same team.

Progress in the online mode runs on two tracks. Reputation points, known as RP, raise a character's rank and unlock weapons, clothing and activities. GTA$, the in-game currency, pays for cars, apartments and gear. Completing jobs earns both.

The release order also shaped how the mode found its audience. GTA Online did not need to attract buyers on its own. Its potential player base was everyone who already owned GTA V on PlayStation 3 or Xbox 360.

GTA Online launched in October 2013 with serious connection failures and lost character saves. Rockstar Games answered by giving affected players GTA$500,000 in in-game currency as an apology.

The trouble began on day one. GTA Online went live on Oct. 1, 2013, on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. Those were the same consoles Grand Theft Auto V had reached two weeks earlier. Players opened the online mode from inside GTA V and did not buy it separately. Many could not connect at all. Others got in, only to find the game had failed to save the characters they had built.

Lost saves struck at the core of the mode. GTA Online characters are created by players and are separate from Michael, Franklin and Trevor, the three protagonists of the GTA V story mode. Each one is a persistent character who earns money, buys property and climbs in rank over time. A failed save erased that progress. A player who lost a character in the first week had to start again from the beginning.

Rockstar released patches over the following weeks to address the connection and save problems. The compensation was part of that recovery. Instead of cash refunds, the studio paid players in GTA$, the fictional currency used throughout GTA Online. GTA$ exists only inside the game and cannot be exchanged back into real money.

The payment fit the way the mode works. Players spend GTA$ on cars, weapons, apartments and other items in Los Santos, the game's fictional version of Los Angeles. Apartments also serve as a base, with garage space for the cars a player collects. A payment of GTA$500,000 gave affected players a head start on those purchases.

The broken start did not end GTA Online. The mode recovered from its October 2013 failures and kept its players. Rockstar went on to support it with new content for years.

Shark Cards let GTA Online players spend real money to receive GTA$, the in-game currency. That currency buys the cars, weapons, apartments and clothing sold inside the game. The cards form the direct link between GTA Online's virtual economy and real-world revenue.

Rockstar Games added Shark Cards in the weeks after GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013. The online mode came included with Grand Theft Auto V at no extra charge. The cards gave Rockstar a way to earn money from players after the initial game sale.

The cards are sold in tiers named after sharks, including Red Shark, Great White Shark and Megalodon. Larger tiers deliver more GTA$ for a higher price. Megalodon takes its name from an extinct prehistoric shark and sits at the top of the range.

The purchase itself is simple. A player picks a card, pays in real currency and sees the GTA$ added to their in-game balance. Cards can be bought through a platform's digital storefront or through the store menu inside the game.

The GTA$ is then spent at in-game shops and on the game's fictional websites. Legendary Motorsport, the in-game site for high-end cars, is one example. Property and vehicle purchases go through these same menus whether the money was earned or bought.

Shark Cards do not unlock a separate catalog. GTA$ bought with a card is the same currency players earn by completing jobs, missions and races. A player who never spends real money can reach the same items by playing longer.

That earn-or-buy choice defines how the cards work. Players with limited time can skip hours of repeated jobs. Players with more time can earn the same currency without paying.

Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, Rockstar's publisher and parent company, reports this kind of ongoing in-game spending under a category it calls recurrent consumer spending. The cards turned GTA Online into a product that could keep earning money long after a player bought the base game.

The Heists update arrived in GTA Online on March 10, 2015, about a year and a half after the mode opened. It added cooperative, multi-stage robberies that a crew plans and carries out together. Each stage feeds into a final job.

Heists were not new to the Grand Theft Auto series. The single-player campaign of Grand Theft Auto V is built around them, with its three protagonists planning and pulling off large scores. Online players waited until 2015 for a version of that structure designed for groups.

The update shipped with five heists: The Fleeca Job, The Prison Break, The Humane Labs Raid, Series A Funding and The Pacific Standard Job. Each one follows the same basic pattern. A crew completes a set of setup missions, then attempts a finale that carries the main payout. Setup missions range from stealing vehicles to collecting equipment the finale depends on.

Most of the heists call for four players. The Fleeca Job, the first in the sequence, needs only two. Lester Crest, a character from the story mode, offers the jobs.

Planning happens on a board inside a high-end apartment. A player has to own one of these properties to host a heist. Apartments are bought with GTA$. The host also pays the setup costs before any missions begin.

That host acts as heist leader. The leader assigns players to roles and decides what share of the final payout each crew member receives. Roles change from one job to the next. One player might fly or drive while another hacks a security system or provides cover.

The update came out on PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One at the same time. It gave every console version of the online mode the same new long-form content on the same day. Grand Theft Auto V had not yet reached PC at that point.

Rockstar Games releases new GTA Online content as free updates instead of selling it as paid expansions. Revenue comes afterward, when players spend GTA$ on the vehicles, weapons, properties and other items those updates introduce.

That arrangement differs from a paid add-on. A player downloads an update at no cost and gets access to its new missions and activities. Many of the items inside it carry an in-game price tag, though. To own them, the player needs enough GTA$ in the bank.

There are two ways to get that money. Players can earn GTA$ by completing missions, races and other jobs inside the game. They can also buy it with real money through Shark Cards, the currency packs Rockstar sells for GTA Online. Both routes lead to the same GTA$ balance.

This structure links each content release to Shark Card sales. A new car or property gives players a specific GTA$ target. A player short of that total can keep earning through jobs or buy the difference with real money. The update costs nothing, but what it unlocks can lead to a real-money purchase.

Free updates also keep the online player base together. Paid expansions divide players into those who bought the add-on and those who did not. When every player receives the same content, new missions and items reach the whole audience at once. A new vehicle or activity is open to everyone who plays GTA Online, not only to buyers of a specific pack.

Rockstar used the paid model with its previous game. Grand Theft Auto IV received two paid episodic expansions in 2009, The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony. GTA Online took a different path, offering its additions as downloads with no separate charge.

The approach has carried through the mode's major releases. Large cooperative missions, property and business updates and later content drops all arrived without a purchase price of their own. Each one added new items with GTA$ prices attached.

Three GTA Online updates pushed players toward buying property and running criminal businesses inside the game. They were Executives and Other Criminals in 2015, Gunrunning in 2017 and After Hours in 2018.

Each update added expensive properties and businesses. Players paid for them with GTA$, the currency used throughout the mode. The updates themselves came free. The price sat inside the game rather than at the point of release.

Before these releases, a GTA Online player mostly took on jobs and finished them. The business updates added ownership to the mode. A player now had property to buy and an operation to run.

Executives and Other Criminals came first. As its name signals, the update cast the player as the head of a criminal enterprise. The player was no longer only a lone operator picking up work.

Gunrunning followed in 2017. Its theme was arms dealing. It carried the ownership idea into a second line of illegal work.

After Hours arrived in 2018 and became known as the nightclub update. Its new content revolved around a nightclub that players could own. That made it the third business type in the series, after the criminal enterprise and the arms trade.

Price links the three releases. Each one put a large GTA$ cost on the property or business at its center. Those costs gave players a concrete target for the currency. A player saving for a business had a specific item in mind, not just a growing balance.

The updates also built on one another. Each arrived as a new business type rather than a replacement for the last one. A player who bought into an earlier business did not lose it when the next update arrived. Each release instead added another option to spend GTA$ on.

From 2015 to 2018, owning an in-game business became a recurring theme of new GTA Online content rather than the subject of one release.

Grand Theft Auto V and GTA Online were re-released for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in November 2014, then for PC on April 14, 2015. Each new version brought another group of players into the same online mode.

The console re-release came about 14 months after the original game went on sale. The PC version followed roughly 19 months after that first launch.

None of these releases created a separate online game. Players on the new platforms entered the same GTA Online that had opened in October 2013. They joined its missions, its in-game economy and its GTA$ currency.

That meant newcomers did not arrive at a blank start. By November 2014, the mode had been running for more than a year. Its missions, prices and GTA$ economy were already in place when the new versions went on sale.

That structure ties each re-release to the mode's revenue model. GTA Online earns money when players use real money to buy GTA$ through Shark Cards. Those cards were already on sale when the new versions arrived. A new platform adds more people who can make those purchases. Rockstar Games did not have to build a new multiplayer game to reach them.

The PC release also followed a major content drop. The Heists update came out on March 10, 2015. The PC version arrived about five weeks later. PC players joined with the cooperative heist missions already live. They could plan and carry out those multi-stage missions with other players from their first weeks. The newest content and the newest platform reached players within weeks of each other.

Rockstar Games developed each version, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO published them. The same online mode carried on across every format. Players on every system bought the same GTA$ and spent it on the same kinds of in-game items. Each release widened its audience without changing how it made money.

The Diamond Casino & Resort update arrived in GTA Online in July 2019. It added an in-game casino that served two roles: a social space where players could gather, and a new source of content inside the mode.

Rockstar Games, which develops GTA Online, released the update nearly six years after the multiplayer mode opened on Oct. 1, 2013. Take-Two Interactive $TTWO publishes the game and is Rockstar's parent company.

Many earlier updates centered on missions, properties and businesses. The casino offered a different kind of content. It was not another job to finish or another business to manage. It was a destination inside the game world where players could meet and spend time together.

The update also sits at a specific point in the mode's timeline. It came the year after After Hours, the 2018 nightclub update. It arrived before the Cayo Perico Heist, which followed in December 2020.

Like other GTA Online content, the casino reached players as a free update to the existing mode. It was not sold as a separately priced expansion.

The Cayo Perico Heist launched in GTA Online on Dec. 15, 2020. It was set on a private island, and players could complete it alone or with a group.

That solo option broke from how GTA Online heists had worked before. The Heists update of 2015 was built around a crew. Its missions were cooperative jobs that players planned and carried out together. Cayo Perico made those other players optional rather than required.

The change removed a practical hurdle for players without a regular crew. A heist no longer depended on finding teammates, matching schedules or waiting for others to join. Players who preferred company could still bring a group along.

The design widened the audience for a major piece of content. A crew-only heist served players who already had organized groups. A heist one person could finish was open to anyone who logged in to the mode.

The private island also gave GTA Online a new setting for a heist. Earlier updates had expanded the mode with businesses, properties and a casino. Cayo Perico added a destination of its own.

The release date shows how long the mode had stayed active. The heist arrived more than seven years after GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013. It came about five years and nine months after the original Heists update of March 10, 2015. It followed the Diamond Casino & Resort update of July 2019 by about 17 months.

Those gaps point to a mode that kept growing rather than being replaced. Rockstar Games added a new heist to the same online world that had opened in 2013, instead of moving players to a new game.

Cayo Perico reached players the same way as other GTA Online content. Rockstar Games delivered it as a free update. Players did not buy the heist as a separate expansion. Like other GTA Online activities, the heist paid out in GTA$, giving solo players a way to earn the currency through play.

GTA V and GTA Online arrived on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR|S on March 15, 2022. Rockstar Games paired the release with two changes to how players could get into the online mode and pay for it. The first was a standalone GTA Online download on PlayStation 5. The second was a subscription called GTA+.

The release moved GTA Online onto a newer generation of home consoles than the PS4 and Xbox One versions of November 2014. The mode had opened on Oct. 1, 2013, so the new versions came about eight and a half years into its life. Rockstar Games developed the game, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO publishes it.

The standalone version split the multiplayer mode off from the GTA V story campaign. On PS5, a player could download GTA Online by itself instead of buying the full game. For the first three months after release, that download was free.

The free entry point fit a game that earns its money from spending after the download. Every new player joins the same online world, where GTA$ pays for vehicles, properties and businesses. Players can earn that currency through play or buy it with real money through Shark Cards. Under that model, the revenue comes from what players buy once they arrive, not from the download itself.

Rockstar launched GTA+ the same month. It is a paid subscription service for GTA Online that bills players on a recurring basis. It added another way to pay, alongside buying the game and buying Shark Cards.

Both changes kept the core of the model intact. New content stays free to play, and spending happens inside the game. The standalone download widened the way in, and GTA+ added a recurring way to pay once there.

#5479. Mirendil raises $1B in funding to speed up AI model development

Mirendil Inc., a provider of software that speeds up artificial intelligence development, has raised $1 billion in early-stage funding.

The startup stated on Thursday that Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital jointly led the Series A investment. They were joined by more than a half-dozen others including Google LLC.

Mirendil was launched last year by two former Google DeepMind and Anthropic PBC researchers. Chief Executive Officer Behnam Neyshabur is a co-inventor of SAM, a popular algorithm that makes AI models better at tasks they were not specifically trained to perform. Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pretraining projects. Pretraining is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow.

Mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company says that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents.

Large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically.

Earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil says that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete.

The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality.

The LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the company unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10 million input tokens per prompt, or 10 times more than Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the equivalent of about a half-million lines of code.

Fern is based on a version of Mirendil-Base with 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Late last month, the company previewed two upgraded versions of the latter model with between 500 billion and 10 trillion parameters. Mirendil plans to use those algorithms to develop more capable LLMs.

#5478. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

#5477. Jensen Huang's failed bid and Rene Haas's IPO: 10 things to know about Arm

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How Arm chip licensing works, explained in 10 parts covering architecture licenses, core designs, royalties, Jensen Huang's failed Nvidia bid and Rene Haas's leadership

Arm Holdings does not manufacture a single chip, yet its technology runs inside processors designed by Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Nvidia $NVDA and Samsung. The company, based in Cambridge, U.K., sells something less tangible than silicon. It licenses the rules a processor follows and, in many cases, ready-made blueprints for the processor cores themselves. Partner companies turn those designs into finished chips. Contract manufacturers such as TSMC $TSM then fabricate them.

That division of labor lets a company with no factories of its own shape the design of chips that other companies build and sell. Arm leaves the expensive work of building and running fabrication plants to others.

Understanding how Arm chip licensing works starts with two kinds of payment. A company that wants to use Arm technology generally pays an upfront license fee. It then pays a royalty on each chip it ships. Arm earns money when a partner signs on and again when that partner's products reach customers.

The rights a company buys vary. Some companies license ready-made core designs and build their chips around them. Others, such as Apple, hold an architecture license that lets them design their own cores to Arm's instruction set. The choice affects how much control a company has over its chip's design. It also sat at the center of a legal dispute between Arm and Qualcomm.

The business has changed hands and leaders in recent years. In September 2020, Nvidia agreed to buy Arm from SoftBank for $40 billion. Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder and CEO, led the company at the time. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission sued to block the purchase in December 2021. U.K. and EU regulators had also raised concerns. Nvidia abandoned the deal in February 2022. That same month, Rene Haas became Arm's CEO, succeeding Simon Segars. Under Haas, Arm listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ in September 2023, and SoftBank kept a majority stake.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of the pieces that make up the Arm licensing model. They explain what an instruction set architecture is, how the company began and which license types chipmakers choose. They also look at how RISC-V and x86 compete with Arm. Each slide covers one part of what Arm does and can be read on its own.

Arm does not manufacture semiconductors. The company, based in Cambridge, U.K., creates processor designs and sets the rules those processors follow. It then sells other companies the right to use that work.

Arm owns no chip factories. What it produces is intellectual property — detailed specifications and circuit designs that exist as digital files rather than as physical silicon. A customer receives those files, not a box of finished parts.

Other companies design the chips that carry Arm technology. Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Nvidia $NVDA and Samsung are among the companies that build chips on Arm's foundation. Each one takes Arm's work as a starting point and turns it into a product of its own.

A finished processor for a phone or laptop usually contains far more than Arm's contribution. Chip designers combine Arm-based processor cores with their own graphics units, memory controllers and other circuits on a single piece of silicon. The industry calls that combined design a system-on-chip. The Arm portion handles general computing tasks. The rest of the chip reflects each company's own engineering.

Manufacturing is a separate step, handled by yet another company. When a chip designer finishes its layout, it sends the design to a foundry for fabrication. TSMC $TSM, short for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., is a contract foundry that fabricates chips for other companies. Its customers include many of the same companies that license Arm technology.

Companies that design chips but outsource production are described as fabless. Qualcomm and Nvidia work this way. Arm sits one layer further back in the chain. It supplies the designs that those chip companies start from.

The three-way split lets each company specialize. Arm concentrates on processor design. Chip companies concentrate on complete products. Foundries concentrate on production technology. A single Arm design can appear in chips from many different companies at the same time.

Arm's revenue comes from that same chain. The company collects money from the businesses that use its technology, not from selling hardware. Its income therefore depends on what its partners design, build and ship.

Arm started in 1990 as Advanced RISC Machines Ltd, a joint venture formed by Acorn Computers, Apple $AAPL and VLSI Technology. The company grew out of processor work at Acorn, a British computer maker. Its name was later shortened to Arm.

Acorn was based in Cambridge, U.K. It was best known for the BBC Micro, a home computer used widely in British schools during the 1980s. For its next generation of machines, Acorn designed its own processor instead of buying one from another supplier. Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber led that design work. The first chip, the ARM1, ran its first code in 1985.

At that stage, the letters ARM stood for Acorn RISC Machine. Acorn used the chip family in its Archimedes computers, launched in 1987. Its simple design also meant the chip drew relatively little power. That trait later suited battery-powered devices.

The 1990 spinout changed who the processor was for. The design moved out of Acorn and into a separate company that could supply it to others. Each of the three founders brought something different. Acorn contributed the processor design and the engineers behind it. Apple was a prospective customer for the chips. VLSI Technology, a U.S. chip company, brought manufacturing capability.

Apple's interest centered on the Newton, its handheld personal digital assistant. The Newton MessagePad, released in 1993, ran on an ARM processor. The device never sold in large numbers. It still gave the young company an early commercial product in the market.

Robin Saxby became the company's first chief executive. Under his leadership, the company licensed its designs to other firms instead of building and selling chips itself. In 1998, it listed its shares in London and on Nasdaq $NDAQ.

That period as a listed company ended in 2016. SoftBank, the Japanese technology investor, acquired Arm that year for about £24 billion, or roughly $32 billion. The deal took Arm private.

The Arm instruction set architecture is the list of basic commands an Arm processor understands and carries out. It acts as the shared language between software and hardware. Any program meant to run on an Arm chip must first be translated into those commands.

An instruction set architecture is usually shortened to ISA. It defines operations such as adding two numbers, loading data from memory or jumping to another part of a program. It also sets out the registers a processor exposes and how memory is addressed.

The ISA is a specification, not a physical circuit. Two chips can look very different inside and still run the same software, as long as both follow the same ISA.

This separation explains why compilers matter. A compiler converts code written in a language such as C or Rust into machine instructions for one specific ISA. A program compiled for Arm will not run natively on an x86 processor from Intel $INTC or AMD $AMD. The reverse is also true. Developers either recompile their code for each architecture or rely on translation software.

The Arm architecture follows RISC, short for reduced instruction set computing. The RISC approach favors a small set of simple instructions that each do one job. Arm is also a load/store design. Arithmetic happens on values held in registers, and separate instructions move data to and from memory.

The x86 family follows the complex instruction set computing, or CISC, approach. Some of its instructions combine a memory access and a calculation in a single step. Its instructions also vary in length.

Arm's 64-bit era began with Armv8, which introduced the AArch64 execution state. AArch64 instructions are a fixed 32 bits long. A fixed size makes them simpler for a processor to decode. AArch64 also provides 31 general-purpose registers. Armv8 kept a separate 32-bit state, called AArch32, so older software could still run on many chips.

Armv9 was announced in 2021 as the next major version of the architecture. It includes Scalable Vector Extension 2, known as SVE2. This feature lets a single instruction work on many pieces of data at once. That style of processing is used in machine learning, image handling and signal processing.

Each new version builds on the previous one rather than replacing it. Software written for earlier 64-bit Arm chips generally continues to run on newer ones.

Arm earns money in two stages. A company pays an upfront license fee to gain access to Arm's designs, and then it pays a royalty on each chip it ships that uses that technology.

The license fee comes first. A chip company pays it when it signs an agreement, long before any product reaches a customer. The fee buys the right to use Arm's intellectual property. That property can be the instruction set itself or a finished processor core design. With it, the licensee can start building a chip around Arm technology.

The royalty comes later. It applies to each unit the licensee sells once its chip is in production. A processor in a smartphone, a microcontroller in a household appliance and a server chip in a data center can each generate a royalty for Arm.

That timing creates a gap between a deal and the money it produces. Designing a chip, verifying it and moving it into manufacturing at a foundry takes time. An agreement signed today may not produce royalty income until the resulting chip ships. That can be years later.

The gap runs the other way at the end of a product's life. A chip design can stay in production for years after launch. Every unit shipped during that time adds to the royalty stream. An older license can keep paying Arm long after the original fee was collected.

The two streams track different things. License fees reflect how many companies are starting new projects with Arm. Royalties reflect how many chips those companies actually sell. A licensee that ships chips in large volumes generates more royalty income than one that ships few.

This structure ties Arm's income to its partners' sales. When companies such as Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Samsung and Nvidia $NVDA ship more Arm-based processors, Arm collects more in royalties. When demand for those products slows, royalty income slows too.

The specific fees and royalty terms are set in contracts negotiated between Arm and each licensee. The basic two-part model applies whether a company licenses a ready-made core or designs its own cores to Arm's instruction set.

An Arm architecture license gives a company the right to design its own processor cores from scratch, as long as those cores run Arm's instruction set. Apple $AAPL and Qualcomm $QCOM are two of the best-known companies that use this route to build custom CPU designs.

Fewer companies take this path than license Arm's ready-made cores. Many Arm customers do not design cores at all. They license finished core designs from Arm and place them inside their chips. An architecture licensee takes on that engineering work itself. It decides how the core is organized internally, how it processes instructions and how it balances speed against power use.

Compatibility is the part that does not change. A custom core built under this license must execute the same Arm instructions as any other Arm processor. Software compiled for Arm can therefore run on it. The licensee gains control over the hardware design without giving up access to the wider pool of Arm software.

Apple is one example. Its M1 chip, announced in November 2020, used Apple-designed cores built to Arm's instruction set. The M1 began Apple's shift away from Intel $INTC processors in its Mac computers. The custom approach lets Apple shape its chips around its own devices and operating systems.

Qualcomm is another. Its newer custom CPU designs trace back to Nuvia, a chip startup that Qualcomm acquired. Nuvia held its own architecture license with Arm before that deal.

Those designs became the subject of a court fight. Arm sued Qualcomm in 2022 in a dispute over which license terms applied to the Nuvia-based designs after the acquisition. A jury in Delaware returned a verdict in December 2024 that went mainly in Qualcomm's favor.

The case put the terms of an architecture license in public view. It showed that the specific wording of such a license, including which company holds it, can decide who may use a design after a change in ownership.

The custom route also carries practical trade-offs. Designing a competitive CPU core requires large engineering teams and years of development. The companies that take this path are generally those that want processors tuned closely to their own products rather than a design shared with competitors.

A core license gives a chip company a finished processor design from Arm that it can place directly into its own chip. Arm sells these ready-made cores in families aimed at different markets. They include Cortex-A for phones, Cortex-M for microcontrollers and Neoverse for servers and data centers.

The licensee does not have to design a processor core from scratch. It takes Arm's completed core and builds a larger chip around it. That chip can also include graphics processors, memory controllers, wireless modems and other circuits the company designs or sources elsewhere.

Cortex-A is the family built for application processors. These are the chips that run full operating systems, such as Android on a smartphone or tablet. Phone chips often combine several Cortex-A cores of different sizes on one piece of silicon. Larger cores take on demanding work. Smaller cores handle lighter tasks and use less power.

Cortex-M targets microcontrollers. These are small, low-power chips that control a single device or a narrow set of tasks. They show up in appliances, sensors, wearables and industrial equipment. They typically run simple firmware or a small real-time operating system. That is far lighter than the software found on a phone or laptop.

Arm also sells Cortex-R cores for real-time systems. These are used where a chip must respond within strict time limits, such as in automotive systems and storage controllers.

Neoverse is Arm's line for servers, cloud computing and networking infrastructure. It is meant for chips that sit in data centers rather than in consumer devices. Amazon $AMZN's Graviton processors, which power servers in Amazon Web Services, are one example. Amazon designs the Graviton chips itself but builds them around Neoverse designs.

A ready-made core removes a large engineering task from a licensee's project. Creating an original processor core requires a specialized engineering team and extensive testing. Licensing a finished core lets a company focus its effort on the surrounding circuits instead.

The trade-off is control over the core. A company using a standard Arm core gets the same core design that its competitors can license. It can still set its product apart through the other components on its chip, its software and its manufacturing choices. Companies that want to change the internal design of the core itself take a different route, through an architecture license.

Arm Flexible Access, launched in 2019, lets a company try out a wide range of Arm designs before signing a full license for any of them. Compute Subsystems take a different approach to a related problem: they bundle several Arm designs into one pre-integrated package that a chip team can build around.

Both programs aim to lower the cost and effort of building an Arm-based chip. Under the traditional model, a company negotiates a license for a specific design and pays for it before engineering work goes far. For a large chipmaker, that is routine. For a startup, a university lab or a small device maker, it can mean committing money before knowing which design fits.

Flexible Access changes the order of those steps. A participant gets access to a portfolio of Arm intellectual property, along with tools and design support. Engineers can evaluate cores, run simulations and build prototypes using several options side by side. The company pays a license fee only for the designs it decides to take into production. Royalties still apply once finished chips ship.

The program is built for companies that have not yet settled on a processor. A maker of connected sensors, for example, might compare several microcontroller-class cores before choosing one. Under a conventional arrangement, each of those comparisons could require its own license negotiation.

Compute Subsystems address a later stage of the design process. A modern processor is more than its CPU cores. The cores have to connect to each other, to memory and to other parts of the chip. Integrating and verifying those pieces takes significant engineering time.

A Compute Subsystem packages Arm cores with surrounding components that Arm has already integrated and tested together. A licensee starts from that working foundation instead of assembling the pieces itself. The aim is to cut the integration and verification work a chip team would otherwise do on its own.

The trade-off is control. A company that builds on a pre-integrated bundle accepts more of Arm's design choices. A company that assembles individual cores, or designs its own under an architecture license, keeps more room to differentiate its chip.

Nvidia $NVDA's $40 billion agreement to buy Arm from SoftBank, announced in September 2020, was abandoned in February 2022 after regulators in the U.S., U.K. and EU objected. Their central worry was that one chipmaker would own the designs its rivals license.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it as CEO since then. The company built its business on graphics processors. Those chips later became widely used hardware for training AI models. Buying Arm would have added a widely licensed CPU architecture to a company already known for GPUs.

SoftBank had owned Arm since 2016. SoftBank does not design or sell chips. Under the proposed deal, Arm would have moved to an owner that designs and sells chips in large volumes. That change sat at the center of the regulatory fight.

Arm's model depends on licensing the same technology to many companies, including firms that compete with one another. Several of those licensees also compete with Nvidia. The deal raised the question of whether Arm could stay neutral under an owner with its own chip products to sell.

In December 2021, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission sued to block the acquisition. The agency's complaint argued that the merger would give Nvidia control over computing technology and designs that its rivals rely on. The lawsuit meant the deal faced a court process in the U.S. on top of reviews in other jurisdictions.

Regulators in the U.K. and the EU had also raised concerns. Arm's headquarters in Cambridge, U.K., placed the deal under British review. With objections on several fronts, the companies walked away from the agreement. That came about 17 months after the deal was announced.

The collapse did not end Nvidia's use of Arm technology. Nvidia remains an Arm licensee. Its Grace CPU, designed for data centers, is built on Arm designs. Nvidia kept access to the architecture through the same licensing route that other chip designers use, rather than through ownership of Arm itself.

Rene Haas has run Arm as chief executive since February 2022, when he succeeded Simon Segars. Under Haas, Arm listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ on September 14, 2023, under the ticker ARM, with shares priced at $51.

Haas was promoted from inside the company. Before becoming CEO, he led Arm's IP products group. IP stands for intellectual property. At Arm, that term covers the processor designs and instruction set rights the company licenses to chipmakers. The group Haas ran was responsible for the products Arm sells to its customers.

Earlier in his career, Haas worked at Nvidia $NVDA. Jensen Huang co-founded that company and serves as its CEO. Nvidia is one of the chip designers that license Arm technology.

Haas took charge in the same month that Nvidia abandoned its agreement to buy Arm from SoftBank. With that sale off the table, SoftBank, which had acquired Arm in 2016, remained the owner. The Nasdaq listing followed in September 2023.

That listing was an initial public offering. In an IPO, a privately held company sells shares to outside investors. Those shares then trade on a stock exchange. The $51 figure was the offering price, set before trading began. Once trading opened, the share price was set by buyers and sellers on the market.

SoftBank kept a majority stake after the offering. Holding more than half the shares means SoftBank owns more of Arm than all other shareholders combined. Public investors gained a piece of the company, but control stayed with SoftBank.

The ticker ARM is the short code investors use to buy and sell the stock on Nasdaq. Nasdaq is a U.S. exchange based in New York. Arm's shares trade there even though the company's headquarters are in Cambridge, U.K.

The listing changed who owns Arm. It did not change the licensing business at the center of the company. A public listing does add a daily share price. That price gives investors a running measure of how they value the business Haas oversees.

Arm faces competition from two architectures that sit at opposite ends of the licensing spectrum. RISC-V is an open instruction set that companies can use without paying license fees. x86, at the other end, is a closed architecture made by Intel $INTC and AMD $AMD.

RISC-V began as a project at the University of California, Berkeley. Like Arm, it follows the reduced instruction set computing approach, which relies on a small set of simple instructions. The difference lies in ownership. The RISC-V specification is published openly. Any company can design a processor that implements it without signing a license with an architecture owner.

That openness offers a direct alternative to the Arm licensing model. Arm charges companies for the right to use its instruction set and designs. A chipmaker that builds on RISC-V does not pay an architecture owner for the instruction set itself.

Free access to the specification does not mean free chips. A company choosing RISC-V still has to design its own processor cores or obtain finished designs from another supplier. It also has to make sure compilers, operating systems and applications run properly on the result. That engineering work carries real cost. It is also part of what Arm sells when it offers ready-made designs.

x86 presents a different kind of competition. Intel created the architecture, and Intel and AMD are its principal makers. The two companies design and sell their own x86 processors. They do not license designs to a wide pool of customers the way Arm does. Decades of desktop, laptop and server software were written for x86. That installed base keeps the architecture entrenched in PCs and in many data centers.

Arm's position against both rivals rests less on any single chip than on its ecosystem. Operating systems, development tools and applications have been compiled for Arm over many years. Software is built for a specific instruction set. A large library of programs that already runs on Arm makes switching away more costly for device makers.

The same principle works against Arm where x86 holds the advantage. Moving PC or server software to Arm requires recompiling it or running it through translation. The contest among these three architectures turns largely on which software already runs where. It also turns on what it costs a chip designer to change.

The Ripple-associated coin is having a terrible time against Bitcoin during the current crypto market crash.

It's down by a brutal 4.9% in the past 24 hours, according to data from CoinGecko. XRP is priced at around $1.10 at the time of writing.

The weekly losses have climbed to an eye-popping 12.4%.

Bitcoin, on the other hand, is down by just 1.4% over the past 24 hours. BTC is down 4.9% over the past seven days.

This means that XRP has lost nearly 8% of its value against Bitcoin in the past seven days alone.

XRP is also doing much worse compared to Ethereum, which is down by 7.4% over the past week.

Solana has lost 8.6% of its value over the past seven days.

The recent crypto market sell-off has been further fueled by shocking news about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Huang recently confessed to cheating on his wife amid reports that he was having an affair with a businesswoman accused by U.S. intelligence of having connections with Chinese espionage.

Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation into whether or not Nvidia's CEO was the victim of a foreign intelligence operation.
