#5475. From interim CEO to Form 8-K: 10 steps boards take after a sudden CEO exit

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How companies replace a CEO after a sudden exit, from naming an interim chief executive to running a board search and filing the required disclosures

A sudden CEO exit tests a board's preparation more than its judgment. When a chief executive resigns without warning, dies, falls seriously ill or is dismissed, directors rarely have time to deliberate from scratch. The decisions they make in the first days are shaped by work they did, or failed to do, long before.

The stakes reach well beyond the boardroom. Employees want to know who is in charge and whether their projects will survive. Investors want evidence that the company has a plan and that strategy will not drift. Customers and suppliers watch for signs of disruption. For a U.S. public company, regulators also expect prompt disclosure of the change.

Understanding how companies replace a CEO after a sudden exit means looking at several moving parts at once. Boards must put an accountable leader in place quickly. They must decide whether that person is a placeholder or a contender for the permanent job. They also need a process for finding a successor that staff and shareholders find credible.

The tools available to directors are well established. Many boards keep an emergency succession plan alongside their longer-term CEO succession planning. They can promote a sitting executive or ask a director to step into an executive role. They can also bring in an outside search firm to build a slate of candidates. Each route carries tradeoffs between continuity and change.

The legal and financial side matters too. A departing chief executive usually leaves behind an employment agreement, equity awards and possibly severance terms that the board must review. The interim leader and the eventual successor each need a pay package. Public companies must also manage what they say, when they say it and to whom.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of common steps boards take during an emergency CEO succession. They are not a complete or ranked list, and the order is not fixed. In practice, many of these steps run in parallel during the first weeks of a chief executive transition. Each slide explains one step, why boards use it and what it involves.

When a chief executive leaves without warning, the board's first move is usually to name an interim CEO. That appointment gives employees, investors and customers one accountable leader while the search for a permanent successor begins.

A company cannot run for long without someone holding the chief executive's authority. Contracts need signatures and budgets need approval. Managers need a person who can settle disputes and make final calls. Payroll, regulatory obligations and customer commitments do not pause for a leadership change. Naming an interim closes that gap and makes clear who is in charge.

Speed matters outside the company as well. Investors, lenders, customers and suppliers watch a leadership change closely. An announcement that pairs the departure with a named replacement shows that the board has acted. A long silence between the two can invite speculation about why the previous CEO left.

Interim chief executives usually come from one of two places: the board or the senior management team. A director tends to know the company's strategy, finances and governance history. A senior executive brings day-to-day knowledge of operations, staff and customers. The board weighs which of those strengths the business needs most in the moment.

The interim holds the CEO's authority, but the board usually sets the terms of the role through a formal resolution. Those terms cover whom the interim reports to and how long the arrangement is expected to last. Some boards also require their own approval for transactions above a set size.

Some interims state from the start that they will not seek the permanent role. That clarity can let other executives focus on the transition instead of on competing for the top job. Other interims stay open to the position. In those cases, the board may evaluate the interim alongside outside and internal candidates in the formal search.

The title varies from company to company. Some boards use "interim CEO," while others prefer "acting CEO." A few split the job temporarily between two senior executives as co-CEOs. That structure requires the board to spell out which parts of the business each executive oversees and how they resolve disagreements.

Many boards keep a confidential emergency succession plan that names who takes charge if the chief executive leaves without notice. Putting that plan into action lets directors carry out a decision they made in calm conditions, rather than improvising one in a crisis.

An emergency plan usually answers a short list of practical questions. It names the person or people who can step in on short notice. That is often a senior executive or a sitting director. The plan may also say who convenes the board, who speaks for the company and which outside advisers get called first.

This document differs from long-term CEO succession planning. A long-term plan develops candidates over years and prepares for an orderly retirement. An emergency plan deals with a narrower problem: who runs the company tomorrow.

The person named for an emergency is not always the board's preferred permanent successor. Keeping the two roles separate lets the board fill the gap without locking in a long-term choice. It also leaves directors room to run a fuller search later.

Confidentiality is part of the design. Boards generally keep the plan private to avoid signaling who is in line for the top job. A leaked name can unsettle other executives or create expectations the board never meant to set.

A plan works only if it stays current. Executives change roles, get promoted or leave the company. A name on the plan can go stale as a result. Boards review and update these plans periodically, often through the full board or its governance or nominating committee. Directors may also confirm that the named stand-in is still willing and able to serve.

The absence of a plan carries its own cost. Without one, directors must debate who leads while employees, customers and lenders wait for answers. That debate can stretch from hours into days. It also leaves room for internal rivalries to surface during the transition.

After a sudden CEO exit, boards commonly set up a small committee of directors to run the search for a permanent successor. The committee manages the process day to day and brings a recommendation back to the full board, which keeps the final vote.

A full board is too large, and meets too rarely, to run a search on its own. A smaller group can schedule interviews quickly and review candidates in detail. It can also keep sensitive information within a tight circle. Some boards hand the job to an existing nominating and governance committee. Others create an ad hoc committee for this search alone and dissolve it once a new chief executive is in place.

Independent directors usually make up the committee. These are directors who are not company employees and have no material business ties to the company. A lead independent director or a non-executive chair often leads the group. That person typically serves as the main contact for candidates, advisers and the rest of the board.

Membership comes with a conflict rule. A director who wants to be considered for the CEO job generally steps off the committee. The same applies to an interim chief executive who may compete for the permanent role. Keeping candidates off the committee separates the people doing the judging from the people being judged. It also strengthens the board's ability to defend its choice later.

One of the committee's first tasks is to write a candidate profile. This document sets out the experience, skills and leadership qualities the next CEO needs. It reflects the company's strategy, its current challenges and the circumstances of the departure. A profile agreed early gives the committee a fixed standard for comparing candidates.

The committee then sets the process and the timetable. It decides how candidates will be sourced, who interviews them and in what order. It also oversees reference and background checks on finalists. Those checks carry extra weight after an abrupt exit tied to misconduct.

Confidentiality shapes the committee's work. Candidate names, interview notes and deliberations stay inside the committee and its advisers. A leak can cost the company a candidate who is employed elsewhere.

The committee reports to the full board at regular intervals throughout the search. Its decision rights stop short of the appointment itself. It recommends a finalist, and the full board votes to name the new CEO.

Promoting a sitting executive, such as the chief operating officer or chief financial officer, is a common way for a board to fill a sudden CEO vacancy. An insider already knows the business, the people and the numbers. That shortens the time before the company has a working leader.

The appeal starts with familiarity. A COO typically oversees day-to-day operations and already manages many of the teams that report up to the chief executive. A CFO knows the balance sheet, the lenders and the investor base. Either one can step into the top job without a long orientation period.

Existing relationships also count. Customers, suppliers, lenders and major shareholders often already deal with the internal candidate. That prior contact can make the leadership change easier to explain to each of them. Employees may read an internal appointment as a sign that the company's direction is not about to be overturned.

An insider also brings a track record the board has watched directly. Directors have usually seen the executive present at board meetings, defend budgets and respond to problems. That direct view removes some of the guesswork that comes with a candidate the board has met only in interviews.

The tradeoff is change. An executive who helped build the current strategy may be less inclined to question it. If the exit followed poor results or misconduct, a board may judge that an insider is too close to the problem.

Promotion also creates a second vacancy. If the COO becomes chief executive, someone still has to run operations. Companies often fill that seat with an acting appointment from the next management layer. Others split the duties among existing leaders for a period. A company that promotes its CFO must keep financial reporting and internal controls running without a gap. A public company also faces periodic filing deadlines that do not pause for a leadership change.

Readiness is the last test. Running one function is different from running the whole company. A COO may have limited experience facing investors. A CFO may have little exposure to product development or sales. Boards weigh those gaps before deciding. Some pair the new chief executive with an experienced chair or outside adviser. Others set out a defined development plan covering the areas where the executive has less experience.

A board sometimes asks its chair or another director to take on a temporary executive role after a sudden CEO exit. The appeal is speed and familiarity. The cost is that the person meant to supervise management now helps run it.

Directors who step in already know the company's strategy, finances and open risks from board meetings. They have usually worked with the senior team and the largest investors. That background lets them take charge without the orientation an outside hire would need. It also gives the board a leader whose judgment it has already seen up close.

The arrangement takes two main forms. In one, the chair becomes executive chair and takes on operating duties alongside the remaining executives. The CEO seat then stays vacant or goes to an internal officer. In the other, the chair or another director is named interim CEO outright. Both forms place a board member inside management, and both are meant to be temporary.

The tension is built into the board's role. Directors hire, oversee, evaluate and, when necessary, remove the chief executive. A director serving as interim leader ends up overseeing their own work. Questions about performance, pay and strategy become harder for the board to examine at arm's length.

Boards use several safeguards to manage that conflict. A common step is naming a lead independent director, or strengthening the role if one exists. That director runs executive sessions of the non-management directors and acts as a check on the interim leader. Under NYSE and Nasdaq $NDAQ listing standards, audit committee members must be independent. A director who takes on paid executive duties generally steps off the audit committee and often the compensation committee as well.

Time limits are another safeguard. Boards often set a defined term or tie the role to the end of the permanent search. A stated end point tells employees and investors that the arrangement is a bridge, not a new leadership structure. It also keeps a split role from becoming the default.

The board also has to settle whether the director in the executive seat is a candidate for the permanent job. Boards often decide that early. A director who is a contender generally steps away from the search committee's deliberations. A director who is not can say so publicly. That statement tells internal candidates the search is open.

Once a permanent CEO arrives, the director typically returns to a non-executive role. Some boards keep the director on as executive chair for a set period to support the handoff. The board then revisits committee assignments and independence determinations. The specifics depend on the company's bylaws, governance guidelines and listing requirements.

Boards often retain an executive search firm to find and vet candidates for a permanent chief executive. Spencer Stuart, Russell Reynolds Associates, Heidrick & Struggles and Korn Ferry are among the firms that take on this kind of board-level assignment.

The firm works for the board, not for management. It typically reports to the committee of directors that oversees the search. That reporting line matters after a sudden exit, when an interim leader may also be a contender for the permanent job.

A search usually begins with a role specification. The firm and the directors agree on what the next CEO needs to deliver. That brief draws on the company's strategy, its financial position and the circumstances of the previous leader's departure. The resulting document shapes which industries, functions and backgrounds the firm targets.

The firm then maps the market. Consultants identify executives who fit the profile, including sitting CEOs, division heads at larger companies and leaders at competitors. Many of those people are not looking to move. The first approach is therefore typically discreet and framed as a conversation rather than a job offer.

Confidentiality runs in both directions. Candidates employed elsewhere often cannot afford to have their interest become public. The hiring company, for its part, may not want rivals or its own employees to learn who is under consideration before the board decides.

Assessment goes beyond the résumé. Search firms conduct structured interviews and check references. They also examine how a candidate performed in situations similar to the one the company now faces. Some boards ask the firm to evaluate internal candidates as well. That gives directors a common yardstick for comparing insiders and outsiders.

CEO searches are generally run on a retained basis. Under that model, the firm is paid for conducting the search rather than only when a candidate is hired. Fee terms are set in each engagement letter and vary by firm and assignment.

Boards also ask about conflicts. Search firms commonly observe off-limits arrangements that restrict them from recruiting executives out of their own current clients. A large firm's client list can therefore narrow the pool of executives it is able to approach.

The firm's output is a short list of finalists, not a decision. Directors interview the candidates, often over several rounds, and the full board votes on the appointment. The board, not the search firm, remains accountable for the final choice.

The choice between an internal and an external CEO candidate turns on one question: does the company need continuity or a change in direction? No fixed rule settles it. Boards weigh each sudden exit on its own circumstances.

The reason for the departure shapes the answer. A CEO who leaves because of illness or death may leave behind a strategy the board still supports. In that case, a leader who already knows the plan can carry it forward with less disruption.

A dismissal tied to misconduct or weak results points the other way. If the board has lost confidence in the direction of the business, an insider may look too close to the decisions that caused the problem. Directors then have to judge whether a familiar face can credibly signal a break with the past.

Internal candidates come with a known record. Directors have usually watched them present to the board, manage budgets and lead teams. They already understand the company's products, customers and culture. That familiarity lowers the risk of a poor fit. It can also limit fresh thinking.

External candidates offer a different set of tradeoffs. An outsider arrives without loyalty to past strategy or to particular executives. That independence can make it easier to restructure, exit a business line or reset relationships with investors.

The cost is a learning curve. A chief executive hired from outside has to learn the organization, its people and its informal ways of working. Until that happens, acting with confidence on major decisions is harder.

Culture adds another layer to the comparison. A company with a strong internal culture may resist a leader who does not share it. A company whose culture contributed to the exit may need someone willing to challenge it.

The depth of the internal bench also narrows or widens the field. If no executive is ready for the top role, the debate moves quickly toward outside candidates. If several insiders are credible, the board can compare them directly against an external slate rather than choosing one pool at the outset.

Timing is another variable. An insider can usually step into the permanent role faster. A wider external search can take longer. That extends the period the company spends under interim leadership.

A U.S. public company generally must report a CEO departure, and the appointment of an interim or permanent replacement, on SEC Form 8-K under Item 5.02. The standard filing deadline is four business days after the triggering event.

Form 8-K is the Securities and Exchange Commission's current report. Companies file it to tell investors about significant events that occur between quarterly and annual reports. Item 5.02 governs the departure and appointment of directors and certain senior officers. The principal executive officer, usually the CEO, falls within it.

A typical filing states who is leaving, when the change takes effect and who is taking charge. For a newly appointed officer, the disclosure includes background such as age and business experience. It also describes any material compensation arrangement tied to the appointment.

The four-day window is a deadline, not a waiting period. Companies often announce the news by press release on the same day and attach that release to the 8-K as an exhibit. A quick announcement shortens the stretch in which rumors circulate without an official account.

Regulation Fair Disclosure, known as Reg FD, shapes how the news goes out. The rule bars a public company from selectively sharing material nonpublic information with analysts or certain investors ahead of the general public. A sudden change at the top can be material. That pushes companies toward one broad public announcement rather than a round of private calls.

Foreign companies listed in the U.S. as foreign private issuers follow a different route. They generally furnish reports on Form 6-K rather than Form 8-K. Companies without SEC reporting obligations file no 8-K at all. Their boards still decide how and when to inform lenders, investors and staff.

Inside the company, timing is a practical problem. Employees who learn about a leadership change from a headline may question whether anyone is in control. Boards and communications teams therefore tend to schedule an all-staff message close to the public announcement.

That message usually names the person now in charge and explains what happens next. It often confirms that the board has started a search, without committing to a date. Companies generally avoid speculating about the reasons for an exit, especially while lawyers are still reviewing the circumstances.

Customers, suppliers and lenders form a third audience. Sales teams and account managers may need prepared language for their contacts. The board may also need to check whether any financing or commercial agreements require formal notice of a leadership change.

After a sudden CEO exit, the board reviews the departing executive's employment agreement to settle severance, equity awards, clawback rights and any non-compete. It also sets pay for the interim leader and, later, for the permanent successor.

The compensation committee usually leads this work, often with outside legal counsel. Its first task is to establish what the contract actually says. Employment agreements differ from company to company. The signed documents set the baseline, and departing from them usually means negotiating new terms with the former executive.

The reason for the departure shapes almost every term. Chief executive agreements commonly treat a termination "for cause" differently from one "without cause." A resignation for "good reason," as the contract defines it, often carries the same benefits as a dismissal without cause. Death and disability usually have their own provisions. A board that labels an exit incorrectly can invite a legal dispute with the former executive.

Equity awards are often the largest piece of value at stake. Unvested stock options and restricted shares may be forfeited, continue to vest or vest immediately. The outcome depends on the equity plan and the individual award agreements. Performance-based awards can carry separate rules tied to whether targets are met after the executive leaves.

Clawback provisions let a company recover pay that should not have been awarded. In the U.S., stock exchange listing standards adopted under SEC Rule 10D-1 require a clawback policy. That policy must cover erroneously awarded incentive pay after an accounting restatement. Some company policies reach further and cover misconduct.

Restrictive covenants come next. These can include non-compete, non-solicitation and confidentiality clauses. Whether a non-compete can be enforced depends on the jurisdiction. The board's lawyers assess that question for each case.

Many departures end in a negotiated separation agreement. In exchange for severance, the former CEO typically signs a release of legal claims against the company. The agreement may also cover a short transition period, a consulting arrangement or a mutual non-disparagement clause.

The committee then turns to the interim leader. An executive who steps up temporarily may receive added cash pay, a one-time equity grant or both. Those terms reflect the extra duties and the uncertainty of a temporary role. The permanent successor's package is negotiated later, as part of the search itself.

Public companies also face scrutiny of the payout. U.S. proxy statements describe the potential payments named executive officers would receive on termination. Shareholders can compare that disclosure with what the departing CEO actually receives.

During a CEO transition, an interim leader usually keeps strategy steady, holds the senior team together and leaves major long-term bets for the permanent chief executive. Retention arrangements for key executives are a common tool for limiting departures while the search runs.

A sudden exit leaves a gap at the top, and the people just below it often feel the uncertainty first. Senior executives may wonder whether the next CEO will keep them, reshape their roles or bring in a new team. Some may hear from recruiters or competitors during this period. Losing several leaders at once would add to the disruption the board is trying to contain.

The interim CEO's job is partly to answer that uncertainty. An interim leader often meets early with each member of the executive team to clarify reporting lines and decision rights. Those conversations confirm which projects continue and who owns them. That clarity lets managers keep running their units rather than wait for direction.

Retention pay is another lever. A board may offer selected executives cash bonuses or additional equity. These awards pay out only if the person stays through the transition or for a set period after it. The terms vary by company and by individual. The aim is to give critical leaders a concrete reason to stay until the new CEO is in place.

On strategy, interim leaders typically focus on carrying out the existing plan. They tend to defer decisions that would bind the next CEO for years. Examples include large acquisitions, major restructurings or a shift in the company's core direction. Routine operations, approved budgets and customer commitments continue. Postponing the biggest choices preserves options for whoever takes the permanent role.

That caution has limits. A business facing a crisis, a regulatory deadline or a fast-moving competitor cannot simply pause. In those cases the board and the interim leader decide which time-sensitive matters must move forward. The board often stays more involved than usual while those decisions are made.

The final stage is the handoff. Once the permanent CEO is named, the interim leader typically briefs the successor on open issues, pending decisions and the state of the executive team. An interim drawn from management may return to a previous role or leave the company. An interim drawn from the board may go back to serving as a director. The new chief executive then sets the longer-term direction. That includes any changes to the leadership team or strategy that the transition period left open.

#5474. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

See the full list of 2026 grant recipients here.

#5472. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5471. How MLB's qualifying offer works, from salary formula to pick compensation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The MLB qualifying offer ties a one-year salary to draft pick compensation, and these 10 explainers cover who gets it, what it pays and what happens when players decline

A club about to lose a free agent can turn his departure into draft pick compensation. The price of that option is the risk that he accepts a one-year salary instead. For the 2023-24 offseason, that salary was $20.325 million. The mechanism behind the trade-off is the MLB qualifying offer, a one-year contract a team can extend to its own impending free agent.

The offer cuts both ways. A club collects compensation only if the player declines and signs with another team. If he accepts, the club owes him the one-year salary. A player who declines gives up a guaranteed salary to test the open market. He also enters that market carrying a cost for any rival club that signs him.

The system dates to the 2012 collective bargaining agreement between the league and its players. It replaced the older Type A and Type B classifications, which relied on player rankings. The salary is not negotiated player by player. It is pegged to the average salary of the 125 highest-paid players in the majors and recalculated every offseason. That formula ties the offer to the top of the market rather than to any one player's performance.

A player generally must spend the full season with the same club to be eligible. A player traded midseason is not eligible. A player can also receive an offer only once in his career. When a player declines and signs elsewhere, the signing club gives up draft picks and, in some cases, international bonus pool space. The exact cost depends on whether the clubs involved receive revenue-sharing money or pay the luxury tax. The size of the contract also matters.

Those costs have shaped individual free agencies. Kyle Lohse, a free agent after 2012, remained unsigned into spring training 2013. The draft pick cost attached to him was a factor. Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales each turned down the 2013 offer of $14.1 million. Both signed in June 2014, after the draft, when the pick compensation no longer applied. Drew went to the Red Sox, and Morales went to the Twins.

The 10 slides below cover the offer piece by piece, from its definition and salary formula to eligibility, acceptance, departure and the compensation rules.

The MLB qualifying offer is a one-year contract that a team may extend to one of its own players who is about to become a free agent. The player then chooses between two paths: accept the deal and stay, or decline it and test the open market.

The offer is optional. A club decides player by player whether to make it. Nothing requires a team to extend one to any departing free agent.

The arrangement exists to give clubs something back when a player leaves. If the player turns the offer down and then signs with a different team, his former club receives draft pick compensation.

That conditional link sits at the center of the system. Declining alone does not trigger anything for the original club. Compensation depends on whether the player goes on to sign with another team, not on the rejection itself.

For the player, the offer is a fallback and a decision point at once. Accepting locks in a one-year salary with his current club. Declining keeps every other option open. It also attaches a cost in draft selections to any other team that signs him.

For the team, the calculation runs the other way. Making the offer creates a path to compensation if the player walks. It also carries the possibility that he says yes. In that case, the club is committed to a one-year salary it chose to put on the table.

The qualifying offer arrived with the 2012 collective bargaining agreement. It took the place of an older approach to free agent compensation that sorted players into Type A and Type B classes based on rankings.

The newer system ties compensation to a team's decision to make an offer, rather than to where a player sat in a ranking. A player becomes subject to compensation because his club offered him the one-year deal and he turned it down.

The qualifying offer salary equals the average salary of MLB's 125 highest-paid players. The league recalculates that average every offseason.

The player receiving the offer has no effect on the amount. A team cannot lower it for a modestly paid player or raise it for a star. Every qualifying offer made in a given offseason carries the same one-year salary.

The figure is also the same for every club. A team with a small payroll and a team with a large one face an identical number. That single salary takes up a bigger share of a smaller budget. The same offer can therefore be a heavier commitment for one club than for another.

That makes the offer a fixed price rather than a negotiated contract. A club considering one is not bargaining over terms. It is deciding whether the player is worth that single figure for one more season.

A fixed price also means a club has to be prepared to pay all of it. A player who accepts receives the full amount, whatever he earned the year before.

The benchmark draws on the highest salaries in the sport. When the largest contracts rise, the average rises with them. When pay at the top levels off, the figure follows.

Because it is an average across 125 salaries, no single contract sets the figure. One record-setting deal shifts the average by only a fraction of that deal's size. Broad movement across many top contracts is what moves the number.

The yearly recalculation means the price can change from one winter to the next. A club weighing an offer in one offseason may face a different figure than a club weighing a similar player a year earlier.

For a player, the formula provides a known number. He can compare that guaranteed one-year salary with the offers he expects from other clubs before he responds.

A qualifying offer can go only to a club's own impending free agent. That player generally must have spent the entire season with the same club. A player who changes teams in a midseason trade is not eligible to receive one.

Both conditions have to be met. The first is contract status. The offer is meant for a player whose deal is ending and who is about to reach the open market. A player still under contract for the following season falls outside the system, no matter how long he has been with his club.

The second condition is tenure. The rule generally ties eligibility to a full season with one organization. The club extending the offer has to be the club the player spent the whole year with.

A midseason trade breaks that link. A pending free agent who is dealt during the season cannot receive a qualifying offer from his new team. His old team cannot make one either. He is no longer its own free agent when the offseason arrives.

That limit carries over to trades of pending free agents. A club that acquires one during the season gets his play for the rest of that year. It does not gain the option of making him a qualifying offer once the season ends. The club that trades him away loses that option as well.

Eligibility also decides whether draft pick compensation is possible. Compensation goes only to a club whose offer was declined and whose player then signed with another team. A player who was never eligible for an offer carries no such cost. The club that signs him does not forfeit draft selections under this mechanism.

Eligibility does not oblige a team to act. A club may extend the offer to an eligible player. It may also let him leave without one, in which case no draft pick compensation follows.

A Major League Baseball player can receive a qualifying offer only once in his career. After a club makes him that one-year offer, no team can make him another, whether he accepted it or turned it down.

The limit follows the player, not the club that made the offer. It does not reset when he changes teams. A club that signs him later cannot extend a fresh offer to a player who has already had one.

The limit shapes his later free agency. Draft pick compensation for a departing free agent flows only through a declined qualifying offer. A player who can no longer receive one carries no pick cost the next time he hits the open market.

A club that wants to sign him at that point does not give up draft picks or international bonus pool space to do it. His former club, in turn, cannot collect compensation when he leaves.

The rule applies to players who accept. An accepted offer is a one-year contract. The player can return to free agency a season later. When he does, his club cannot issue a second offer.

Joc Pederson and Martin Perez accepted offers in the 2022 offseason, as did Hyun-Jin Ryu in 2019 and Brandon Belt in 2021. Each of those acceptances used up that player's single offer.

The same limit covers players who decline. Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales both turned their offers down. Having received one, neither could be given another later in his career.

The limit also holds as the offer's value climbs. A player who received an offer at an earlier, lower amount cannot be tagged again when the figure is higher.

For a player, the compensation attached to his name is a one-time event. For a club, making the offer is a single chance to tie draft pick compensation to that player's departure.

The MLB qualifying offer was worth $13.3 million in 2012, the year the system began under that year's collective bargaining agreement. By the 2023-24 offseason, the figure had climbed to $20.325 million.

Two more figures mark points along the way. The offer was $14.1 million in 2013. For the 2022-23 offseason, it was $19.65 million.

Those four numbers are snapshots rather than a full year-by-year record. Two sit at the start of the system, in its first two years. The other two come from back-to-back offseasons much later. Read in order, each figure is higher than the one before it.

The direction follows from how the number is set. The offer is an average of top salaries, so it moves when that group of salaries moves. Bigger contracts at the high end of the market push the next offer up. A quiet offseason for top-end deals would hold the figure down. The number reflects where elite pay stood in a given offseason. It is not a reward tied to any single player.

The same sum applied to every club that made a qualifying offer in a given offseason. A team with a modest payroll faced the same one-year figure as a team with a large one. That fixed figure takes up a bigger share of a smaller payroll than of a larger one.

A higher number changes what is at stake on both sides. It means a larger guaranteed salary for any player who accepts. It also means a larger one-year bill for the club that made the offer.

That raises the bar for extending an offer. A club has to be willing to pay the full figure for one season if the player says yes. A player weighing the offer compares that one-year sum with what he expects to find on the open market. The higher the figure, the more the guaranteed side of that comparison is worth.

A player who accepts the qualifying offer signs a one-year contract with his current club at that offseason's set salary. He skips the open market, and the club keeps him for one more season instead of collecting draft pick compensation.

Joc Pederson and Martin Perez both took that route in the 2022 offseason. Each accepted $19.65 million, the qualifying offer figure for the 2022-23 offseason. Two players signed at an identical salary in the same winter because the offer carries one price for everyone who receives it that year.

Hyun-Jin Ryu accepted a qualifying offer worth $17.8 million in 2019. Brandon Belt accepted $18.4 million in 2021. Both figures sit below the $19.65 million that Pederson and Perez took. The amount a player accepts depends on the year he receives the offer, not on his own salary history.

Acceptance also changes what happens on the club side. Draft pick compensation exists only when a player declines and then signs with another team. Once a player accepts, that path closes. His club receives no extra draft selection. No rival club forfeits picks or international bonus pool space to sign him.

What the club gets instead is another season of the player's services at a fixed, known price. The deal covers one year only, with no multiyear commitment attached to the offer itself.

For the player, accepting means trading the uncertainty of free agency for a guaranteed salary. He gives up the chance to test what other clubs would pay him. In return, he avoids a market where any signing team would have to give up draft picks to land him.

The choice also carries a career-long consequence. A player can receive a qualifying offer only once in his career, and a player who accepts has used that one offer. When his one-year deal ends, his club cannot attach a second qualifying offer to him. He reaches his next free agency without that draft pick cost following him.

A player who turns down the qualifying offer becomes a free agent on the open market. His former club receives draft pick compensation only if he signs with a different team.

The decline alone earns the original club nothing. Compensation depends entirely on where the player lands. If no other club signs him, no picks change hands.

Turning down the offer means walking away from a guaranteed one-year salary. In exchange, the player can negotiate terms with any club in the league.

That single trigger shapes the calculation for the club that made the offer. Extending it places a price on the player's departure. The club collects that price only when a rival team decides to sign him.

The decline also travels with the player. Any team weighing a contract with him has to account for what it would give up to sign him. The size of that cost varies from club to club.

Each side makes its own trade-off. The player exchanges a guaranteed salary for access to the open market. The original club exchanges its hold on the player for the possibility of draft picks. The signing club gives up some of its draft capital to add him.

When a player turns down a qualifying offer and signs with a new team, that new team gives up draft picks. In some cases it also surrenders international bonus pool space. The size of that cost depends on whether the clubs involved receive revenue sharing or pay the luxury tax, and on how large the contract is.

The forfeiture is one half of an exchange. The club that made the offer receives draft pick compensation, but only if the player signs with a different organization. If he never signs elsewhere, no picks move in either direction.

Three variables shape the exchange. The first is whether a club is a revenue-sharing recipient. The second is whether a club is a luxury-tax payer. Both questions apply to each club in the transaction — the team that loses the player and the team that signs him. The third variable is the size of the contract the player signs.

Those factors mean the price of signing a player who declined a qualifying offer is not uniform across MLB. Two clubs pursuing the same free agent can face different forfeitures based on their financial standing. The compensation that flows back to the team that lost him also depends on that club's own status.

None of the three variables is a direct measure of the player's performance. Two describe the finances of the clubs involved. The third reflects the deal he signs.

The possible loss of international bonus pool space means the penalty for some signings reaches beyond the draft. A single free-agent signing can draw down two separate resources at once.

For a front office, the cost of a free agent tied to a declined offer has two parts. One is the contract itself. The other is the picks, and in some cases the bonus pool space, that the club gives up to sign him. The size of that contract can also change the second part.

Kyle Lohse, Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales are three examples of how draft pick compensation can weigh on a free agent's market. All three stayed unsigned for long stretches while pick compensation was attached to them.

Lohse reached free agency after the 2012 season. He remained unsigned into spring training in 2013. The draft picks a new club would have had to surrender to sign him were a factor in that wait.

Drew and Morales went through a similar wait. Both declined the 2013 qualifying offer of $14.1 million and entered the open market.

Both players signed in June 2014. By then the draft had already taken place. The pick compensation tied to each of them no longer applied. A club could add either player without forfeiting a draft selection.

Drew signed with the Boston Red Sox. Morales signed with the Minnesota Twins.

In all three cases, the cost sat with the club doing the signing. Any team that wanted Lohse, Drew or Morales before the draft would have given up draft selections to get him. Their former clubs stood to collect compensation only if each player signed somewhere else.

That cost fell on the buyer, but it still shaped each player's options. A club weighing a contract for one of them had to count the picks it would lose alongside the salary it would pay. For Lohse, that added cost was a factor in a wait that stretched into spring training.

The Drew and Morales signings show the other side of that calculation. Once the draft passed, the compensation attached to them ended, and the extra cost to a signing club went with it.

The cases also show the risk a player takes by saying no. Declining means giving up a guaranteed one-year salary for an uncertain market. Drew and Morales each passed on $14.1 million and then spent months without a contract.

The 2012 collective bargaining agreement replaced MLB's old Type A and Type B free agent classes with the qualifying offer. Compensation stopped hinging on where a player ranked and started hinging on a one-year salary offer he could accept or decline.

Under the earlier system, a player's class came from his place in player rankings. Compensation followed from that classification. The qualifying offer took rankings out of the equation.

In their place, the 2012 agreement put two decisions. The club makes one, and the player makes the other.

The club decides first whether to extend a one-year contract to its own impending free agent. A club that makes no offer has no claim to compensation if that player leaves. Under the new structure, compensation starts with an action the club takes, not with a label attached to the player.

The player then chooses between that guaranteed one-year salary and a search for a deal on the open market. His answer, not his ranking, determines whether compensation comes into play at all.

The offer is not tailored to the individual. In a given offseason, every club extending one offers the same amount. A league-wide salary formula sets that figure, not the player's own record. Two players with very different track records face the same number.

That uniform price turns the question of a player's value into a test both sides answer. A club weighing an offer has to decide whether the player is worth that salary for one season. A player weighing it has to decide whether the open market will pay him more than that.

That design puts a price on the club's choice. A team that extends the offer must be ready to pay the full one-year salary if the player accepts. If he declines, that salary commitment falls away.

The framework built in 2012 remained in place through the 2023-24 offseason.

#5470. Data center developers brace for new reality as election backlash sinks in

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:25 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Data center developers already knew they had a public relations problem. This month’s midterm elections showed how much of a political problem it has become.

Voters approved data center restrictions in 44 of 45 local measures across a dozen states. Candidates who support stronger regulation of the facilities won 32 of the 34 gubernatorial races called so far. And political campaigns reportedly spent more than $380 million on TV ads referencing data centers, according to the Associated Press.

The results capped a year of accelerating resistance as tech giants plan to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on new facilities.

So what comes next? More outreach, more transparency and the expectation that states and local governments will pass data center rules, said leaders in the Pacific Northwest.

“We’ve been working and adapting our approach to meet the moment,” said John Wilson, chief financial officer of Sabey Data Centers, in an interview. “There used to be a time where we would say that our track record could speak for itself, and that’s clearly no longer the case.”

Communities nationwide have raised concerns about the facilities’ effect on rising electric bills, their water use for cooling electronics and the noise they generate.

Broader fears about artificial intelligence are also stoking the pushback, including worries that it will replace workers and appropriate human-created content, and that it can provide erroneous information, foster unhealthy relationships with users, or facilitate scams or terrorist attacks.

A renewed effort to regulate data centers is expected in January in Washington state — home to the headquarters of Sabey, Microsoft and Amazon.

Earlier this year, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, pushed legislation that included ratepayer protections, transparency on environmental impacts and clean energy requirements. Microsoft and the national Data Center Coalition opposed the bill, which failed.

“It’s going to be a very tech-heavy session,” Doglio said.

Before voters weighed in this month, tech companies launched efforts to assuage public fears.

In January, Microsoft released its “Community First AI Infrastructure” initiative, which includes promises to pay the company’s full power costs, reject local property tax breaks, replenish more water than it uses, train local workers and fund AI education and community programs.

Last month, Amazon announced its “Built Together” program, pledging to invest $1 billion over five years in the U.S. communities where it operates data centers, including support for education and civic projects. The initiative offers similar commitments to Microsoft’s on transparency and covering its energy costs.

Wilson said Sabey also works with communities to understand and meet their needs. When a proposed campus in Indianapolis triggered significant pushback, the company brought community members to Quincy, a central Washington data center hub, to tour a Sabey facility and hear from locals about their experience.

“It requires a lot of patience. It requires a lot of transparency in our communication,” Wilson said. Sabey’s Decatur Technology Park in Indianapolis is moving ahead, and the company aims to bring it online in 2030.

But the even bigger challenge now is statewide moratoriums and data center bans — a scale of resistance that is difficult to address even when there is local support.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. Umatilla, where Sabey is developing its first Oregon campus, declared a local state of emergency over the potential loss of investment and revenue, the Oregon Capital Chronicle reported.

Even with the surge in resistance, “we’ve been able to find our way through on every project that we’ve had,” Wilson said. “I’m knocking on wood as I say that.”

Corporate commitments alone may no longer be enough to win public confidence, said Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, in a GeekWire interview. Communities increasingly want laws requiring all data center developers to build responsibly — a shift he called a “watershed” moment, “but one we anticipated.”

“[P]eople want to see everyone who builds a data center do it in a responsible way,” Smith added, “and they feel that the only way that one can obtain that result is to have some new laws that are put in place.”

Come next year, that could include Washington and impact local tech giants, Sabey and others. Baxtel, a data center industry research firm, lists 29 Microsoft facilities operating in Washington and four under construction, with Sabey operating eight facilities.

Amazon plans to build its first large-scale data centers in Washington, with proposed campuses in Walla Walla County and the Tri-Cities. Amazon did not respond to repeated requests for comment on this story.

Doglio said the next version of her bill will be more stringent. “We have to have a strong bill,” she said, adding that the public and members of her party are calling for it. Microsoft did not publicly specify which provisions triggered its opposition to the previous bill.

Wilson hopes any legislation, in Washington or elsewhere, allows flexibility and recognizes that data centers vary widely in size, impact and application. Sabey provides data center space and infrastructure for customers ranging from major cloud companies to corporations and community organizations.

“Describing all data centers as one thing is just not accurate,” Wilson said, “and it doesn’t understand the realities of the industry itself.”

Smith expressed optimism that U.S. lawmakers can find a middle ground that meets the needs of communities and tech companies.

“There’s plenty of room to draft laws that enable people to go forward and build responsible data centers without chilling the economic contributions these data centers make, especially to local communities,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5469. Nvidia Hit With $5.4 Million Leveraged Short on Hyperliquid

An enigmatic crypto whale has opened a giant leveraged short position in Nvidia (NVDA) on the decentralized trading exchange Hyperliquid amid the bombshell controversy surrounding the chipmaker's CEO, Jensen Huang.

As reported by blockchain analytics firm Lookonchain, a mysterious trader opened a 10x leveraged short position involving 30,000 NVDA contracts, equivalent to around $5.44 million.

The whale's massive bearish trade emerged soon after the Nvidia CEO publicly admitted to infidelity in the wake of explosive reports alleging that Jensen Huang was a target of Chinese intelligence.

The mysterious trader reportedly opened the position at around $181.33 per contract. With 10x leverage, the whale would need to deposit about $544,000 as initial collateral to control a $5.44 million position.

The shocking development comes as Nvidia faces one of the gravest controversies surrounding its leadership in recent times.

On Sunday, Nov. 8, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a startling confession to employees about being unfaithful to his wife.

The revelation comes after The New York Times broke a bombshell story about Jensen Huang and his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who was formerly employed by Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company.

The Times noted that U.S. intelligence believes Alice Huang was enlisted by China's Ministry of State Security to spy on the Nvidia CEO.

The publication reported that a classified intelligence memo sent to top Trump administration officials said Beijing was looking to collect information on U.S. artificial intelligence technology.

Moreover, the purported intelligence operation was reportedly trying to sway Nvidia's stance on limiting the sale of its top AI chips to China.

Meanwhile, Megaspeed, a buyer of Nvidia's high-end chips, has also drawn the attention of U.S. authorities amid suspicions that AI chips restricted by the U.S. government might end up in China.

Nonetheless, the allegations of espionage have yet to be proven in the public domain.

Nvidia-related securities suffered substantial losses ahead of the U.S. market open following the scandal.

Nvidia's stock has fallen by around 8.8% over the past five trading sessions, although it rebounded by 2.8% on Friday.
