#5468. From Palestine to Gibraltar, 10 cases of home games played elsewhere

Free daily briefing on global business news.

National teams playing home games abroad usually face war, travel limits or failed stadium checks, and these 10 cases from football and cricket show why

A home game is a line on a fixture list before it is a place on a map. The team named first usually wears its first-choice kit and uses the home dressing room. Nothing in that arrangement requires the match to be played inside the team's own borders. When a country cannot host, the fixture moves abroad and keeps its home label.

That gap between label and location explains why national teams playing home games abroad have become a recurring feature of international sport.

The decision rarely rests with the team alone. In football, FIFA and continental confederations such as UEFA set rules on where competitive internationals may be staged. Those rules cover security, stadium inspections and licensing. In cricket, a home board needs visiting teams willing to tour. Without them, it must find another venue.

Three causes recur across these cases. The first is war or a security threat serious enough that teams, officials and fans cannot be protected. The second is restricted movement, which can stop players from reaching a venue or crossing borders to train together. The third is infrastructure. A stadium can fail an inspection or lack the license a competition demands, even in a country at peace.

The 10 cases that follow are a selection, not a complete list. Nine come from international football and one from cricket. They cover Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, the Caribbean and Central and South Asia. Some relocations followed a single event, such as the 2009 attack on the Sri Lanka team bus in Lahore. Others grew out of long-running conflict or security restrictions, as in Libya and Iraq. Gibraltar's case had nothing to do with security.

A relocated home match still counts as a home fixture in the competition's records. What changes is the setting. The team plays on a pitch abroad, and the size of its crowd depends on which supporters can travel or live nearby. Several hosts in this selection are neighbors, such as Jordan for Palestine, Tunisia for Libya and Tajikistan for Afghanistan. Others sit farther away, such as Malaysia for Syria and Hungary for Israel.

Taken together, the cases show a fixture list responding to events outside sport: conflict, restricted movement and stadium standards.

Palestine's national football team has repeatedly staged home fixtures outside Palestine because of movement and security restrictions. Jordan has hosted some of those matches at the Amman International Stadium.

The team also has a home venue inside the West Bank. The Faisal Al-Husseini International Stadium in Al-Ram has hosted Palestine home matches as well.

That gives Palestine two kinds of home ground. One sits in Palestinian territory. The other is in Amman, the Jordanian capital, on the far side of an international border.

A fixture at Al-Ram is a home game in both senses. The town lies in the West Bank. A match there is played on Palestinian soil.

A fixture in Amman is a home game on the schedule only. Palestine is still the named host. The stadium, however, is in another country.

The venue for a Palestine home match is therefore not settled by geography alone. Over the years, the team's home fixtures have been played both in the West Bank and in Jordan.

Movement restrictions bear on who can reach a ground. A home international needs players, coaching staff, match officials and the visiting team to arrive and leave on schedule. Security restrictions add a second test: whether the host can protect everyone inside the stadium. When those conditions cannot be met in the West Bank, Amman provides a stadium across the border.

Ukraine could not play competitive home matches on its own soil after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. In Euro 2024 qualifying, its home game against England was played in Wrocław, Poland. Its home game against Italy was played in Leverkusen, Germany.

The obstacle was security, not facilities. Ukraine had stadiums built to international standards, including Kyiv's Olimpiyskiy Stadium, which hosted the Euro 2012 final. Air-raid alerts and missile strikes ruled out staging a fixture with visiting players, officials and fans inside the country.

Wrocław sits in southwestern Poland, near the German and Czech borders. It was one of the host cities when Poland and Ukraine jointly staged Euro 2012. Its stadium was built for that tournament and already met UEFA standards.

Leverkusen is a city in the western German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. It is home to the Bundesliga club Bayer Leverkusen. The match against Italy was played at the BayArena, the club's ground. Germany was also the host of Euro 2024, the tournament Ukraine was trying to reach.

Ukraine did reach those finals, though not through its qualifying group. It advanced through the playoffs and then played its tournament matches in Germany.

The displacement extended beyond the national team. Ukrainian clubs could not host European ties at home either. Shakhtar Donetsk had already left Donetsk after fighting began in eastern Ukraine in 2014. After the full-scale invasion, it staged Champions League home matches in Warsaw and later in Hamburg.

Domestic football took a different route. The Ukrainian Premier League restarted in August 2022. Matches were played behind closed doors and halted when air-raid sirens sounded. That kept a league running inside the country while the national team relied on borrowed venues abroad.

The invasion also changed the fixture list for the other side of the conflict. FIFA and UEFA suspended Russia's national teams and clubs from their competitions in February 2022. Russia was left without competitive international fixtures, home or away.

Haiti played its home matches in 2026 World Cup qualifying in Curaçao rather than in Haiti. Gang violence at home ruled out hosting, and the Ergilio Hato Stadium in Willemstad served as the team's stand-in home ground.

The move took the national team away from its usual base. Haiti has traditionally played home internationals at the Stade Sylvio Cator in Port-au-Prince, the capital. Armed gangs have taken control of large parts of Port-au-Prince in recent years. The violence has displaced residents, shut businesses and forced repeated closures of the city's international airport.

The Ergilio Hato Stadium is Curaçao's national stadium and the home ground of Curaçao's own national team. It is named after Ergilio Hato, a goalkeeper from the island.

Curaçao is a small island in the southern Caribbean, off the coast of Venezuela. It is a constituent country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and Willemstad is its capital. Like Haiti, Curaçao belongs to CONCACAF, the confederation that governs football in North America, Central America and the Caribbean. CONCACAF organizes World Cup qualifying for the region.

The arrangement left Haiti without a guaranteed home crowd. Supporters based in Haiti had to leave the country to watch matches billed as Haiti home games.

The 2026 tournament is the first World Cup to feature 48 teams, up from 32. The U.S., Canada and Mexico co-host it, and all three qualify automatically. CONCACAF received six direct places, including the three hosts' automatic spots. The region also received two places in an intercontinental playoff. That expansion opened more routes to the finals for teams such as Haiti.

Haiti's only World Cup finals appearance before the 2026 cycle came in 1974, in West Germany. At that tournament, Emmanuel Sanon scored against Italy, ending goalkeeper Dino Zoff's long run of international minutes without conceding. Sanon also scored against Argentina, giving him both of Haiti's goals at the finals.

Syria played its home leg of the 2018 World Cup Asian qualifying playoff against Australia in Malaysia. The match was staged at the Hang Jebat Stadium in Malacca and finished 1-1.

Syria's civil war, which began in 2011, left the country unable to host international football. Its national team had to find venues abroad for competitive home matches. It also played its other home matches in that final qualifying round outside Syria.

The playoff was a two-legged tie between the third-placed teams from the two groups in Asia's final qualifying round. Australia finished third in one group. Syria finished third in the other, which also included Iran and South Korea. Away goals would break a tie on aggregate. The winner moved on to an intercontinental playoff for a place at the tournament in Russia.

Syria clinched third place on the final matchday. Omar Al Somah scored a late equalizer in a 2-2 draw away to Iran. The country had never qualified for a World Cup. The playoff left its team two rounds from a first appearance.

Malacca is a historic port city on Malaysia's west coast, southeast of Kuala Lumpur. The Hang Jebat Stadium takes its name from a warrior in Malay legend. Hosting there meant the Syrian squad traveled to Southeast Asia for a fixture listed as its own.

Robbie Kruse put Australia ahead in Malacca. Omar Kharbin equalized for Syria with a late penalty. The result left the tie level but gave Australia an away goal heading into the second leg in Sydney.

Australia won that match 2-1 after extra time. Tim Cahill scored both Australian goals. Al Somah gave Syria an early lead and later hit the post with a free kick in extra time. A goal there would have put Syria through on away goals.

Australia went on to beat Honduras in the intercontinental playoff and qualified for the 2018 World Cup. Syria's campaign ended in Sydney.

Libya's national football team has played home matches in neighboring Tunisia. Years of conflict left Libya without venues approved to stage international fixtures.

Those games keep their Libyan label. Libya is still listed as the home side, even with the match played across the border.

The conflict traces back to the 2011 uprising that ended Muammar Gaddafi's rule. Rival armed groups and competing administrations later fought for control of the country.

Venue approval decides where a competitive international can be played. A stadium must be cleared before it can host one. Libya's grounds lacked that clearance during the years of conflict. The national team needed a host abroad.

Tunisia lies along Libya's western border. Its stadiums gave the team a home base in North Africa.

The disruption reached beyond single fixtures. Libya had been chosen to host the 2017 Africa Cup of Nations. The tournament was moved because of the security situation. Gabon staged it instead.

The same conditions that sent individual matches to Tunisia also cost Libya a full continental tournament.

Afghanistan's national football team has played home matches in Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan. Security conditions inside Afghanistan kept the country from hosting those games.

The obstacle was security, not the condition of a stadium. A pitch that meets the regulations is only part of what a competitive international requires. Visiting players, referees and spectators must also be able to travel to the venue and stay there safely.

Dushanbe sits across the border from Afghanistan. Tajikistan shares a frontier with northern Afghanistan, and much of it follows the Panj River, one of the headwaters of the Amu Darya.

The Afghanistan Football Federation runs the national team. It belongs to FIFA and to the Asian Football Confederation. Those two bodies set the rules on where the team's competitive matches may be staged.

A match in Dushanbe still counts as an Afghanistan home fixture in the competition's records.

Pakistan's national cricket team played its home international series in the United Arab Emirates for years after gunmen attacked the Sri Lanka team bus in Lahore in March 2009. Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Sharjah became its main home venues.

The attack took place on March 3, 2009. The Sri Lankan squad was traveling to the Gaddafi Stadium for the third day of a Test match against Pakistan. Several Sri Lankan players were wounded. Pakistani police officers escorting the convoy were among those killed.

International sides stopped touring Pakistan after the shooting. Visiting boards declined to send teams, which left Pakistan with no opponents willing to play on its soil.

The fallout reached beyond bilateral tours. The International Cricket Council removed Pakistan as a co-host of the 2011 Cricket World Cup. The tournament went ahead in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

The UAE already had grounds built for international cricket. The International Cricket Council has had its headquarters in Dubai since 2005. The Emirates are also home to large South Asian expatriate communities, including many Pakistanis.

Each of the three venues has its own history. Sharjah Cricket Stadium staged one-day international tournaments from the 1980s and has hosted more one-day internationals than any other ground. Sheikh Zayed Cricket Stadium in Abu Dhabi opened in 2004. The Dubai International Cricket Stadium, in Dubai Sports City, opened in 2009.

The UAE was not Pakistan's only stand-in host. In 2010, Pakistan staged a two-Test home series against Australia in England. Lord's and Headingley hosted the two Tests.

Domestic cricket moved to the Gulf too. The Pakistan Super League, the country's professional Twenty20 competition, launched in 2016 with its first season played in the UAE.

Cricket relocations differ from football ones in a practical way. A cricket tour often runs for several weeks and can include Tests, one-day internationals and Twenty20 internationals. That means the stand-in country hosts an entire visiting tour, not a single match night.

Gibraltar played home qualifiers at the Estádio Algarve in Portugal because its own ground, the Victoria Stadium, did not meet UEFA's requirements for some competitive internationals. The move had nothing to do with war or security. It came down to whether a venue passed the governing body's standards.

Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory on the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula. It joined UEFA as a full member in 2013. That gave its national team a place in European qualifying competitions. Gibraltar later became a FIFA member in 2016, which opened World Cup qualifying as well. Membership did not come with a stadium ready for every fixture those competitions involve.

UEFA sets infrastructure rules for the venues used in its competitions. Its Stadium Infrastructure Regulations grade grounds into categories. The rules cover areas such as seating, floodlighting, media facilities and the playing surface. A ground that falls short of the required level cannot stage the matches those rules apply to. That holds even if it hosts regular domestic football.

The Victoria Stadium is Gibraltar's main football ground. It sits beside Gibraltar International Airport, on a territory where flat land is scarce. It also stages the territory's domestic league matches.

Portugal provided the alternative. The Estádio Algarve stands between the cities of Faro and Loulé in the country's southern Algarve region. It was built as a host venue for Euro 2004, the European Championship that Portugal staged that year. UEFA accepted it for Gibraltar's qualifiers, and the team played its home fixtures there.

The arrangement meant Gibraltar's supporters had to leave the territory to watch a home match. Spain is the only country that shares a land border with Gibraltar. Portugal does not border it at all. The overland route to the Algarve therefore crosses Spain before reaching the Portuguese border.

For Gibraltar, a home qualifier meant a trip through one country to play in another.

Israel played its home UEFA Nations League matches in Hungary in autumn 2024. The fixtures moved because UEFA matches could not be played safely in Israel during the conflict.

UEFA organizes the Nations League and sets the conditions for its matches. A national association cannot choose any venue it likes for a competitive fixture. The governing body has to accept that a site is safe for players, officials and spectators. When a country cannot meet that test, the match is staged elsewhere.

Israel belongs to UEFA, the governing body for European football, rather than to Asia's confederation. Its national team therefore enters UEFA competitions, including the Nations League. Hungary is also a UEFA member.

Moving the fixtures to Hungary kept them inside UEFA's own membership. The matches stayed under the same competition rules, at a venue that still had to meet UEFA's standards for the Nations League.

The Nations League is UEFA's competition for national teams. It is played during international windows outside the major tournaments. Group results decide standings, as well as promotion and relegation between leagues. A home game in the competition is a competitive fixture, not a friendly. It cannot be dropped from the schedule without affecting the group table.

The matches in Hungary kept their status as Israel's home fixtures in the group. The venue moved, but the fixture's designation did not. Israel's squad traveled to another country to play matches it was formally hosting. Its opponents also traveled to Hungary instead of making the trip to Israel.

The cause sets Israel's case apart from relocations driven by stadium standards or licensing rules. The condition of Israel's grounds was not the reason for the move. The question was whether UEFA matches could be held safely in the country at all during the conflict. A stadium upgrade could not settle that question. The answer depended on security conditions in the country, not on construction work or an inspection.

Iraq played its home football internationals outside the country for years. FIFA had restricted Iraq from hosting competitive internationals because of security conditions.

Those fixtures moved to other countries. Qatar, Jordan and Iran were among the places where Iraq lined up as the home side.

The restriction came from FIFA, football's world governing body, rather than from Iraq's own federation. It applied to competitive internationals, the matches that count toward qualification and tournament standings.

The grounds for the restriction were security conditions inside Iraq. That made the issue one of safety, not a decision Iraqi football officials could reverse on their own.

The hosts differed in their relationship to Iraq. Jordan and Iran share land borders with Iraq. Qatar has no border with Iraq and lies farther down the Persian Gulf.

The restrictions did not end in a single ruling. FIFA lifted them in stages.

Bitcoin snapped a seven-week holding above the 50-week moving average (MA) with a weekly close at $74,968. According to the latest Galaxy Research report, BTC settled 0.7% under this key line, which now sits at $75,488.

Alex Thorn, the firm’s head of research, calls it a fakeout. The history is on his side: it's standard Bitcoin mechanics to slip back under the 50-week MA right after a bear-market bottom, and it's what shapes the structure of the four-year cycle. It has happened exactly twice before.

Losing the trendline again right after reclaiming it is how the biggest cryptocurrency has always behaved. Previous cycles played out like this:

The current chart is running the same script. From the $123,524 peak in October 2025, the coin bled 51.8% into the June cycle bottom at $59,517. A rebound then shoved the price back above the 50-week MA at $81,195. Today’s price is 7.7% off that September reclaim level, yet Bitcoin maintains a comfortable 26% cushion above the June bottom.

Thorn isn’t selling certainty. Two cycles is a thin sample, and bottoms only get confirmed in the rearview mirror. The margin for error is wide: in 2012, Bitcoin broke down again from 18% above the line, while in 2015 it held from just 8% above.

“Bitcoin just closed below its 50 week moving average after holding above it for 7 consecutive weeks. Two other times (2011-12 & 2019-20) btc closed below its 50w after reclaiming its post-bear bottom. Neither of those times did the bear make a new lower low (weekly close data),” the analyst notes.

One level kills the bull case for this 4-year cycle: $59,517. The technical case stays alive as long as Bitcoin reclaims the 50-week MA and holds it within the next month.

#5466. Fintech giant Plaid opening Seattle engineering office, with plans to double local headcount

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 10, 2026 at 11:58 am

Plaid is opening an engineering office in Seattle’s Westlake neighborhood in January and plans to double its local workforce to about 80 people by next summer.

The San Francisco-based fintech company says the new 11,466-square-foot space at 1000 Dexter Ave. N. will serve as a hub for its technical teams, with most open Seattle roles focused on machine learning, data science and engineering.

Plaid said in a blog post that it chose Seattle because much of the cloud and AI technology behind modern financial infrastructure was built in the region. The company is developing AI models trained on its network to understand patterns in how money moves.

Plaid already has about 40 employees in the Seattle area, who currently work remotely, The Seattle Times reported. “There’s just great talent in Seattle, so it’s a little bit of a no-brainer for us,” Meghan Welch, Plaid’s chief people officer, told the Times.

Plaid’s careers page lists more than 50 open roles that include Seattle as a possible location, though most are also open in San Francisco, New York or other cities. About half are in data, engineering or security, with the rest spread across sales, legal, finance and other teams.

Founded in 2013, Plaid was valued at $8 billion in an employee share sale earlier this year, down from a 2021 peak of $13.4 billion. The company says more than 150 million people have used its technology to connect their financial accounts.

Plaid is led by co-founder and CEO Zachary Perret.

The new office will have views of Lake Union, an outdoor deck and event space, along with three catered meals a day, according to the company.

#5465. How the UEFA Nations League works: promotion, relegation and Euro routes

Free daily briefing on global business news.

UEFA Nations League promotion and relegation decide where Europe's national teams play, and the results also open routes to the Euros and World Cup

The UEFA Nations League gives Europe's national teams a tiered competition in which results carry consequences. A strong campaign can lift a team into a higher league, and a weak one can drop it down. Results can also open a route to major tournaments.

UEFA's Executive Committee approved the competition in 2014, and the first edition was played in 2018-19. Teams are sorted into four tiers, League A through League D, according to UEFA rankings. League A holds the strongest national teams and League D the weakest. In the 2024-25 edition, Leagues A, B and C each had 16 teams, split into groups of four.

UEFA Nations League promotion and relegation follow from that tiered structure. A team that wins its group in League B or League C moves up a tier for the next edition. A team that finishes fourth in a League A or League B group drops down one tier. Third-placed teams in those two leagues face two-legged play-offs against runners-up from the tier below. A place in the higher league is at stake.

League A carries its own prize. Since the 2024-25 edition, the top two teams in each League A group have advanced to two-legged quarter-finals. The four winners then meet at a finals tournament in a single host country. Portugal, France and Spain have all lifted the trophy, and Portugal has won it twice.

The results also reach beyond the Nations League itself. For Euro 2024, play-offs gave Nations League group winners that missed out in the main qualifying groups a second route to the European Championship. Georgia, Ukraine and Poland all reached Euro 2024 that way. For the 2026 World Cup, four Nations League group winners that finished outside the top two of their qualifying groups received places in UEFA's play-offs.

The 10 slides below take each part of the format in turn. They cover why UEFA created the competition, how the leagues are seeded and how groups and knockout rounds work. They then explain how teams move between tiers and how the competition links to Euro and World Cup qualifying. The final slide lists every winner from 2019 to 2025.

UEFA created the Nations League to replace many low-stakes international friendlies with competitive matches between national teams of similar strength. UEFA's Executive Committee approved the competition in 2014, and the first edition was played in the 2018-19 season.

Before the competition began, friendlies filled many of the dates reserved for national-team football outside tournament qualifying. A friendly result earns no points, no trophy and no qualification place. Nothing carries over beyond the match itself.

That absence of consequence shaped how the games were used. Coaches could treat them as a chance to try fringe players or new tactics. Opponents could be picked for convenience rather than competitive balance. That sometimes left a strong side facing a much weaker one.

The Nations League takes over many of those calendar slots and attaches stakes to them. Each match feeds into a group table. Final positions carry consequences for the next edition of the competition. In some cases they also affect qualification for major tournaments.

Matching teams of similar strength is the other half of the design. UEFA does not throw every European national team into a single pool. It sorts them into tiers using its own rankings. A team therefore plays its group matches against opponents near its own level.

That structure changes what an international break offers at both ends of the scale. A smaller football nation gets competitive games it has a realistic chance of winning. A leading side gets regular meetings with other leading sides, with something riding on the result.

The Nations League did not end friendlies altogether. National teams still arrange them, particularly as warm-up matches before major tournaments.

It also did not replace the qualifying campaigns for the European Championship and the World Cup. Those campaigns continue, and the Nations League runs alongside them as a separate competition.

UEFA places each national team in the Nations League into one of four tiers — League A, League B, League C or League D — based on its UEFA ranking. League A contains the strongest sides, and League D contains the weakest.

The letters run from the top down. A team's letter reflects its standing among Europe's national sides at the start of an edition.

Ranking-based tiers put teams of similar strength in the same league. That follows UEFA's aim of matching national sides against opponents close to their own level.

The top three tiers were the same size in the 2024-25 edition. Leagues A, B and C each had 16 teams that season. That put 48 national sides in those three tiers combined.

League placement tells fans what level of opposition a side will meet. A team in League A plays other top-ranked nations. A team in League C or League D plays nations closer to its own standing, not the strongest sides on the continent.

The assignment is not permanent. Results in one edition decide which league a team enters for the next. The rankings set the starting order, and the matches reshape it over time.

Every team in Leagues A, B and C begins the Nations League in a group of four. Each side plays its three group opponents twice, once at home and once away, for six group matches in all.

The double round means no pairing is settled by one game at one team's ground. Each team hosts every opponent once and visits every opponent once. That gives every side an even split of three home matches and three away matches. Home advantage is therefore shared equally across the group.

A group of four contains six distinct pairings. With each pairing played twice, every group stages 12 matches.

Those 12 matches fit into six matchdays. On each matchday, all four teams in a group are in action across two games. No team sits out a round while its rivals play.

League A shows how those numbers scale. In the 2024-25 edition, League A was divided into four groups. Each League A team met three other League A sides home and away. Together, the four League A groups staged 48 matches.

Leagues B and C used the same layout in 2024-25, with four groups each. That made 12 groups across the top three leagues. Those 12 groups accounted for 144 group matches between them.

Because each league is a single tier, all three of a team's group opponents come from the same level of the competition. A League A side does not meet a League C side in the group stage.

Every team in a group finishes with the same number of games played. No side ends the group stage with a game in hand. The final standings compare teams on equal terms.

The final group table decides what happens next. A team's finishing position can send it forward, up or down, and the consequences differ by league.

League A teams compete for the UEFA Nations League title through a knockout bracket. Since the 2024-25 edition, the top two finishers in each League A group advance to two-legged quarter-finals. The four winners move on to a finals tournament hosted by one country.

League A is the top tier of the competition, and only its teams can win the title. Its four groups each send their top two forward, producing eight quarter-finalists. Those eight teams meet in four ties.

Each quarter-final is played over two legs. Every team plays once at home and once away. The aggregate score across both matches decides who advances. That gives each side a home fixture before the competition moves to one host nation.

The four quarter-final winners then travel to the Nations League Finals. This stage is a short tournament held in one country. It includes two semi-finals and a final, and the winner of the final takes the trophy.

The current bracket replaced a simpler route. Before 2024-25, only the four League A group winners qualified for the finals. There were no quarter-finals. Finishing second in a League A group therefore ended a team's chance of winning the title.

The change doubled the number of teams with a path to the trophy, from four to eight. A runner-up can now reach the finals without winning its group. A group winner no longer goes straight through. It has to win a two-legged tie first.

The format also lengthens the campaign for the strongest sides. On top of its group fixtures, a side that reaches the final plays four more matches: two quarter-final legs, a semi-final and the final itself.

Group position in League A therefore carries two kinds of stakes. The top two in each group chase the trophy through the knockout rounds. The bottom two play for their place in the top tier, through direct relegation or a play-off.

Group winners in League B and League C are promoted. Each one moves up a single tier for the next edition of the UEFA Nations League.

The step is always one league. A League B group winner joins League A, the top tier. A League C group winner joins League B.

No team can skip a tier. A side starting in League C needs to win its group in two consecutive editions to reach League A. The first group win lifts it to League B. The second lifts it to the top tier.

Only first place brings automatic promotion. A runner-up in either league does not go up directly, and neither does a third-placed team.

League B and League C each contained four groups in the 2024-25 edition. That meant four teams earned direct promotion from League B and four from League C, eight in all.

The reward is a higher level of opposition. A side promoted from League B spends its next campaign in League A, against the highest-ranked national teams in the competition. A side promoted from League C moves into the tier directly below League A.

Promotion to League A also changes what a team can win. Only League A teams can reach the quarter-finals and the finals tournament. A side that climbs out of League B becomes eligible for the trophy in its first season in the top tier.

The system means a team's league is not set by its ranking alone. Group results in one edition decide where it plays in the next.

The team that finishes fourth in each League A group drops straight to League B for the next edition. The same rule applies one level down: fourth place in a League B group means automatic relegation to League C.

Fourth place is the bottom of the group. In the 2024-25 edition, every group in Leagues A and B had four teams. Each side played the other three home and away, for six matches. A team that finishes last after those matches does not enter the promotion and relegation play-offs. Its move to the lower tier is settled once the group stage ends.

League A had four groups in 2024-25. That meant four League A teams went down directly. League B also had four groups, which sent four more teams from League B to League C. Across the top two tiers, direct relegation covered eight teams in that edition.

Relegation from League A carries a specific cost. League A holds the strongest national teams under UEFA's ranking-based placement. It is also the only tier that plays for the Nations League title. A team that drops to League B has no route to the quarter-finals or the finals tournament in the following edition. It must first win promotion back before it can contest the trophy again.

Relegation from League B to League C is a drop to the third of four tiers. The relegated team then plays opponents from a lower tier in its next campaign.

Relegation does not have to last long. A relegated team that wins its group in the lower league is promoted for the next edition. That means a side can return to its old tier after a single campaign.

Direct relegation applies only to fourth place. Third-placed teams in Leagues A and B are not relegated automatically. They play two-legged play-offs against runners-up from the tier below. The winner of each tie takes the place in the higher league.

The Nations League settles some movement between its top three tiers through play-offs. Third-placed teams in League A face League B runners-up, and third-placed teams in League B face League C runners-up. Each tie runs over two legs, with a place in the higher league at stake.

These ties sit between the automatic outcomes. Group winners in League B and League C move up without extra matches. Fourth-placed teams in League A and League B go straight down. The teams in between get either a last chance to stay up or an extra route to climb.

For a League A side, finishing third means it has to defend its place. If it wins the tie, it stays in League A for the next edition. If it loses, the League B runner-up takes its spot, and the League A team drops a level.

The same structure applies one tier lower. A League B team that finishes third must beat a League C runner-up to remain in League B. If the League C side wins instead, it is promoted, and the League B team moves down.

League B is the only tier involved in both sets of ties. Its runners-up play upward against League A opposition. Its third-placed teams play downward against League C opposition. As a result, no finishing position in a League B group keeps a team in League B automatically. The winner moves up, the fourth-placed side drops, and the two teams in between go into play-offs.

League A is arranged differently at the top. In the current format, its first- and second-placed teams advance to the quarter-finals. Their place in the top tier is not in question. Only the bottom two in each League A group face any risk of dropping.

A League C runner-up has two ways to reach League B. It can win its group outright, or it can finish second and then beat a League B side over two legs.

The two-legged format gives each team one home match and one away match. The outcome depends on the combined result across both games, not on a single match.

Nations League results give national teams a second path to the European Championship. A team that misses out through the main qualifying groups can still reach the tournament through play-offs filled on the basis of Nations League performance.

Group winners get first claim on those play-off places. When a group winner has already qualified through its group, its place passes to another team based on Nations League results.

The main qualifying groups remain the primary way into the European Championship. The play-offs come into play only for teams that miss out there. A team's Nations League campaign decides whether it gets that second chance.

For Euro 2024, which Germany hosted, the 2022-23 Nations League set the play-off field. Twelve teams entered three separate paths. Each path had one-off semi-finals and a final, and each path winner took one of the tournament's 24 places.

Georgia beat Greece on penalties in its path final in Tbilisi after a 0-0 draw. That result sent Georgia to its first major tournament. Both teams had reached the play-offs as League C group winners.

Ukraine won another path final, beating Iceland 2-1 in Wroclaw, Poland. Ukraine played that home tie in Poland because of Russia's invasion.

Poland beat Wales on penalties in Cardiff after a 0-0 draw to take the third place. Each of the three winners reached Euro 2024 after falling short in the main qualifying competition.

Two of the three deciding matches — Georgia against Greece and Poland against Wales — went to penalty shootouts. In both, a full European Championship place rested on a single shootout.

The route also changes what a poor qualifying campaign means for a team. Finishing outside the automatic places in a qualifying group does not end a team's Euro bid if its Nations League results earned a play-off spot. The two competitions run as separate tracks. A strong result in one can make up for a weak result in the other.

Nations League results carried over into qualifying for the 2026 World Cup. Four Nations League group winners that did not finish in the top two of their World Cup qualifying groups received places in UEFA's play-offs.

The rule gave those teams a fallback after their main qualifying campaigns fell short. A finish below second place in a qualifying group would otherwise have ended their chances. A Nations League group title kept them in contention instead.

The route depended on how a team's qualifying group ended. Teams that finished in the top two of their qualifying groups did not use it. A Nations League group title mattered most to teams whose qualifying campaigns went poorly.

The 2026 World Cup is co-hosted by the U.S., Canada and Mexico. It is the first edition with 48 teams, up from 32 at the 2022 tournament in Qatar. UEFA's share of that field is 16 places.

The link gave Nations League matches weight beyond the competition's own standings. A single group game could shape a team's chances of reaching a World Cup. That stake sat alongside the promotion and relegation consequences of the same result.

A play-off place does not guarantee a spot at the finals. Teams that enter through the Nations League must still come through the play-offs to qualify.

The World Cup rule mirrors the route UEFA already offered for European Championship qualifying. In both cases, Nations League form serves as a safety net when main qualifying falls short.

Portugal has won the UEFA Nations League twice, in 2019 and 2025. France and Spain have each won it once, and Spain has played in more finals than any other country.

Portugal took the first title in 2019 with a 1-0 win over the Netherlands in Porto. The first champion won the trophy in one of its own cities.

France claimed the 2021 title. It beat Spain 2-1 in a final played in the Italian city of Milan.

Spain won in 2023 after its final against Croatia in Rotterdam went to penalties. That title came two years after Spain lost the 2021 final to France.

Portugal added its second title in 2025. The final against Spain in Munich finished 2-2, and Portugal won the shootout. No other country has won the Nations League more than once.

Spain has played in three of the four finals, in 2021, 2023 and 2025. It won one and lost two, to France and then Portugal. That makes Spain the only country to lose more than one Nations League final.

The Netherlands and Croatia have each reached one final and lost it. The Netherlands fell to Portugal in 2019. Croatia lost to Spain in 2023.

Penalties settled two of the four finals: Spain against Croatia in 2023 and Portugal against Spain in 2025. The other two were decided by a single goal. Portugal won 1-0 in 2019, and France won 2-1 in 2021.

Each final so far has been played in a different country. The hosts run from Portugal in 2019 to Italy in 2021, the Netherlands in 2023 and Germany in 2025. Portugal is the only host nation to win the final on home soil.

Every champion has come from League A. It is the only tier whose teams can reach the finals tournament.

#5463. Microsoft awards $20K grants to 25 Seattle-area nonprofits amid state budget crunch and tax debate

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 10:48 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:27 am

The Lighthouse for the Blind is adding braille displays to its computer lab. Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery is taking its lessons to low-income schools. And Lake Washington High School’s band boosters are replacing marching capes that date to the MS-DOS era.

Those are among 25 King County nonprofits that received $20,000 apiece from Microsoft in grants announced this week. It’s the first round of the company’s Community-First Grants, a $1 million program launched in September.

Microsoft said it received 813 applications.

“Boy, I think we hit a nerve,” said Jane Broom, Microsoft’s senior director of Community Affairs, during an event Monday recognizing the nonprofits on the company’s Redmond campus, featuring Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh and the team’s mascots.

The grants are meant for immediate needs, such as replacing a broken-down van or a failed freezer, Broom explained. Nonprofits that already received or were invited to receive Microsoft corporate grants in 2026 weren’t eligible.

Funding and the tax debate: Nonprofits are dealing with rising costs and tighter budgets. As a group, their largest funding source is the state government, which is in the middle of an ongoing debate with members of the business community over taxes and economic competitiveness amid a budget crunch.

Microsoft is among the companies asserting that current and proposed taxes are hurting the business climate. It’s also the second-largest funder of the state’s nonprofits, behind only the state itself, said Brad Smith, the company’s president and vice chair.

“In my view, a healthy nonprofit community actually has aspects of support from more than one source,” Smith said in an interview after the event, noting that state grants are often at risk when a recession forces budget cuts.

Where the money goes: Demand is climbing for many of the grant recipients. At Community Lunch on Capitol Hill, which serves free hot meals, it’s up 40% this year, and the diaper bank at Byrd Barr Place has grown from 720 families in 2021 to 1,600, Microsoft said at the event.

Friends of the Issaquah Salmon Hatchery gives more than 700 tours during the salmon season. It will use its grant to bring lessons to classrooms, mainly at Title I schools, which serve large numbers of low-income students and often can’t afford a field trip to the hatchery, said Mark Clemens, the group’s executive director.

“If they can’t bring the school to the hatchery, we will go out to the school,” said Clemens, a former Scientific American art director, who was creative director of the Modernist Cuisine cookbook project before taking over the nonprofit in 2023.

One bonus for the group, which goes by the clever acronym of FISH, was the appearance of the Mariners’ salmon mascots, which joined the group onstage for a photo op when Clemens and his colleagues accepted its grant.

The Lighthouse for the Blind, a Seattle-based nonprofit that employs blind people in manufacturing, retail and other jobs, will use its grant to upgrade its computer training lab with Windows 11 PCs, braille displays and wireless keyboards, said Antonio Rozier, the nonprofit’s IT director.

The goal is to keep employees current on screen readers and other tools so they can work alongside sighted colleagues, Rozier said. The Lighthouse also has computer labs at its three manufacturing plants, and employees can use them for personal tasks, since some don’t have that equipment at home.

Rozier called the upgraded lab “a game changer for the future.”

The Lake Washington High School Band and Jazz Boosters will buy 150 uniforms for the school’s marching band, which returned in 2025 after a 40-year absence and has been performing in capes from 1981.

Microsoft’s company culture: Most of the company’s local giving is directed by its employees. Microsoft matches their donations and adds $25 for every hour they volunteer, up to a combined $15,000 a year per person, Smith said.

That program accounts for most of the $1.9 billion that Microsoft and its employees have given to about 13,000 Washington nonprofits over the past 30 years, he said.

“We let our people decide where the money goes,” Smith said.

Microsoft’s employee base is going through a period of major change. After layoffs in July and September, the company offered voluntary buyouts last month to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its global workforce. Employees have described mounting pressure to use AI, stagnant pay and a growing sense of job insecurity, The New York Times reported.

Asked about the buyouts, Smith said it’s a good time for Microsoft to keep investing in the employee experience, and he described the giving program as part of that.

Silicon Valley companies may offer more free food as a perk, he said, but Microsoft matches employee donations, giving workers who often move to the region from elsewhere a way to get involved in the community.

This year’s Microsoft Give campaign in October, the company’s biggest month for employee donations, was again a success, Smith said, showing that “employee participation and employee giving is alive and well.”

Microsoft plans to open a second round of applications for the Community-First Grants in the spring of 2027.

#5462. The NFL injury report explained: what questionable, doubtful and out mean

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The NFL injury report explained, from questionable, doubtful and out designations to practice participation, the Friday report and game-day inactives, and why the labels matter

The NFL injury report is a league-mandated public disclosure. Every team must file one for each regular-season game. The result is that everyone sees the same official information at the same time. It shows which players are hurt, what is wrong with them and whether they are expected to take the field.

Opposing coaches read it while preparing for a game. Fantasy football managers read it to set lineups. Bettors read it before placing wagers. Reporters read it to explain why a starter is missing. Each group works from the identical official list.

The report has a simple structure. Each entry names a player, the body part or illness involved and how much he took part in practice that day. Teams submit the report to the league, and the league makes it public. Later in the week, the report adds a game status for players whose availability is in question.

The game statuses each carry a specific meaning, and they are not interchangeable. Questionable signals uncertainty. Doubtful signals that a player is unlikely to play. Out means the player will not play in that game. A fourth label, probable, once sat at the top of the scale, but the league dropped it starting with the 2016 season.

The labels do not tell the whole story on their own. Practice participation — full, limited or did not participate — adds context that a game status alone does not provide. Timing matters too. For a typical Sunday game, teams release reports on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Only the Friday report carries game designations. The final answer arrives on game day, when teams submit their inactive lists about 90 minutes before kickoff.

Injured reserve sits outside this weekly system. It is a roster move, not a game status, and it works under its own set of rules.

The 10 slides below walk through each piece of the system. They cover who files the report, what each label means and how the weekly schedule unfolds. They also explain where injured reserve fits and why the league requires accurate information. Read together, they explain how a single injury listing moves from a Wednesday practice note to a game-day decision.

The NFL injury report is a required public disclosure that every team must file for each of its regular-season games. It names the players who are hurt or ill, identifies the body part or illness involved and records how much each player took part in practice.

The requirement covers every club in the league. No team is exempt. The obligation attaches to each game on the regular-season schedule rather than to the season as a whole. A team therefore produces a new report for every matchup it plays.

Both clubs in a game carry the same duty. Each matchup therefore produces two reports, one from each side, covering the players on each roster who are dealing with a problem that week.

Each entry links a named player to a specific problem. An injury is listed by the part of the body affected, such as a knee, an ankle or a hamstring. A player who is sick rather than hurt is listed with an illness instead.

Listing by body part keeps each entry brief. It also means an entry does not reveal a diagnosis or its severity. A knee listing alone does not show whether the problem is minor or serious.

The second core element is practice participation. Alongside the injury itself, the report shows how fully each listed player practiced. That pairing gives readers two separate pieces of information about a player's condition in the same entry.

Teams do not publish the report through their own channels. Each club submits it to the league, and the league then makes it public. The information reaches fans, media and opposing teams through a single official route.

The report is a statement about players, not about the whole roster. A player who is healthy and practicing normally does not need to appear on it at all. Appearing on the report does not mean a player will miss time.

Practice participation is the part of the NFL injury report that records how much work each listed player did on a given day. Teams describe it with one of three labels: full participation, limited participation or did not participate.

These labels describe what happened at practice. They do not say whether a player will suit up for the game. Game-status designations sit in a separate part of the report and serve a different purpose.

Full participation means the player took full part in practice. It is the strongest signal of health this section offers. A player can still appear on the report with a full listing because the injury itself remains on file.

Limited participation means the player practiced, but not fully. The label covers a wide range of workloads. It does not show which drills a player sat out or how much of the session he missed. Two players with the same limited listing may have done very different amounts of work.

Did not participate means the player stayed out of practice that day. The label on its own does not explain why. The body part or illness listed beside the player's name usually supplies that context.

Some absences have nothing to do with health. Teams can mark an entry as not injury related. A rest day or a personal matter falls into this group. A did-not-participate entry marked this way says little about a player's physical condition.

Teams do not always hold a real practice. When no real practice takes place, the report lists estimated participation instead. In that case, the team reports the level of work it expects each player would have managed in a normal session.

An estimate is a judgment, not a record of work done. A limited listing on an estimated report reflects the team's assessment rather than a session that actually happened. That distinction matters when a reader compares one day's entry with another's.

Questionable is the NFL injury report's label for a player whose availability for the upcoming game is uncertain. It does not predict that the player will sit or play. It signals only that the team has not ruled him in or out when the report is filed.

Older versions of the report attached a percentage to each game-status label. The league no longer does that. Questionable now carries no official numerical chance of playing. Any figure attached to it today is an outside estimate, not league policy.

Without a number, questionable covers a wide range of situations. A player managing a minor problem and a player facing a real chance of missing the game can carry the same label. The designation itself does not distinguish between them.

Players working through the league's concussion protocol can carry the questionable tag late in the week. A player in the protocol cannot return until both the team physician and an independent neurological consultant clear him. That clearance can come after the team files its final weekly report.

Practice participation helps narrow the picture. A questionable player who closed the week with full participation presents a different case from one who did not practice on any day. A player who moved from did not participate to limited also shows a different trend from one who stayed limited all week.

The designation reflects the team's view when the last report of the week is filed. A player's condition can still change before kickoff. Teams can downgrade a questionable player to out after that report. A downgrade means he will not play.

The inactive list settles the matter on game day. A questionable player left off that list is available to suit up. One who appears on it will not play, whatever the earlier report said.

For fantasy managers and bettors, questionable marks an open question rather than a final verdict. The practice record, any late downgrade and the inactive list together carry more information than the label alone.

Doubtful means a player is unlikely to play in the upcoming game. On the NFL's game-status scale, it sits between questionable, which signals genuine uncertainty, and out, which means the player will not suit up.

The label shows which way a team is leaning. A questionable player could go either way. A doubtful player carries a clear lean toward missing the game, but the team has not ruled him out.

Doubtful is not a final decision. The team keeps the option of playing him. He stays on the roster and can still be named active on game day. The definitive answer comes with the inactive list the team submits shortly before kickoff.

A team can also settle the question earlier. If it decides before game day that the player will not play, it can downgrade him from doubtful to out. That change tells everyone the absence is confirmed.

Doubtful appears only on the week's final injury report, the one that carries game designations. Earlier reports in the week list a player's injury and practice work but no game status. A player can therefore be on the report all week and pick up the doubtful tag only at the end.

Doubtful is a game-status designation, not a practice label. Reading it next to the player's practice entries gives a fuller picture. A doubtful player who sat out every session that week presents a different case from one who was limited late in the week. A late-week limited session shows the player was back on the field in some capacity.

The designation applies to one specific game. A player listed as doubtful this week starts fresh on the next week's report, where he may carry a different label or none at all.

Like the other game designations, doubtful can be attached to an illness as well as an injury.

For anyone planning around the game, the label works as an early signal of a likely absence. A doubtful listing is the team's public notice that it does not expect the player on the field.

An out designation means the player will not play in that game. It is the most definitive game-status label on the NFL injury report. It leaves no room for a late decision.

Questionable and doubtful both describe a degree of uncertainty. Out removes it. Once a team lists a player as out, his availability for that game is settled.

The label covers one game at a time. On its own, it does not say how serious an injury is or how long recovery will take. A player can be ruled out with a minor strain one week and practice fully the next. Another player can carry the same label for several straight games while a longer injury heals.

Each new game brings a new report. The status does not carry over automatically. A player listed out this week has his availability assessed again for the next game.

The entry also shows why the player is out. The report names the body part or illness involved, such as a knee, a hamstring or a concussion. Readers see the status and its cause on the same line.

Practice participation sits alongside the designation. The report records whether a player practiced fully, in a limited way or not at all during the week. Those entries describe how the week went. The out designation records the outcome for the game.

Out does not change a player's roster status. He stays on the team's roster even though he will not play. That separates the label from roster transactions, which move a player into a different category altogether.

The certainty matters on both sidelines. A team that rules a player out can build its game plan around his absence before kickoff. The league publishes the report. The opponent therefore works from the same information.

The label is read closely outside the stadium as well. An NFL player who does not appear in a game earns no fantasy points. Fantasy managers treat an out designation as a signal to change their lineups. Bettors read it the same way — as a confirmed absence rather than a possibility.

The NFL stopped using the probable designation starting with the 2016 season. Probable had told readers that a player was likely to play. Its removal left the injury report with three game-status labels instead of four.

Before the change, the report used a four-step scale. Probable sat at the top, followed by questionable, doubtful and out. Each label signaled a different level of confidence that a player would be available on game day.

With probable gone, the scale has three steps: questionable, doubtful and out. Questionable is now the least severe label a team can assign.

Players who once would have carried a probable tag did not disappear from the report. A player who is expected to play but still has an injury is usually listed with his practice status and no game designation. His name, the injury and his participation level still appear. The game-status column next to him stays blank.

That blank space carries meaning. A player on the report without a designation is generally someone the team expects to have available. A player with questionable next to his name is someone whose availability is still uncertain.

The change shifts more of the reading work onto the practice entries. Under the old system, one word summed up the team's outlook for a lightly injured player. Now readers build that outlook from the participation notes logged across the practice week.

Older news coverage, archived reports and past fantasy football advice can still mention probable players. Those references describe a system that ended before the 2016 season began. They do not reflect how current injury reports are written.

Anyone comparing injury reports across seasons should keep the switch in mind. A probable listing in 2015 and an entry with no game designation in 2017 could point to the same expectation that a player would suit up. The two entries record it under different reporting rules.

For a typical Sunday game, NFL teams file three injury reports during the week: one on Wednesday, one on Thursday and one on Friday. The Friday report is the one that carries game-status designations such as questionable, doubtful and out.

The Wednesday and Thursday reports serve a different purpose. They record which players are hurt or ill, the body part or illness involved, and how much each player took part in that day's practice. They do not assign a game status. A player listed on Wednesday is not being ruled in or out for Sunday at that point. Teams submit each of these daily reports to the league, which then makes it public.

Each report captures a single day. Read together, the three releases form a sequence. A player whose practice participation rises from Wednesday to Friday shows a different trend from one whose participation stays flat or drops. A name that appears on Thursday but not on Wednesday points to an injury or illness that surfaced midweek.

Friday changes the nature of the document. Alongside the practice information, teams attach a game designation to players whose availability is in doubt. That makes the Friday release the main public statement of a team's expectations before the weekend.

The Friday report is still not the last word. Game status can shift between Friday and kickoff. A team can still update a player's status after the Friday release, such as downgrading him to out. The final list of players who will not suit up comes later, on game day itself.

Not every game falls on a Sunday. Teams that play on a Monday, a Thursday or another day follow a shifted version of the same cycle. The specific release days move with the date of the game. The Wednesday-to-Friday pattern does not carry over unchanged.

For a non-Sunday matchup, the timing of that week's reports differs from the standard Sunday pattern.

Every NFL team must submit its list of inactive players about 90 minutes before kickoff. That list is the final, official word on who will not suit up. It can also differ from the game designations a team gave on its Friday report.

The inactive list answers a narrower question than the weekly injury report. The injury report describes health and practice work across a week. The inactive list simply names the players on the active roster who will not dress for that specific game.

Those two documents do not always line up. A player listed as questionable on Friday has no settled status until inactives arrive. He either appears on the list or he does not. That ends the uncertainty for that game.

Change can run in either direction. A player who seemed likely to play can suffer a setback over the weekend or in pregame warmups and end up inactive. A player carrying a game designation can also be cleared and take the field.

Not every inactive player is hurt. Teams cannot dress their entire active roster, so some healthy players sit out each week. Coaches decide who stays in uniform based on depth at each position and the needs of that matchup. A name on the inactive list does not, by itself, signal an injury.

The timing matters to anyone tracking player availability. Fantasy football managers and sports bettors watch for the list closely. It is the last official update before the game begins. For a player listed as questionable, it is often the first definitive one.

A player's status can remain open until that deadline. As a result, a Friday questionable tag can leave fans waiting into game day for an answer. The requirement applies to every game, whether it kicks off on a Sunday afternoon, a weeknight or in prime time.

The inactive list is also separate from roster transactions. A player on it remains on the team's active roster. He can be available the following week without the team making any move. That distinction separates a one-game inactive from longer-term absences handled through formal roster changes.

Injured reserve is a roster transaction, not a game-status label. A player marked out on the weekly injury report is ruled out of one game. A player placed on injured reserve must sit out a minimum number of games before he is eligible to return.

The two terms describe different things. Out is a designation tied to a single upcoming game. It tells the public that the player will not take the field that week. It says nothing about the weeks after that. The following week, the player goes through the reporting cycle again, and his status is set fresh.

Injured reserve runs on a different timeline. Moving a player there changes his roster status rather than his availability for one game. Once the move is made, the player cannot come back simply because he has healed. He has to wait out the required minimum first.

That minimum has not stayed the same. The NFL has changed the number of games an injured reserve player must miss over the years. To work out how long a specific player will be sidelined, check the rule in force for that season.

The two terms also surface in different places. Out appears on the weekly injury report, next to the player's practice participation. A move to injured reserve is announced as a roster transaction. A player on injured reserve is already ineligible to play. He does not need a weekly game designation to confirm it.

The terms carry different expectations as well. An out designation leaves open a quick return, sometimes as soon as the next game. Injured reserve signals that the team expects the player to be unavailable for at least the minimum stretch. A team can also list a player as out for several straight weeks without ever moving him to injured reserve.

For anyone following a team, each term answers its own question. Out answers whether a player will appear this weekend. Injured reserve answers a longer question: the earliest point at which he is allowed to return to the field.

The NFL requires teams to report player injuries accurately, and the league can discipline a club that fails to do so. That requirement turns the weekly injury report from a courtesy into an obligation.

Accuracy applies to every element a club files. A game status has to reflect the team's honest read of a player's availability. A practice entry has to reflect the work the player actually did, not a softer or harsher version of it. The obligation holds for each report a team releases during the week, not only the one that carries game designations.

Misreporting can run in either direction. A club might hide an injury to keep an opponent guessing about a key starter. It might also list a healthy player with an injury to create doubt that does not exist. Both versions mislead the opposing staff and anyone else relying on the report.

Competitive fairness is the main reason the rule matters. Both teams in a game prepare with the same official information about each other. A club that shades its report gains an edge its opponent cannot see or correct before kickoff.

Public trust is the second reason. The report reaches a far wider audience than the two coaching staffs. For readers outside the building, the report is the league's official record of who is hurt. Their confidence in the report depends on the league holding clubs to it.

The rules also give teams an honest outlet for absences that have nothing to do with injury. A player can be listed as not injury related. A club therefore has no reason to invent an ailment to explain a missed practice.

Enforcement rests with the league itself. The NFL receives each club's report, publishes it and can act when a filing falls short. Penalties can include fines against the club.

#5461. XRP Whales Move $900 Million in Biggest Inflow Since 2024

XRP's price correction has continued to deepen, with the leading altcoin retesting its multi-month low around $1.08, causing trading activity to intensify, especially among large holders.

Latest onchain data from crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant shows that large XRP holders are moving an unusually high volume of tokens to Binance, stirring speculation about increased selling activity among whales.

Notably, the data shows that whales have deposited about 691 million XRP into Binance within 24 hours, marking the largest single-day inflow recorded since 2024.

While XRP was trading around $1.3 during the period, the total XRP that flowed into the exchange that day was worth about $900 million, drawing attention from market analysts.

The massive XRP inflow has stirred panic among investors about the asset's potential performance, as it has surpassed the previous inflow record seen during a major market correction in February 2025.

It is important to note that the surge is not limited to a single day, as XRP's 90-day moving average of daily whale inflows has also surged above $100 million following recent market declines.

As such, the metric has reached its highest level in nearly six months, suggesting that large holders have been moving increasing amounts of XRP to Binance over an extended period.

The massive increase in XRP whale inflows has come as XRP continues to face a severe market decline, falling far below its local lows.

Following the extensive price decline, XRP has just retested its multi-month low around $1.08, a price level last seen on August 20, sparking fear among traders.

Although whale inflows do not necessarily mean that the whales have sold their holdings, the coinciding price bloodbath points to increased selling activity.

#5460. Seattle mayor lifts pause and will expand police surveillance cameras with new safeguards

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 1:10 pmNovember 10, 2026 at 1:28 pm

The move comes a day after NYU’s Policing Project released an independent audit of the Seattle Police Department’s Real Time Crime Center (RTCC), which Wilson commissioned during the pause. The audit found the city had built “an important foundation” for overseeing the system but that “significant policy gaps remain.” It made 19 recommendations.

Cameras in the Stadium District, installed before this summer’s FIFA World Cup, will be turned on immediately, according to the mayor’s office. Cameras around Garfield High School and in the Capitol Hill nightlife district still need to be bought and installed, which will take months. The City Council approved all three areas in 2025.

Wilson briefly turned on the 22 stadium-area cameras during the World Cup, citing “credible threats” reported by law enforcement, and said they would go off after the tournament. The audit noted that police streamed live feeds throughout the event, despite a department policy against monitoring cameras without an active call or case.

“After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle’s public-safety system,” Wilson said in a statement.

Wilson said the city will adopt most of the audit’s recommendations. The police department will publish a public dashboard on how the crime center is used and tighten its rules on data retention, permissible uses and requests from outside agencies. A new advisory group will help write policies for privately owned cameras, protests and where future cameras go.

No Flock cameras in Seattle, ever. New protections against potential abuses drawn from an outside audit. A handful of cameras in new neighborhoods. Here's what the RTCC looks like from the inside. pic.twitter.com/QeYUg8ZkW3

The Real Time Crime Center, which launched in 2025, pulls live video from hundreds of cameras into a single command room at police headquarters. They include 303 police-owned cameras at 61 sites, 116 security cameras at police buildings, 96 city traffic cameras, and 23 cameras owned by three local businesses that share their feeds with police.

Analysts watch 911 calls as they come in and pull up nearby cameras to give officers details callers may have missed, such as what a suspect is wearing or which way they ran. They also comb through recorded footage to help detectives investigate past crimes. The system runs on Fusus, software from Axon, the Arizona-based maker of police body cameras and Tasers.

Police are barred from using facial recognition with the system. The software does include an AI tool that searches video for people, vehicles and other objects, but analysts told auditors they use it only as a last resort because it is unreliable. In one case, a search for a man in a gray top and gray pants returned an image of a pigeon.

Whether the system reduces crime remains an open question. The Seattle Police Department has said officers and detectives are three times more likely to make an arrest with help from crime center analysts, and that the center assisted in 17 homicide cases in 2025, helping close 10. But the audit notes that the department counts any analyst action as “support,” such as checking a camera, even if it produced nothing useful.

Broader research on crime centers is thin, the audit found, and studies of surveillance cameras on their own show mixed results. A University of Pennsylvania evaluation of Seattle’s program, commissioned by the city’s inspector general, isn’t expected until late 2027.

Critics have warned that footage could end up with federal immigration agents or out-of-state prosecutors pursuing people who come to Washington for abortions or gender-affirming care. The audit found that state and city laws limit such sharing, but they can’t fully prevent it. Outside agencies could still get footage through public records requests or court orders served on the city or on Axon, which stores some of the police department’s video in its cloud.

“Used together, CCTV and RTCC supercharge law enforcement’s capabilities to monitor, track, and reconstruct people’s movements across the city,” Sannon said. Protecting residents, she said, requires strict, enforceable limits on how the technology is used, how long data is kept and who it’s shared with, along with independent oversight.

Wilson said the expansion and the new safeguards go together. “We can gather evidence to hold those who commit violent acts accountable and protect our neighbors targeted by federal overreach,” she said.

“Residents and businesses have sent a clear message: they want our officers to have the tools to keep them safe,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, CEO of Challenge Seattle.

City Councilmember Bob Kettle, who chairs the council’s public safety committee, said the committee will take up the audit’s recommendations, along with those from the city’s inspector general and auditor.

The city also plans to lay groundwork for connecting cameras run by Seattle Center tenants and nearby businesses to the crime center, according to the mayor’s office, citing interest from those businesses after the Bite of Seattle shooting in July. The audit flagged private camera integration as a key area to watch: the police department has bought about 100 devices that let businesses stream video to the center but hasn’t decided who will get them.

The advisory group, which will include members of the Community Police Commission, the Community Surveillance Working Group, police and other city staff, will meet over the next few months. Its recommendations will then go through the police department’s policy review process.
