#5459. How MLB free agency works: 10 rules from opt-outs to compensation picks

Free daily briefing on global business news.

MLB free agency runs on service time, qualifying offers, opt-outs and draft pick rules, and these 10 explainers show how each piece shapes where players sign

Free agency in Major League Baseball is rarely a simple auction. Before a player signs with the highest bidder, a set of calendars, salary formulas and draft penalties comes into play. Those rules decide when he can talk to other clubs and what his signing will cost. They can change what a player is paid and which teams bid on him. They also help explain why one star signs in November while another is still unsigned when spring training camps open in February.

Nearly all of those procedures come from the collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association. The current agreement was reached in March 2022, ending a 99-day lockout. It is scheduled to expire on Dec. 1, 2026. That date matters for anyone reading about the rules. The next round of bargaining could rewrite parts of the system described here.

The system follows a clear sequence. A player first has to earn enough service time to qualify. His club then gets a short head start to negotiate with him. After that, league rules and contract terms shape the bidding. A qualifying offer can attach a draft-pick cost to a player. A non-tender can push a younger player onto the market early. The competitive balance tax can lead a payroll-conscious club to walk away. An opt-out clause can return a star to the market before his contract was due to end.

This slideshow covers 10 of those mechanisms. It is a selection of key pieces, not a complete catalog of every provision in the agreement. Each slide explains one rule on its own terms, from the six-year service-time threshold to the compensation picks a club collects when a top player leaves. The final slide covers the posting system, which lets Japanese clubs make players available to major league teams before they reach free agency at home.

Taken together, the slides offer a working guide to MLB free agency rules for fans who follow the offseason closely and for readers who are new to it. Terms such as qualifying offer, non-tender, club option and competitive balance tax appear in transaction reports every winter. Each has a specific meaning. Each can also change where a player ends up and how much he earns.

A major league player becomes eligible for free agency once he has six full years of service time and his contract has expired. One year of service equals 172 days on the active roster or the injured list.

The regular season lasts longer than 172 days. A player can therefore earn a full year of service without spending every day in the majors. He cannot bank more than one year of service in a single season, however long the schedule runs.

Clubs and agents write service time as years and days. A player listed at 5.171 has five years and 171 days. One more day would give him six years. Without it, he stays under his club's control for another season.

The path to six years has three stages. Early in his career, a player's salary is set by his club at or near the league minimum. He then becomes eligible for salary arbitration, which covers the seasons before he reaches six years. Free agency comes last, when all 30 clubs can bid for him.

The six-year standard grew out of a long fight over the reserve clause. That clause once bound a player to his club from one year to the next. After the 1969 season, outfielder Curt Flood refused a trade from the St. Louis Cardinals to the Philadelphia Phillies. He sued to challenge the clause. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled against him in 1972 in Flood v. Kuhn.

The clause gave way through arbitration rather than the courts. In December 1975, arbitrator Peter Seitz ruled that pitchers Andy Messersmith and Dave McNally were free to negotiate with other clubs. Owners and the players union then wrote free agency into their 1976 labor agreement.

Service time also shapes when clubs promote their best prospects. Keeping a top young player in the minors for the first weeks of a season can delay his free agency by a full year. The 2022 collective bargaining agreement addressed that practice in part with the Prospect Promotion Incentive. Under it, a club can earn an extra draft pick when an eligible top prospect accrues a full year of rookie service. The player must then win Rookie of the Year or finish in the top three of MVP or Cy Young voting before he reaches arbitration.

For five days after the World Series ends, a team holds exclusive negotiating rights with its own free agents. Once that window closes, all 30 clubs can make offers. The open market then runs through the Winter Meetings in December and often well beyond them.

Inside the window, a player can re-sign with his current club before anyone else bids. His club must also decide by the end of those five days whether to extend him a qualifying offer. Rival clubs may not discuss contract terms with him during this stretch.

MLB's anti-tampering rules bar a team from negotiating with another club's player before the market opens. The league can discipline clubs that break those rules.

After the window closes, agents collect offers and clubs compare their options. A reported agreement is not final until the player passes a physical exam and the club announces the deal.

Shortstop Carlos Correa's winter of 2022-23 shows how much rides on that last step. In December 2022, he agreed to a 13-year, $350 million deal with the San Francisco Giants. The Giants raised concerns during his medical review, which focused on a lower right leg injury dating to 2014. The deal fell apart. He then agreed to a 12-year, $315 million deal with the New York Mets. That agreement also stalled over the medical review. In January 2023, he signed a six-year, $200 million contract with the Minnesota Twins.

The offseason calendar has other fixed dates. In November, clubs set their 40-man rosters. That roster decides which minor leaguers are protected from the Rule 5 draft. Clubs also face a November deadline to tender contracts to players still under team control. Players who are not tendered contracts become free agents.

The Rule 5 draft takes place at the Winter Meetings. Clubs also use those meetings for much of their face-to-face business with agents.

The market does not shut down after December. Manny Machado agreed to a 10-year, $300 million deal with the San Diego Padres in February 2019. Bryce Harper's 13-year, $330 million agreement with the Philadelphia Phillies came at the end of that same month. A player's timing tends to reflect what clubs want to spend, what rival bidders can offer and whether a draft-pick penalty is attached to his name.

The rules set the order of events, but they set no signing deadline. A free agent can stay unsigned past Opening Day while he waits for a better offer.

A qualifying offer is a one-year contract that a club can extend to its own departing free agent. The salary equals the average of the 125 highest player salaries in the majors. It was $20.325 million for the 2023 offseason and $21.05 million for both the 2024 and 2025 offseasons.

The figure is recalculated every year because it follows the top of the salary market. Every player who receives an offer that winter is offered the same amount. A club cannot adjust it for age, position or performance. The same salary can sit well above one player's market value and well below another's.

The timing is fixed. A club must extend the offer within five days after the World Series ends. The player then has 10 days to accept or reject it. If he accepts, he returns for one season at that salary. If he rejects it, he enters the open market with draft compensation attached to his name.

Eligibility has limits. The player must have spent the entire season with the club that makes the offer. A player traded at the deadline therefore cannot receive one from his new team. A player can also receive a qualifying offer only once in his career. Any later trip through free agency comes without the tag.

The system dates to the 2012 collective bargaining agreement. It replaced the older Type A and Type B rankings, which used statistical formulas to sort free agents and set compensation. Under the current rule, the club chooses which players to tag.

Clubs weigh two risks. If the player accepts, the club owes a large one-year salary. That commitment can strain a tight payroll. If the club does not make the offer, it gives up any claim to compensation when the player leaves. Teams with room to spend often tag players they expect to depart. Teams with thin budgets tend to hold back when an acceptance looks plausible.

Players face the reverse calculation. Accepting guarantees a high salary for one season. It also returns him to free agency the next winter, when no tag is possible. Rejecting opens the door to multiyear offers. It also adds a draft-pick cost that any signing club must absorb.

Most players who receive the offer decline it. No player accepted until November 2015, when Matt Wieters, Colby Rasmus and Brett Anderson each took that winter's $15.8 million offer. Players who accept have tended to be those facing questions about their age, injury history or demand on the open market.

A club that loses a free agent after making him a qualifying offer receives an extra pick in the next amateur draft if he signs with another team. The new club pays nothing to the old one directly. The reward comes only as a draft selection.

Compensation applies only when the player rejects that offer, the one-year contract his club can extend after the season. Two outcomes produce no pick at all. If the player re-signs with his former club, nothing is owed. If he accepts the offer, he stays under contract, and again there is no compensation.

Two factors decide where the extra pick lands. One is the size of the player's new contract. The other is the financial status of the club that lost him. The $50 million dividing line arrived with the 2016 collective bargaining agreement, and it remained in place under the 2022 agreement.

Under that framework, a club that receives revenue sharing gets a pick right after the first round if the departing player signs for $50 million or more. If he signs for less, its pick comes after Competitive Balance Round B. A club that paid the competitive balance tax in the previous season receives a pick only after the fourth round. Clubs in neither group receive a pick after Competitive Balance Round B.

The placement matters because of how the draft pays out. The draft now runs 20 rounds. Every selection in the first 10 rounds carries an assigned slot value. Those values add up to a club's bonus pool, the total it can spend to sign its picks. An earlier pick means a larger slot value, a bigger pool and an earlier choice among the available prospects.

The 2022 agreement added a lottery that sets the first six selections among clubs that missed the playoffs. Compensation picks sit outside that lottery. They are slotted into fixed positions after the rounds described above.

The system has changed shape before. When the qualifying offer began under the 2012 agreement, compensation picks were placed after the first round, with no payroll-based tiers. The tiered structure that followed ties a club's reward partly to its finances. Revenue-sharing recipients receive the most valuable placements. Tax-paying clubs receive the least valuable ones.

The compensation pick is a newly created selection. It is not taken from the team that signs the player. That club faces its own separate penalty. The two sides of the transaction run on different rules.

Compensation picks also cannot be traded. Only Competitive Balance Round picks can change hands in MLB. A club that earns compensation keeps the pick and makes the selection itself.

A club that signs a free agent who turned down a qualifying offer gives up draft picks and, in most cases, international bonus pool money. The size of that cost depends on the signing club's payroll status. Clubs that pay the competitive balance tax lose the most.

The tiered penalty dates to the 2016 collective bargaining agreement, which took effect for the 2016-17 offseason. The 2022 agreement largely kept it in place. A club that receives revenue sharing forfeits its third-highest pick in the next draft. A club that neither receives revenue sharing nor pays the tax forfeits its second-highest pick. It also loses $500,000 of international bonus pool money. A club that paid the tax in the prior season forfeits its second- and fifth-highest picks, along with $1 million of pool money.

The earlier rules worked differently. Under the 2012 agreement, which governed the 2012-13 through 2015-16 offseasons, a club that signed a tagged free agent generally lost its first-round pick. If that pick fell in the top 10, the club lost its second-round pick instead. That approach put a club's highest available selection at stake, regardless of its payroll.

The tiered system did not remove friction from the market. A club may value a tagged player less once it counts the lost selection. Pitcher Dallas Keuchel and closer Craig Kimbrel both rejected qualifying offers after the 2018 season. Neither signed during the winter or spring. Both agreed to deals on June 7, 2019, after that year's draft had begun. By then, a signing club no longer had to surrender picks for them. Keuchel joined the Atlanta Braves, and Kimbrel joined the Chicago Cubs.

The international bonus pool is the second half of the cost. Each club receives a pool of money for signing amateur players who are not subject to the draft. Those players come from outside the U.S., Canada and Puerto Rico. Losing part of that pool narrows a club's options in the next international signing period.

Clubs can offset the loss only in limited ways. Most draft picks cannot be traded under MLB rules. Picks in the Competitive Balance Rounds are the exception. International bonus pool space can also change hands in trades. A club that forfeited pool money can acquire more from another team to restore its spending room.

An opt-out clause lets a player walk away from the remaining years of his contract after a set season and return to free agency. The player alone makes the choice, typically shortly after the World Series ends.

Each clause is negotiated deal by deal. Some large contracts include one, and others do not. A player who declines to use it keeps playing under the original terms.

For a player, the clause offers a second shot at the market. He may outperform his salary, or prices around the league may climb after he signs. In either case he can leave guaranteed money behind in search of a larger deal. If he gets hurt or struggles, he stays and collects what he was promised.

That imbalance makes the clause a cost for the club. The team carries the risk of a declining player. It also risks losing one who plays well. A club may agree to the clause in exchange for a lower total commitment or other concessions in the deal.

Carlos Correa's contract with the Minnesota Twins shows the clause at work in a short deal. In March 2022 he signed for three years and $105.3 million, with opt-outs after the first and second seasons. He exercised the first one after the 2022 season and returned to the market.

Alex Rodriguez used one on a much larger contract. His 10-year, $252 million deal, first signed with the Texas Rangers, allowed him to opt out after the 2007 season. He did, and then re-signed with the New York Yankees for 10 years and $275 million.

A player who opts out enters free agency on the same footing as other players. If he meets the eligibility conditions, his former club can extend a qualifying offer and attach draft compensation to his signing.

Clubs can act before the deadline arrives. A team can offer extra years or more money to persuade a player to give up the clause. It can also plan its payroll around his likely departure.

The clause changes how a contract's length should be read. A five-year deal with an opt-out after the third season may work like a three-year deal if the player performs well. Contracts and transaction reports sometimes describe a similar right as a player option, and the two labels overlap in practice. The key details are who holds the decision and which years it covers.

An option is an extra contract year that one side, or both, can choose to keep or decline. The player holds a player option, the team holds a club option, and a mutual option requires agreement from both. Club and mutual options usually carry a buyout that is paid if the year is declined.

These decisions come shortly after the World Series, in the same early-offseason stretch when clubs handle the rest of their roster business. A declined option, from either side, sends the player into the market without a contract.

A player option puts the choice in the player's hands. If he believes he can earn more on the open market, he declines it and becomes a free agent. If he would rather keep the guaranteed salary, he exercises it and stays. A player coming off an injury or a weak season has a clear financial reason to keep the money.

A club option reverses that control. The team can pick up the year at the stated salary, or it can decline the year and pay the buyout. Clubs often decline when the salary is higher than the value they expect from the player. Picking up the option does not commit the team to keeping him. Clubs sometimes exercise an option and then trade the player. Club options also appear often in early-career extensions. There, they give a team control over what would have been a player's first free agent seasons.

A mutual option requires both sides to want the same thing at the same time. A player who has performed well tends to prefer the market. A club whose player has struggled tends to prefer the buyout. As a result, these options are rarely exercised, and the buyout often becomes the payment that matters.

The buyout is a fixed sum written into the contract. It counts as guaranteed money, so a club that declines an option still pays something. It also counts toward the contract's guaranteed value.

Vesting options add a performance trigger. The extra year becomes guaranteed automatically if the player reaches a target in the prior season, such as a set number of innings pitched or plate appearances. That structure shields a club from paying for an injured player's final year while still paying a healthy one.

Options also affect how headline figures read. A deal reported as seven years may include a club option on the final season, which means only six are guaranteed. The contract terms show how many years a team actually owes.

The competitive balance tax charges clubs whose payrolls pass a set threshold. Under the 2022 collective bargaining agreement, that threshold was $230 million for 2022 and $241 million for 2025. Clubs pay tax on every dollar above it.

The rate climbs with repetition. A club over the threshold for the first time pays 20 percent on the excess. A second consecutive year raises the rate to 30 percent. A third or later year raises it to 50 percent. Clubs that exceed the threshold by wider margins also pay surcharges on top of those base rates.

The higher rates do not last forever. A club that finishes a season under the threshold returns to the first-time rate the next time it goes over. The New York Yankees stayed under the 2018 threshold, which reset their rate after years as a repeat payer.

The tax payroll is built from average annual value, not the cash a player receives in a given season. A club takes the total guaranteed money in a contract, including any signing bonus, and divides it by the number of years. That figure counts against the threshold in every season of the deal. A front office can calculate a signing's tax effect before it agrees to terms.

Deferred money changes that calculation. In December 2023, Shohei Ohtani agreed to a 10-year, $700 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers. He is scheduled to receive $2 million a year during the contract. The remaining $680 million is deferred and paid from 2034 through 2043. Deferred dollars are discounted to present value for tax purposes. The deal counts about $46 million a year against the Dodgers' tax payroll.

The penalties reach beyond cash. A club whose payroll sits $40 million or more above the first threshold has its highest draft pick moved back 10 places in the next amateur draft. If that pick falls among the first six selections, the club's second-highest pick moves back instead.

The threshold also shapes the market below the stars. A club just under it may pass on a mid-tier free agent whose salary would push its payroll over. A club with room beneath the line can absorb the same contract without a tax bill.

Salary arbitration sets pay for players with three to six years of major league service time. A non-tender sends a player to free agency before he reaches the six-year mark. Both processes shape which players are available each winter.

A player in the arbitration window cannot sign with any club he chooses. His team still controls his rights. He can, however, ask a neutral panel to set his salary when he and the club disagree.

The format is known as final-offer arbitration. The player and the club each submit one salary figure, typically in January. If they do not settle, a panel of three arbitrators chooses one of the two numbers at a hearing. The panel cannot split the difference or pick a figure in between.

That all-or-nothing design raises the cost of an unrealistic filing. A club that files too low risks losing the hearing outright. A player who files too high faces the same risk. Most cases settle before anyone enters a hearing room. Hearings that do go forward are held in February. The panel weighs factors such as the player's performance and the salaries of comparable players.

Some players reach arbitration a year early under a rule known as Super Two. The group includes players with at least two years of service but fewer than three. To qualify, a player must rank in the top 22 percent of that group in service time. He must also have accrued at least 86 days of service in the previous season. A Super Two player gets four arbitration years instead of three. His salary begins to climb a year sooner as a result.

The tender deadline in November is where arbitration and free agency meet. By that date, a club must offer a contract to every arbitration-eligible or otherwise reserved player it wants to keep. A player who does not receive one is non-tendered. He becomes a free agent immediately, with no qualifying offer or draft compensation attached.

Clubs non-tender players for practical reasons. A projected arbitration salary may exceed what the club thinks the player is worth. A player may be recovering from an injury. A club may need to clear a spot on its 40-man roster. A non-tendered player can sign with any team, including the one that let him go.

The non-tender list adds a group of established major leaguers to the market weeks before the Winter Meetings. Unlike veterans who reached six years of service, many of these players are still in their arbitration years when they hit the open market.

A separate group arrives through minor league free agency. These players have spent a set number of seasons in the minors without being added to a 40-man roster. Most sign minor league contracts with new organizations. Some of those deals include invitations to major league spring training.

The posting system lets a Nippon Professional Baseball club make one of its players available to MLB teams before he reaches international free agency. If a major league team signs him, that team pays a release fee to his Japanese club.

The decision to post belongs to the NPB club, not the player. Once a player is posted, he has a 45-day window to negotiate with major league teams. Every MLB club can make an offer. If no deal is reached before the window closes, he returns to his Japanese team for the coming season.

The release fee is tied to the size of the contract and rises on a sliding scale. It equals 20 percent of the first $25 million, 17.5 percent of the next $25 million and 15 percent of any amount above $50 million. The signing team pays the fee on top of the contract. It does not come out of the player's salary.

Posting offers an earlier route than waiting out a career in Japan. NPB players can become international free agents on their own after a set number of years of service with their clubs. A Japanese club that expects to lose a star may post him a year or two early. That way it collects a fee instead of watching him leave without one.

Pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto took this route. The Orix Buffaloes posted him, and he agreed to a 12-year, $325 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers in December 2023. The fee went to Orix and was not part of the contract total.

Age and experience change the rules. A foreign professional must be at least 25 and have six seasons in a recognized foreign league to sign a standard free agent deal. A younger or less experienced player counts as an international amateur. His signing bonus is limited by each club's international bonus pool.

The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Shohei Ohtani in 2017. He was younger than 25, so he came to the majors under those amateur limits when he signed with the Los Angeles Angels. He then completed six years of major league service. After the 2023 season, he entered free agency as an established player with no bonus pool restrictions.

XRP Ledger co-creator David Schwartz dropped his $1.7 million tax bill on X to settle a long-running fight over the token’s value. Ripple’s CTO Emeritus was swatting away haters who accused him of dumping XRP on the market. One commenter called XRP “a terrible investment,” adding that nobody would blame the engineer for heading for the exit. Schwartz kept it short: “The $1.7 million I paid in capital gains tax says otherwise.”

In 2025, Schwartz sold about 2.5 million XRP, according to his own words. Nearly all of it came from bonuses for his work in 2020 and 2023. Posting the numbers was no accident. Schwartz is killing rumors about what Ripple’s "big guns" really pocket and proving he has nothing to hide.

The sale is one chapter in a bigger personal saga Schwartz has been unpacking piece by piece from 2024 through 2026. At his peak he held around 26 million XRP. By August 2026, that stack had shrunk to just 2 million. Describing the 92% drawdown, he chose his words carefully: “I think I’m down from about 26 million at my peak to about 2 million now.”

Some went out as gifts and transfers, but he sold most of it on the open market.

He started taking profits the moment the price touched $0.10. Schwartz admits he never believed the coin would break $0.25. The same paranoia made him dump his entire 40,000 ETH position at a measly $1.05 apiece.

“Obviously, I wish I hadn’t done those things,” the developer says of the billions he left on the table.

Schwartz opposes the approach many attribute to as "diamond hands". He openly says he “really, really hates risk” and doesn’t count himself among long-term holders. He and his wife had an ironclad rule to sell a fixed slice of their holdings every time the price printed a new all-time high. Cashing out is simply the cost of being able to “sleep better at night.” These days, volatility barely touches him as his net worth is now largely cut loose from price swings.

Based on his own admission, Schwartz moved most of his savings into Ripple stock. The shares are illiquid, sure, but they give direct exposure to the tech giant’s wins and fully insulate his personal capital from exchange chaos.

#5457. Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 7:15 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:30 am

Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years.

The Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup. It was the first investor in Overland AI, the maker of autonomous military vehicles, and an early backer of subsea geothermal startup Endurance Energy, among others.

Ascend Fund III will back more physical AI startups building robots, energy systems, defense technology and other ventures that blend software and hardware — part of a larger bet on what the Ascend team likes to call Seattle’s “Third Act.”

Winfield said raising a third fund in this market shows that Ascend has “arrived on the national stage,” along with Seattle’s rise as a hub for this new class of startups. He said the firm’s track record puts it in the same league as the country’s top seed investors.

“We are not just some nice guys in the corner of the country helping out our neighbors,” said Winfield, who works closely with Jen Haller, Ascend partner and chief of staff, and Nate Bek, a principal at the firm.

Who’s backing the fund: The new institutional investor is FirstLook Partners, a firm that invests in smaller venture funds. Josh Porter, FirstLook’s co-founder and managing partner, said the firm, which is “very bullish on the Seattle ecosystem,” looked at several startup markets outside San Francisco and New York and met many investors in Seattle, “but all roads kept leading back to Kirby.”

Porter said Winfield has “lived the founder journey” and has “the operational chops to sit across the table from a founder and empathize with what they’re going through.”

The rest of the fund comes from family offices, founders who have sold companies, and more than a dozen founders of Ascend portfolio companies.

A tough market for small funds: Ascend’s raise comes as smaller venture firms struggle to bring in new money. Their investors, mostly wealthy individuals and family offices, are waiting longer for returns from earlier funds.

Just 211 newer venture firms closed at least one fund through the end of September, down from 927 in all of 2022, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. Established firms took a record 88.2% of the money raised by U.S. venture funds in the first nine months of the year, the report found. Porter said smaller firms have to show “a right to exist and a right to win deals.”

Ascend launched its first fund in 2019 and ultimately raised $15 million. Its second fund closed at $25 million in 2023. The firm generally operates in the $15 million to $25 million range and writes the same size checks regardless of fund size, Winfield said.

“We think Kirby knows his place in the larger ecosystem, knows the value he brings to the table, and has sized his fund accordingly,” Porter said.

The firm has already drawn about 60% of the money committed to Fund III. GeekWire first reported that the firm was raising the fund in April 2025, based on filings at the time. Endurance was one of the firm’s first investments from the new fund, in mid-2025.

Ascend’s track record: Winfield started Ascend after two decades in leadership roles at four startups. He described the first fund as a proof of concept that “stumbled into some unicorns,” including Fabric, an e-commerce software company that was valued at $1.5 billion in 2022. Ascend was in its first round.

With its second fund, Ascend moved away from consumer and marketplace investing to focus on enterprise AI and deep tech. Its most successful investments from that fund, according to Winfield, include Overland AI, Sabi, Yoodli and Zocks.

After Ascend’s first checks, its portfolio companies have gone on to raise more than $1.5 billion from investors including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer, Founders Fund, Khosla and Lightspeed, according to Ascend.

Ascend’s second and third funds rank in the top 10% of funds of $50 million or less, based on current valuations of their portfolio companies, Winfield said, citing figures Ascend shared with its investors at its annual meeting. The firm didn’t disclose specific returns or how much cash it has returned to its investors.

What Ascend looks for: The firm looks for ideas that seem too difficult, too boring, too confusing or too small for big multistage venture firms to evaluate. Ideally, Winfield said, its founders are doing something that makes Series A investors “a little bit nervous.”

That’s why Ascend hasn’t made many more defense tech investments since backing Overland, he said. Valuations for well-known founders in the sector have soared as more investors have piled in.

“The time to invest in defense tech was when nobody was investing in defense tech,” Winfield said.

Porter said Ascend’s focus on Seattle and physical AI is “really the bet we made with Ascend,” adding that Endurance and Overland have the potential to become “generational, category-defining companies.”

Fund III also backs AI software and infrastructure companies, including Seattle-area startup Govstream.ai, which uses AI to speed city permitting.

Seattle’s economic climate: Winfield is a champion of Seattle’s startup scene, known for Ascend’s annual Founders Bash party in the city and his ever-present ☔🔥☔ emojis on social media, symbolizing hot startups in rainy Seattle.

Ascend’s refreshed website and brand, launched with Fund III, nod to the firm’s Seattle roots with its longstanding Seattle Startup Toolkit and a Spotify playlist of Pacific Northwest indie rock and hip-hop.

But Winfield has also been a vocal critic of state and local policies he sees as hostile to startups, including Washington’s new tax on income over $1 million, which takes effect in 2028 and survived a repeal vote last week. He worries the tax could eventually be extended to people earning $150,000 a year, which would make it harder for startups to recruit employees from places like Texas.

“The chilling effect that’s going to have on the ecosystem is real, and it’s happening,” he said.

About 60% of Ascend’s portfolio companies are based in Seattle, according to the firm.

Bek said hardware companies such as Endurance and Overland still have good reasons to be in Seattle, including testing on Lake Union and in Yakima, access to the sea and University of Washington talent. For Overland, he said, that also means proximity to Joint Base Lewis-McChord.

Combined with the region’s history in aerospace, defense and energy, Winfield noted, those advantages make Seattle one of the country’s key hubs for building physical products. He called it “El Segundo Northwest,” a reference to the Los Angeles-area city that has become a hub for defense and hardware startups.

As Winfield notes, Ascend isn’t the only early-stage firm chasing these companies. Pre-seed firms such as Cantos, Ironspring and Silent Ventures are backing similar founders, and some Seattle firms that historically focused on software are becoming more open to investing in hardware.

Ultimately, he said, Seattle still benefits from a long legacy of technical founders, and Ascend is “betting that those folks are going to continue to create companies that are worth hundreds of billions of dollars.”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5456. 10 milestones in Nvidia's growth, from the NV1 to $3 trillion in market value

Free daily briefing on global business news.

This Nvidia timeline traces 10 milestones in the chipmaker's rise, from its 1993 founding and GeForce graphics cards to CUDA, AI data centers and trillion-dollar market value

Nvidia $NVDA started in April 1993 in Santa Clara, California, as a company building 3D graphics for PCs. The founders were Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. On June 18, 2024, it overtook Microsoft $MSFT as the most valuable listed company. Company rankings by market value change daily. That makes the June 2024 milestone a dated one, not a permanent title. The two dates sit 31 years apart.

The link between those two dates is the graphics chip itself. Hardware designed to draw 3D scenes for games turned out to suit other kinds of computing work. Nvidia's CUDA software, introduced in 2006, let developers use its GPUs for general-purpose programs. In 2012, AlexNet showed that the same chips could speed up deep learning. Those two steps pointed the company toward AI systems for data centers. After OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022, demand for Nvidia's data center chips rose.

Not every step moved the company forward. Its first product, released in 1995, did not succeed commercially. The company changed its approach to graphics afterward. A planned acquisition was abandoned after regulators raised objections. Its purchase of Mellanox, by contrast, added data center networking technology. Those setbacks and deals sit in the timeline alongside product launches and market value figures.

This Nvidia timeline covers 10 milestones, from the 1993 founding to the June 2024 day the chipmaker passed Microsoft in market value. It is a selection, not a complete history of the company. The entries run in chronological order and are not ranked. The early entries cover graphics chips for PCs and a game console. The middle entries cover the software and research that opened GPUs to new uses. The later entries cover data center hardware, acquisitions, export restrictions and the market value steps that followed. Market value claims in the timeline are tied to the dates they occurred. Each entry stands on its own, with the date, product, deal or figure that defined it.

Nvidia $NVDA was founded in April 1993 by three co-founders: Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The company was based in Santa Clara, California.

Its early work centered on 3D graphics for personal computers.

The NV1 was Nvidia $NVDA's first product, and it reached the market in 1995. It did not succeed commercially.

The chip arrived about two years after the company's founding. It was Nvidia's first attempt to sell graphics hardware to buyers.

That attempt did not catch on. The commercial failure led Nvidia to change its approach to graphics.

Nvidia $NVDA went public on Nasdaq $NDAQ on January 22, 1999, at $12 a share. In October of that year, it launched the GeForce 256 and marketed the chip as the first GPU, or graphics processing unit.

The listing came less than six years after the company's April 1993 founding. Once its shares began trading on Nasdaq, Nvidia became a publicly traded company.

The product milestone followed about nine months after the listing. In October 1999, Nvidia released the GeForce 256, a graphics chip for PCs.

Nvidia promoted the GeForce 256 as the first GPU. That label was the company's own marketing claim. Nvidia used the term to present the chip as a new kind of graphics product.

The two 1999 events differed in kind. The IPO changed how Nvidia was owned and financed. The GeForce 256 gave the company a new chip and a name for the category it claimed that chip started.

Nvidia $NVDA supplied the graphics processor for Microsoft $MSFT's original Xbox, the game console that launched in 2001. The deal added a console business to the chipmaker's existing sales of graphics cards for PCs.

With the Xbox, Nvidia's graphics hardware reached players through two kinds of products. One was a graphics card installed in a personal computer. The other was a home console sold under Microsoft's brand.

Nvidia $NVDA announced CUDA in November 2006. The platform lets developers run general-purpose programs on Nvidia GPUs, not only graphics code.

The announcement came alongside the GeForce 8800 GTX, a graphics card built on Nvidia's G80 chip. Nvidia introduced the software platform and the new card at the same time.

A GPU had been designed to render images for games. CUDA gave programmers a way to write software that put an Nvidia GPU to work on tasks other than drawing a picture on a screen. That widened the range of jobs the company's hardware could take on.

The GeForce 8800 GTX was a graphics card for PC gaming. Paired with CUDA, the launch addressed two audiences. One was buyers looking for a graphics card. The other was developers who wanted to use a GPU for their own programs.

CUDA's role grew in the years after 2006. It later became the software base for much of AI computing.

That later role traces back to the November 2006 announcement. It marked the point when Nvidia began offering its GPUs for general-purpose computing as well as for graphics.

AlexNet, a neural network built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, won the 2012 ImageNet competition. The three researchers trained it on two Nvidia $NVDA GTX 580 GPUs.

AlexNet was a deep learning model. Its ImageNet result showed that GPUs could speed up that kind of work.

The 2012 win linked Nvidia's graphics processors to deep learning research. The link came through the work of Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, who chose a pair of the chipmaker's GPUs to train their network.

In April 2016, Nvidia $NVDA announced the Tesla $TSLA P100, a GPU built on its Pascal architecture. That same month, it introduced the DGX-1, an AI system. Together, the two launches marked the chipmaker's turn toward the data center.

The two products sat at different levels. The Tesla P100 was a single chip. The DGX-1 was a complete system built for AI work. With it, Nvidia offered a finished machine as well as the processors that go inside one.

In August 2016, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang delivered a DGX-1 to OpenAI. The handover came four months after the system's introduction. It put one of the new machines in the hands of an organization working on artificial intelligence.

Pascal did not stay Nvidia's newest design for long. In 2017, the GPU maker followed it with Volta, an architecture that added tensor cores.

Nvidia $NVDA agreed in March 2019 to buy Mellanox for $6.9 billion. The purchase closed in April 2020 and gave the chipmaker data center networking technology.

About 13 months passed between the announcement and the close. The deal took a business built around graphics processors into the networking side of the data center.

A much larger bid followed. In September 2020, five months after the Mellanox purchase closed, Nvidia announced a $40 billion deal to buy Arm.

That agreement never closed. It stayed pending for about 17 months. In February 2022, the companies abandoned it after regulators raised objections.

The two deals ended differently. Mellanox became part of Nvidia, and its networking technology stayed with the chipmaker. The Arm bid ended without Nvidia acquiring the company.

Nvidia $NVDA announced the H100, a data center GPU built on its Hopper architecture, in March 2022. Demand for Nvidia's data center chips rose after OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022.

Hopper is the name of the architecture. H100 is the name of the data center GPU built on it. Nvidia announced the chip in March, before ChatGPT reached the public that November.

ChatGPT was an OpenAI product, not an Nvidia one. The demand that rose after its release was for Nvidia's data center chips. The H100 belongs to that category.

U.S. export rules also limited where those chips could be sold. In October 2022, the U.S. imposed restrictions on exports of advanced chips to China. The rules covered the A100 and the H100, two of Nvidia's data center GPUs.

The H100 therefore came under U.S. export restrictions for China in the same year Nvidia announced it.

Nvidia followed Hopper with another architecture. In March 2024, the company announced Blackwell.

This stretch of Nvidia history runs from the H100 announcement in March 2022 to the Blackwell announcement in March 2024. The October 2022 export restrictions and the November 2022 release of ChatGPT fall between those two dates.

Nvidia $NVDA's market value first passed $1 trillion in May 2023. It crossed $2 trillion in February 2024 and $3 trillion in June 2024. On June 18, 2024, the chipmaker overtook Microsoft $MSFT as the most valuable listed company.

Market value, also called market capitalization, is a company's share price multiplied by its number of shares outstanding. It moves with the stock on every trading day. Each threshold records how investors priced Nvidia on a given date. It is not a fixed measure of the business.

Market value is also separate from a company's sales or profit. A higher market value does not mean a company sold more or earned more than another. It reflects the price investors paid for its shares, multiplied across all of them. When Nvidia passed Microsoft, the comparison was between two stock market valuations on the same day.

The word "listed" matters in that comparison. The ranking covers companies whose shares trade on public stock exchanges. A privately held company has no daily share price. It cannot be measured on the same daily basis.

The two trillion-dollar steps took different lengths of time. Nvidia needed about nine months to go from $1 trillion in May 2023 to $2 trillion in February 2024. The climb from $2 trillion to $3 trillion took about four months and ended in June 2024. Each step added the same $1 trillion in market value. The second step took less than half as long as the first.

The Microsoft milestone came in the same month as the $3 trillion crossing. The lead was a position held on a particular trading day. A company that ranks first on one day can fall behind on the next as share prices move.

The dates mark first crossings only. They show when Nvidia's value reached each level, not whether it stayed above that level afterward. Round numbers such as $1 trillion are reference points for share-price valuation. They are not figures the company reported in its earnings.

#5455. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

Zcash has set a new high in its network hashrate just days after the NU7 upgrade, which slashed block times by a third to 25 seconds. Zcash activated its NU7 upgrade on November 6, 2026, at block 3,543,405.

Zcash network hashrate: 32.62 GSol/s, up 5.8% in 30 days. ⛏️ An all-time high. https://t.co/1vNROBAvd2

Zcash hashrate refers to the total computing power of all miners on the ZEC network. It is calculated by the current network difficulty, the average block find time set by the cryptocurrency network and/or the effective block find time of the latest blocks.

ZEC got 3x faster following the NU7 upgrade, which launched on November 6, with block times down from 75 to 25 seconds, and the Sprout pool retired, marking a new era for Zcash.

Faster blocks mean more room for shielded transactions. NU7 adds per-block limits: 330 Orchard or Ironwood actions, 300 Sapling inputs and outputs, a shared budget of 330 across pools, and no new Sprout JoinSplits. These limits more than double Orchard protocol throughput while reducing the worst-case sync load a spammer can push onto light wallets by about 37%.

NU7 does not raise Zcash's fixed 21 million cap; halvings will now come every 5,040,000 blocks instead of 1,680,000, so the issuance schedule holds at roughly four years per halving. NU7 also starts allocating funds for future mining rewards. Some 60% of aggregate transaction fees will flow into a public reserve that pays later mining rewards.

In what comes next after the NU7 upgrade, Zcash developers have proposed cutting block times in a potential NU7.1 upgrade just days after NU7 went live. The proposal would reduce target block times from 25 to 20 seconds, aiming to speed up transaction confirmations and improve user experience and network latency.

#5452. Ethereum (ETH) Gas Estimates Are Broken: Explaining the Fix and the Issue

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Ethereum transactions can appear successful, but there might be a problem hiding behind the scenes.

A Geth developer has proposed a fix to the client's gas estimation, according to draft pull request #36084 on GitHub. The patch addresses an issue in the current estimator, which could result in incorrect gas limits due to failed internal calls (calls from one smart contract to another) being ignored.

Although the transaction could still be completed, there is no evidence that the action the user wanted has actually happened.

The issue lies in a mechanism where a smart contract calls another smart contract, catches an error, and then proceeds to a refund, records the failure, or skips an item entirely. Technically, the transaction was successful, but the outcome is different for the user.

This could potentially result in wallets suggesting a gas limit that is enough to finish the transaction, but not enough to complete the work inside it. The developer also noted that EIP-8037 could make this behavior more common, since gas returned from failed internal execution can help fund the fallback.

According to the pull request, the change includes a stricter definition of success for gas estimates. This version of Geth would improve the way it deals with internal failures, counting failed internal calls and contract creations instead of checking only whether the transaction completes.

Even if the transaction completes, the estimate would get rejected if it produces more internal failures than a reference execution with a higher gas limit.

Nonetheless, the developer stressed that an internal call that always fails should not push the estimate higher indefinitely. The reference execution enables the estimator to keep existing failures without allowing additional ones caused by insufficient gas. The proposal also introduces a separate Amsterdam reference, preventing unnecessary increases made purely to access the state gas reservoir.

The developer states that they've replayed 432 mainnet transactions with the new set of rules from the Amsterdam update and that the suggested change fixed 64 out of 67 cases.

The gas limit increased by 4%. 254 additional estimates were unaffected due to the lack of the problem, with 3 cases being undetected.

For regular investors, the proposed change should improve the reliability of wallet estimates and reduce transactions that complete without delivering the intended result, despite introducing higher gas limits in some cases. Luckily, there is no proven link between higher gas limits and higher fees.

#5451. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am

AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.
