#5444. Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?

In the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning departure from the company, employees received an email from someone most of them had probably never heard of before, even though he’d been affiliated with the company and its board for decades. His name is Harvey Jones, and he was writing to tell them that he’d just been appointed the company’s first-ever Chair of the Board, and that Nvidia CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO.

“I’m writing to share an important update,” Jones’ note began, according to leaked screenshots of the email. He then tried to reassure employees no doubt left shaken by the past weeks’ revelations and the sudden departure of Jensen Huang, a man who co-founded the company and, until today, had been synonymous with its success. “The Board takes seriously our duty as steward of this great company,” Jones said.

That sense of calm and confidence is something Jones is known for, according to two longtime friends and former coworkers. Although Jones, 73, may not be a household name, he has worked in the technology industry, and in semiconductors, for over 30 years, according to his biography on the Nvidia website. He founded two companies, served as CEO of another, and since 2004 has been managing partner of investment firm Square Wave Ventures. He’s been on Nvidia’s board since 1993, the year Huang founded the company.

Jones comes from a successful Connecticut family—his full name is Harvey Jones III—with an “old school, conservative” way about him, Penny Herscher, who has known Jones since 1984 and used to work for him, tells Fortune. His father was a U.S. Army Colonel and church-goer, who then became a vice president at the Walt Disney World Company. Jones himself is a billionaire, which Forbes says is “almost entirely due to his Nvidia director’s compensation” and the fact that he owns 0.03% of the company.

“Harvey has a deep sense of history,” Chris Rowen, who cofounded the semiconductor processor company Tensilica with Jones in 1997, tells Fortune. He has a house on Nantucket and enjoys sailing classic yachts and fine art. “He has a smooth polish,” Rowen said. But Rowen also said that, despite outward appearances, there’s nothing effete about Jones. “He is such a gentleman, so articulate, and so well-sanded on the outside that you might worry there isn’t a deep fierceness and technical insight inside, but beneath that smooth exterior is a really bright, insightful, aggressive guy.”

At a time of great turbulence, Jones can offer Nvidia a “steady pair of hands” to “sort out” its next chapter, Herscher said. She described him as a “charming elder statesman” who at this point in his career is likely “very hard to ruffle.”

Jones and Rowen played distinct roles during their time at Tensilica. As the CEO, Rowen was an enthusiastic technical and operational leader overseeing the team. As chairman, Jones offered a reassuring presence. “His experience was such that he exuded this confidence and experience,” Rowen said. “If he thought we were on the right track, people were instantly comforted. He really communicated a sense of the larger picture and gave people a great deal of confidence that the wider world needed and approved of what we were doing.”

“He’s very strategic,” Herscher said. “I’m sure he’s right now figuring out the right strategy and steps going forward. He’s always looking around corners.”

Jones’ experience and board tenure also begs the question of how he failed to identify the enormous reputational risk of Huang’s affairs, three of which are known as of this writing. Huang also notoriously had many reports, up to 60 at one point, and no clear successor or succession planning.

“Jones may be the right person to steady the ship, but his longevity is both his greatest qualification and the strongest reason to scrutinize his leadership,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult tells Fortune. “The board cannot simply present itself as the solution without examining its role in creating the problem.”

Case in point: Huang’s affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, was known inside the company, and appears to violate its code of conduct, The New York Times reported. The code of conduct instructs all employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships.” The board promises to promptly investigate all reports of misconduct. What happened?

“Major companies often brief their key leadership about potential risks including the theft of intellectual property, legal and regulatory risks, and reputational risks,” Nick Reese, a former Department of Homeland Security employee and assistant professor at NYU SPS’ Center for Global Affairs, tells Fortune. “It is unimaginable to think that Nvidia, a company building geostrategically impactful technology, was not aware of these threats and would not have briefed its principles about them.”

Jones will likely lead the process to select Nvidia’s next CEO, Herscher said, though she had not spoken to him about it directly, and Nvidia did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. But that’s typically how the process would work in a situation like this, Herscher said, drawing on her knowledge from sitting on three public boards, and being the co-founder of The Chairs Circle, which runs educational programs for board chairs.  The fact that Jones also sits on Nvidia’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee makes it even more likely that he will lead this process, she said, as usually that committee is involved in the process.

The search will likely take at least a few months, Herscher said. The board will likely hire a recruiter to identify candidates—something Bloomberg reported this week that Nvidia has already done. That firm will likely do the first outreach, Herscher said, and then Jones will speak to the most promising candidates, along with the rest of the internal search committee.

All signs point to Jones being an effective recruiter, with a wide net of contacts in the industry, Herscher said.

Longtime technology executive Chi-Foo Chan described Jones as “a very persuasive guy” in a 2019 oral history interview with the Computer History Museum, referring to the conversations the two had when Jones convinced Chan to join Synopsys, the electronics company Jones led from 1987 to 1998.

Nvidia shareholders are hoping those skills can wrangle a big fish to come in as Nvidia’s next CEO. Potential successors may include Rene Hass, who is currently the CEO of the chipmaker Arm.  President Trump, who allegedly did not act on reports of Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy, suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook might be a good pick.

Whoever it is, they’ll need the right operational and product development chops to keep the GPUs flowing.

#5443. Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”

#5442. How boards investigate a CEO: 10 parts of an internal probe

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn how boards investigate a CEO, from special committees and outside counsel to interviews, disclosure rules and the outcomes directors can choose when an internal probe ends

Every company has one executive whom the board alone hires, pays, evaluates and can remove: the chief executive. That makes an inquiry into the CEO different from any other internal investigation. The person under review often controls the budget, the legal department and much of the information directors depend on. Corporate governance practice has developed a set of safeguards to work around that conflict.

Understanding how boards investigate a CEO starts with a familiar sequence. Independent directors take charge. They retain outside lawyers who report to them instead of to management. They write down what the inquiry will examine, lock down relevant records, interview witnesses and follow the money. At each stage, they decide what the company owes regulators, investors and the public.

Two Delaware court decisions define the legal stakes. Delaware is the state of incorporation for many large U.S. companies. Its courts expect directors to make a good-faith effort to oversee major risks. The Delaware Court of Chancery set out that oversight duty in its 1996 Caremark decision. In 2019, the Delaware Supreme Court applied it in Marchand v. Barnhill, a case arising from food safety problems at Blue Bell Creameries. Directors who overlook warning signs about a chief executive can face shareholder claims. A poorly run inquiry carries its own costs. It can put attorney-client privilege at risk, cause a company to miss a filing deadline or invite closer scrutiny from regulators.

This slideshow breaks the process into 10 parts. The first four cover who leads the probe, which lawyers do the work, how the scope is defined and how evidence is preserved. The next four explain witness interviews, forensic accounting, whistleblower complaints and the disclosure rules that apply to public companies. The final two describe how the CEO is kept out of the board's deliberations and what directors can do once the findings arrive.

The descriptions reflect common U.S. practice and established law. Bylaws, corporate charters and executive employment contracts differ from company to company. Practice varies from one investigation to the next.

Each slide is written to stand on its own. A reader interested only in Upjohn warnings, clawbacks or Form 8-K deadlines can skip directly to that entry.

When allegations reach the chief executive, a board usually assigns the inquiry to a special committee made up only of independent directors. These directors have no business, family or financial ties to the CEO. That lets them weigh the facts without a conflict of interest.

The committee can be created for the occasion or drawn from a body that already exists. The audit committee is a frequent choice when the allegations concern financial reporting. It already oversees the outside auditor and the company's internal controls. Claims about workplace conduct or personal behavior may instead go to a purpose-built committee. They can also go to the full board, meeting without the CEO.

Independence is judged by actual relationships, not only by a director's formal status. A director whom the CEO recruited may be left off the committee. The same goes for a director who serves alongside the CEO on another company's board, or one with a long personal friendship with the executive. Boards commonly ask counsel to review each prospective member's ties before the work begins.

Delaware case law gives directors reason to take care. Under the oversight duty recognized in In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation, directors must make a good-faith effort to ensure the company has information and reporting systems. The Delaware Supreme Court applied that duty in Marchand v. Barnhill, a case involving Blue Bell Creameries. The court stressed that boards must make this effort for the risks most central to the business. Shareholders can bring derivative claims against directors who fail to meet that duty.

A committee needs formal authority as well as independent members. A board resolution, often called the committee's charter, gives it the power to hire its own advisers. The same document lets it demand company records and speak with any employee. It also sets the reporting line, which in most cases runs to the full board minus the CEO.

The choice of committee leader carries weight. A lead independent director or a non-executive chair often acts as the main contact for the outside lawyers. That arrangement keeps the CEO and other senior managers out of the chain of communication. It also helps shield the inquiry from accusations of interference by the executive under review.

A special committee investigating a CEO hires its own outside law firm. That firm takes instructions from the committee rather than from the chief executive or anyone in management. The separate reporting line gives regulators, auditors and shareholders a reason to trust what the investigation finds.

Boards generally avoid the company's regular outside law firm for this work. A firm that earns large fees from routine corporate matters can look like it has a stake in the result. So can a firm whose partners deal with the CEO regularly. Committees tend to pick a firm with no history of advising the executive under review. They also run a conflicts check on the firm's other clients before signing.

The engagement letter names the committee as the party the lawyers answer to. That wording helps support attorney-client privilege. The privilege can shield confidential communications between a lawyer and a client from disclosure in later lawsuits. It belongs to the company itself. In this setting, the committee typically decides on the company's behalf whether to keep it or give it up.

The protection can be lost. Handing findings to a government agency or another outside party may lead a court to rule that privilege has been waived for that material. Some committees ask for oral briefings instead of a long written report for that reason. Others want a document they can share with regulators and accept the waiver risk that comes with it.

Investigation teams at these firms often include former federal prosecutors. Those lawyers know how the Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission judge whether a company's internal inquiry was independent and thorough. The firm can also bring in specialists, such as e-discovery vendors, and supervise their work.

The company pays the legal bills. That puts the CEO's own organization in the position of funding an inquiry into its leader. Committees handle the problem by approving the fee terms themselves and having invoices sent straight to them. Management has no role in setting the budget or signing off on the bills.

Counsel also guides the committee's process from the first meeting. The lawyers advise on the order of steps, how to document decisions and when to brief the outside auditor or regulators. That record can matter later if a court or agency examines how the board handled the matter.

Before any witness is interviewed, the special committee puts the scope of a CEO investigation in writing. That mandate names the allegations under review, the time period covered, the people and records involved and the authority the investigators hold.

The document is usually a committee resolution, an engagement letter with outside counsel or both. Its terms need to be precise. An allegation that the CEO misused a company aircraft calls for different records and witnesses than an allegation of harassment. Pressure on the finance team to hit a quarterly target would call for yet another set.

A defined scope also keeps the inquiry from drifting. A review of expense reports can surface questions about related-party deals or a vendor contract. Each new thread adds cost and time. With a written mandate in hand, the committee can choose to widen the inquiry, keep it narrow or open a separate review with its own terms.

The mandate states who receives the findings. In most cases that is the special committee, which then decides what to pass to the full board. The document can bar the CEO from receiving drafts. Counsel still reviews the executive's employment agreement and the company's bylaws. Either one may grant the CEO a right to information or a chance to respond.

Access is another core term. A typical mandate gives the investigators authority to reach any employee, any company system and any document the business holds. It also directs management to cooperate. Corporate codes of conduct and employment contracts often require staff to assist internal inquiries, and the mandate can cite those obligations.

The document also covers unexpected discoveries. Investigators may find signs of a separate problem, such as possible bribery or an accounting error. The mandate can require them to alert the committee at once. The committee then decides whether to bring in other advisers or notify the outside auditor.

A mandate is not fixed. When the facts change, the committee amends the scope in writing. Each expansion or narrowing then appears in the record as a deliberate decision rather than an accident.

That record has a later use. The company may face shareholder litigation or questions from regulators. A written mandate and dated committee minutes show what the committee asked for, when it asked and why.

Locking down evidence is the first concrete step in a CEO investigation. Early in the process, the company sends a legal hold notice telling employees to keep relevant records intact. Its IT team also switches off the routine deletion of email, files and chat history.

The chief executive's own data comes first. Investigators move early to secure the CEO's company email, calendar, phone, laptop and cloud accounts. A common method is a forensic image, which is a complete copy of a device's contents made in a way that can be verified later. A copy taken at the outset makes it harder for anyone to argue afterward that material was altered or removed.

Personal phones and messaging apps are harder to reach. Executives may conduct business over text messages, WhatsApp or Signal. Some of these apps can be set to erase messages after a period of time. The U.S. Department of Justice addressed this problem in March 2023, when it updated its Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs. The revision covers how companies govern personal devices, communication platforms and messaging applications, including those that make messages ephemeral.

Losing data carries legal consequences. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) deals with electronically stored information that should have been kept but was lost. If a party failed to take reasonable steps to preserve it, a court can order measures to cure the resulting harm. Where the loss was intended to deprive another party of the information, the court can impose harsher sanctions. Those include instructing a jury that the lost information was unfavorable to the party that lost it, or dismissing the case.

The hold notice goes to a defined group known as custodians — the people likely to hold relevant records. In a CEO probe, that list usually starts with the executive, direct reports and assistants. It then extends to finance staff and others involved in the matters under review. Counsel adds names as interviews and documents point to other people who handled the material.

Records generated by company systems matter as much as messages. Access logs, badge swipes and expense approval trails show who acted and when. Investigators use them to test what witnesses say against what the systems recorded. Some systems overwrite their logs on a rotating schedule. The hold covers them for that reason.

Collection follows preservation. E-discovery vendors process the gathered data into a searchable form. Lawyers then search it using keywords, names and date ranges drawn from the scope of the investigation.

Outside counsel typically opens each witness interview in a CEO investigation with an Upjohn warning. The lawyer tells the employee that counsel represents the company, not the individual, and that the company controls the privilege over the conversation.

The warning is named for Upjohn Co. v. United States, a 1981 U.S. Supreme Court decision. The Court held that attorney-client privilege can protect conversations between a company's lawyers and its employees. The protection applies when those conversations help the lawyers give legal advice to the company. The Court rejected a narrower "control group" test, which had limited the privilege to senior managers. That ruling lets investigators question staff well below the executive suite and still treat the exchanges as privileged.

The warning is sometimes nicknamed a "corporate Miranda," although it is not a constitutional right. Its job is to prevent a misunderstanding. An employee who assumes the company's lawyer is also a personal lawyer may speak more freely than intended. A later claim that a personal attorney-client relationship existed can cloud the company's control over the interview.

A standard warning covers a handful of points. The lawyer works for the company. The conversation is confidential. The company can waive the privilege and share the employee's statements with regulators or prosecutors without the employee's consent. Counsel usually confirms that the employee understands before asking about the facts.

An employee who wants personal advice can hire a separate lawyer. Some companies pay for that representation under their bylaws or an indemnification agreement.

The order of interviews follows a pattern. Counsel generally reviews documents first and then speaks with people on the edges of the events. Witnesses closer to the conduct come next. The CEO is often interviewed near the end. By then, the lawyers can test the executive's account against emails, records and other testimony.

Interviews are usually not recorded or transcribed. Lawyers take notes and write memoranda that reflect their own impressions and analysis. That approach can strengthen work-product protection for the materials. The memoranda summarize rather than quote, and witnesses do not usually sign them.

Counsel often reminds employees that company policy forbids retaliation for taking part. Witnesses are also asked not to discuss the interview with colleagues. That request helps keep later accounts independent. It cannot stop an employee from reporting possible violations to the Securities and Exchange Commission, which bars companies from impeding such communications.

The CEO occupies a different position as the subject of the probe. The executive can bring a personal lawyer and may negotiate the timing and format of the interview. The special committee decides whether to insist on a face-to-face session or accept a written response.

Forensic accountants trace where company money went in a CEO investigation. They examine expense reports, wire transfers, vendor payments and sign-off records. The goal is to test whether spending followed company policy and whether the required approvals were actually given.

Their work starts with specific questions. Were the chief executive's travel and entertainment claims backed by receipts? Did company money reach vendors connected to the executive or to family members? Were contracts broken into smaller pieces to slip under approval limits? Did anyone override a control, and who was aware of it?

To answer those questions, the accountants line up ledger entries against bank statements, invoices and email. A payment recorded in the books with no matching invoice becomes a lead for the lawyers. So does a spending approval that cannot be traced to the person who was supposed to give it.

Data analytics widens the search. Software can sort through large volumes of transactions to flag duplicate payments, round-number entries, payments made at unusual times and money sent to new vendors. None of those patterns proves misconduct by itself. Each one points investigators toward documents to pull and witnesses to question.

Related-party transactions draw close scrutiny in an inquiry focused on a chief executive. These are deals between the company and an insider, or someone close to an insider. U.S. public companies must disclose some of these arrangements in their securities filings. A deal that was left out or described inaccurately can become a reporting problem separate from the original allegation.

The accounting firm is usually hired by outside counsel rather than by the company directly. That structure draws on United States v. Kovel, a 1961 decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. The court recognized that attorney-client privilege can extend to an accountant who helps a lawyer understand financial information in order to give legal advice. Whether the protection holds in a given case depends on how the engagement is set up and used.

The company's outside auditor plays a different part. The auditor stays independent of the investigation. It may still ask what the board's special committee has found. Alleged executive misconduct can affect the auditor's view of management's integrity and of the financial statements. The committee and its lawyers decide when and how the auditor is briefed.

The accountants' conclusions flow into the committee's final report. They put a dollar figure on the amounts at issue. They also help directors distinguish a policy breach from an accounting error or an intentional scheme.

Many CEO investigations begin with a tip, such as a hotline report, an employee complaint or a letter sent directly to a director. U.S. law requires listed companies to keep a channel open for these reports, and it protects the people who use it.

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 gave that job to the audit committee. Audit committees of listed companies must set procedures for receiving, keeping and handling complaints about accounting, internal controls and auditing. Employees must be able to raise those concerns confidentially and anonymously. Many companies hire an outside vendor to run the hotline.

Section 806 of the same law addresses retaliation. It protects public-company employees who report conduct they reasonably believe is fraud or a securities law violation. A worker who is fired or demoted after reporting can file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Labor's Occupational Safety and Health Administration within 180 days. Boards that receive a complaint typically document how the complainant is treated from the first day.

The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 opened a second path. Its whistleblower program lets the Securities and Exchange Commission pay tipsters a share of what it recovers. Awards run from 10 percent to 30 percent of money collected in actions with sanctions above $1 million. An employee can go to the agency at the same time as the board, or without telling the board at all.

The agency's rules reward internal reporting without requiring it. A whistleblower who reports inside the company and then contacts the agency within 120 days can be treated as having reported on the date of the internal complaint. The agency's Rule 21F-17 bars anyone from taking steps to impede a person from communicating directly with agency staff about a possible securities law violation. That ban covers enforcing or threatening to enforce a confidentiality agreement.

The practical result is that a board does not fully control the timeline. A committee that receives a credible tip moves quickly and records when the information arrived. It avoids any step that could look like an effort to unmask or silence the source.

Routing is the first decision. A complaint that names the CEO or the general counsel should bypass both and go straight to independent directors, usually starting with the audit committee chair. That director judges whether the allegation, if true, is serious enough to warrant an independent probe. Investigators typically speak with the complainant early. They protect the person's identity as far as the law and the facts permit.

A public company does not have to announce an internal investigation of its CEO when the inquiry begins. Certain outcomes do trigger fast reporting. If the chief executive leaves, the company generally must file a Form 8-K with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) within four business days.

Form 8-K is the SEC's current report for major corporate events. The governing provision for a CEO exit is Item 5.02. It covers the departure of directors and certain senior officers, including the principal executive officer. The filing must state that the executive resigned, retired or was terminated, along with the date. A reason is not required. If the company chooses to give one, that description has to be accurate and not misleading.

The same item covers the other side of a leadership change. When the board appoints a new principal executive officer, Item 5.02 calls for a filing on that appointment too.

Financial findings carry a deadline of their own. The board or audit committee may conclude that previously issued financial statements should no longer be relied on. Item 4.02 of Form 8-K then requires a filing within four business days. A probe into executive spending or revenue practices can lead to that conclusion.

Staying quiet about an inquiry still carries legal risk. Rule 10b-5, adopted under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, bars materially false statements. It also bars omitting facts needed to keep other statements from being misleading. A company that praises its leadership while aware of serious allegations can expose itself to liability. Counsel reviews earnings releases, filings and executive remarks with that risk in view.

Executive certifications add pressure. Sections 302 and 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 require the CEO and chief financial officer to certify the company's periodic reports. When an investigation casts doubt on those reports, the committee, the outside auditor and disclosure counsel assess whether the earlier statements still hold.

Reporting to authorities is a separate decision from public disclosure. A company may choose to tell the SEC or the U.S. Department of Justice about possible violations. The Justice Department has published corporate enforcement policies describing credit for voluntary self-disclosure, cooperation and remediation. The board weighs that option with its lawyers.

Stock exchange rules also apply. The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq $NDAQ expect listed companies to release material news promptly. A CEO exit or a restatement can meet that standard.

A small group controls the message. The committee, outside counsel and the corporate secretary agree on what is said to employees and the public. Conflicting accounts can create legal problems of their own.

During an internal investigation, the chief executive is cut out of every decision about the probe. The CEO does not attend special committee meetings, does not see the committee's papers and has no say over the investigating lawyers. In many cases, the executive continues to run the business day to day.

The arrangement is harder to manage when one person is both CEO and board chair. In that case, the lead independent director or another independent director chosen by the board presides over any discussion of the inquiry. The chair's usual control over meeting agendas and board materials does not extend to the investigation.

Listed companies already have a forum for these conversations. New York Stock Exchange rules require non-management directors to meet in regularly scheduled executive sessions without management present. Nasdaq $NDAQ rules require regularly scheduled executive sessions of independent directors. Those meetings give directors a routine place to discuss the probe without the executive in the room.

Recusal covers votes as well as attendance. The chief executive abstains from any board decision about the investigation, including its budget and its conclusions. The general counsel may also have a conflict. That officer usually reports to the CEO. Committees often limit the general counsel's role to logistics, or keep the general counsel out of the inquiry entirely.

Directors also decide how the executive will operate while the work continues. One choice is a leave of absence. Another is to remove the CEO's authority over particular areas, such as the finance function or the employees being interviewed. A third is to make no change when the allegations are narrow. The committee weighs the risk of interference against disruption to the company.

The executive keeps rights during the process. A CEO under investigation can hire a personal lawyer and is normally given a chance to answer the allegations. Company bylaws, indemnification agreements and employment contracts can determine whether the company covers legal costs as they arise. Section 145 of the Delaware General Corporation Law permits companies to advance those expenses to officers. The officer typically must promise to repay the money if a court later finds the officer is not entitled to indemnification.

Succession planning runs on a separate track. Directors identify who could serve as interim CEO and how operations would stay stable if the executive leaves. That discussion is kept apart from the fact-finding. The separation keeps choices about a possible replacement from shaping the investigation's conclusions.

The rest of the board stays informed. The committee briefs the other independent directors at intervals. Those updates let the full board carry out its own oversight duties.

At the end of a CEO investigation, the special committee presents its findings and the independent directors decide how to respond. The options range from clearing the executive entirely to firing the CEO for cause. Reprimands, pay cuts and compensation recovery fall in between.

The CEO's employment agreement usually sets the boundaries of that decision. Many executive contracts define cause to include conduct such as fraud, willful misconduct or serious breaches of company policy. A dismissal for cause can cost the executive severance and unvested equity. Directors and counsel therefore test the facts against the contract's exact wording. Labeling a departure as for cause when the evidence does not meet the definition can lead to a dispute with the former executive.

Recovering pay is a separate track. The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted Rule 10D-1 under the Dodd-Frank Act. It requires listed companies to keep policies for clawing back incentive-based compensation that executives received in error because of an accounting restatement. The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq $NDAQ put the rule into effect through their listing standards. Companies had to adopt compliant policies by December 2023.

Rule 10D-1 has a narrow trigger. A restatement sets it off, not misconduct in general. Recovery applies whether or not the executive was at fault. It covers current and former executive officers. It reaches incentive pay received during the three completed fiscal years before the restatement was required. A CEO who broke conduct rules without affecting the financial statements falls outside it.

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 contains an older recovery provision. Section 304 covers the CEO and the chief financial officer when misconduct leads to a restatement. It reaches bonuses, incentive pay and profits from selling company stock in the 12 months after the misstated filing. The SEC enforces it, not the board.

Company-written clawback clauses can go further. Depending on how they are drafted and what the executive signed, they may reach compensation tied to misconduct. Collecting the money can still require negotiation or a lawsuit.

The committee's conclusions go to the independent directors, who weigh them before voting on any action. Their reasoning belongs in the board minutes. Those minutes become the formal record of how the company handled the allegations.

Remediation follows the decision about the CEO. Committees often order changes to the controls, approval limits or reporting lines that allowed the problem. A documented record of those fixes can matter if regulators later examine how the board responded.

Not every probe ends with a finding against the executive. When the evidence does not support the allegations, the committee says so in its conclusions. The board then records that it has cleared the CEO. That written record shows directors examined the allegations and acted on what the evidence showed.

#5439. AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:19 pm

WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The company this week launched WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate users can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The company has spent the past two years moving away from individual users to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

“We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr said. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the company’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

Dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

He succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The company is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The company’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

“We view [Model Context Protocol], and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago.”

How it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr said AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

WellSaid also says it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

Producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs.

The strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he said.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr said. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the company’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid plans to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”

Customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr said.

The business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr said. Moving away from individual users “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

WellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the company at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr said debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable company,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”

#5438. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

Telegram CEO Pavel Durov has shared new metrics on the Gram wallet integration in the messenger.

According to Durov, over the last 48 hours alone, users activated more than 700,000 non-custodial Gram wallets.

The screenshot shared by the Telegram CEO shows more than 329,000 new addresses a day. According to GRAM documentation, a wallet is created automatically when a user receives their first token transfer.

700K+ self-custodial wallets created on Telegram in the last 48 hours alone. Adoption spreads virally: a wallet activates the moment someone receives Grams. The crypto revolution is going strong. https://t.co/JPO2KVMip0

The growth comes after a series of changes Telegram made to the TON network earlier this year under Durov's "Make TON Great Again" campaign.

Back in 2020, Durov was forced to kill the original Telegram Open Network project and return more than $1.2 billion to investors after a lawsuit from the US SEC.

Community developers kept the open-source code alive as The Open Network (Toncoin).

This year, Telegram became the largest validator of the network. Besides, Telegram cut TON fees sixfold.

In June, the token was renamed back to its original name, Gram, after a community vote, with 81% of voters in favor. In July, Durov announced that Telegram would integrate a native non-custodial Gram wallet into every Telegram app.

The Telegram CEO described it as "the largest deployment of a non-custodial crypto wallet in history" and promised instant zero-fee transactions for more than 1 billion Telegram users.

According to TON developer Andrew Rogozov, the custodial Wallet in Telegram will stay separate from the new wallet. Now, onboarding happens natively within standard chat windows.

Still, while wallet creation metrics break records, liquidity inside the network is lagging behind with total value locked at $42.01 million, according to DefiLlama.

These hundreds of thousands of new addresses are mostly making microtransactions, such as buying Telegram Premium, paying for in-app ads, or settling small P2P transfers.

Besides, Telegram's validator weight is raising centralization concerns among industry critics. At the same time, the native wallet is still unavailable for US users.

At press time, Gram is trading at $1.05. The token is still more than 87% below its 2024 high of $8.25.

"The crypto revolution is going strong," Durov said.

#5436. Ex-Seattle startup DeltaGen acquired by new AI company backed by Veeam co-founder

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a new small-business software company backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron said. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The company relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

“AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.

#5435. Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal

Jane Street, one of Wall Street’s leading quantitative trading firms, more than doubled its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, according to regulatory filings released Thursday and reviewed by Fortune. The securities filings show the firm’s positions as of Sept. 30—just over six weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though.

The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. That’s over double the 11.8 million shares held, worth $2.4 billion, in the second quarter. Nvidia was its second-largest holding behind SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Jane Street declined Fortune’s request for comment.

The filings show what Jane Street held in late September, not what it owns now, and leave out short positions. Jane Street traders could, in theory, have shorted Nvidia after the reporting period ended and made money from the subsequent decline. The filings alone cannot tell us whether they did, though.

Options add another layer of complexity to this. The 13F also discloses that Jane Street holds a large amount of puts and calls, which are reported using the value of the underlying shares, rather than the market value of the options themselves. Those notional figures can make positions look far larger than the sums actually invested, while revealing little about the firm’s overall exposure once offsetting trades are taken into account. A large reported position, in other words, is not necessarily a huge directional bet.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after more than three decades at the helm of the company he cofounded in 1993. In his place, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO. Huang’s departure comes days after bombshell media reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former exec at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence authorities suspect of working for Beijing.

In a message to employees on Sunday, Huang admitted that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and apologized. He also said he supported an independent investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The bad news didn’t stop there for Huang, though. Just three days later, the New York Times reported that the 63-year-old also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Reuters reported Thursday, citing two people familiar with the matter, that he had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee, as well.

Reuters reported in August, citing a person familiar, that Jane Street had so far generated more than $40 billion in trading revenue in 2026. That surpassed its $39.6 billion total for all of 2025 and comfortably beat trading revenues for the nation’s largest banks.

Still, there have been some signs of cracks. That same Reuters report over the summer said Jane Street took a $15 billion hit, partly from its exposure to AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness. Situational Awareness, started by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner, sold the bulk of its equities portfolio to Ken Griffin’s Citadel after the market downturn triggered margin calls. Jane Street told employees that the drawdown had left its investment roughly flat for the year, though it remained profitable over the full period, per Reuters. Jane Street has not confirmed this report.

The story was updated with Jane Street’s decline to comment.

Morgan Chittum is a reporter at Fortune covering finance.

Ripple USD (RLUSD) now tops the chart for short-term volume growth on decentralized exchanges (DEXs), outpacing Ethena's USDe. RWA Foundation, citing Token Terminal data, shows RLUSD's DEX trading volume jumped by $127.4 million over the past seven days.

Other major DeFi stablecoins, Usual's USD0 and Aave's GHO among them, stayed below $20 million.

#5433. Seattle’s Allen Institute helps create a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for brain cells to unlock clues to disease

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm

A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits. The region is linked to psychiatric and degenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Parkinson’s disease.

The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species. The goal is to help researchers compare findings, collaborate and accelerate their understanding of this essential brain region.

“This is groundwork that is necessary to really make progress,” said Michael Hawrylycz, principal investigator with the Seattle-based Allen Institute who helped organize the consortium.

The project, called the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, or BICAN, produced a basal ganglia atlas that is publicly available for basic researchers, clinicians and others to use.

The research is being presented in a package of 26 articles in a special issue of the journal Cell. The data comes from humans, macaques, marmoset and mice. One of the benefits of comparing the basal ganglia between species is understanding which components are uniquely human, providing potential insights into neurological diseases.

Despite the critical and wide-ranging roles, the basal ganglia is relatively small — it’s about 2% of the brain with a volume roughly the size of a large gumball.

For the project, the researchers pulled information from 25.5 million brain cells, including 21 million human cells. They used a variety of techniques to tease out insights, including RNA sequencing to identify gene activity from single cells in precise locations; epigenomic studies revealing where genes are switched on or off; and measurements of electrical activity combined with cell shape and genetic information.

It’s a lot of data to stitch together and make sense of, Hawrylycz said. “AI is a perfect tool” for the job, he said, because it excels at finding patterns.

The findings could help guide future treatments, but the work remains basic research rather than clinical research, Hawrylycz said.

The new research is the first major installment of the third phase of a brain-mapping effort that began in 2014. The first phase demonstrated that scientists could analyze individual cells on a large scale. The second produced an atlas of the mouse brain.

BICAN aims to create a standardized atlas describing cells throughout the brains of humans and other primates. Hawrylycz said the work is expected to take another two or three years.

#5431. ‘People are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin’ as rising inflation leads investors to seek yield

Bitcoin’s escape from the trenches didn’t last long. The cryptocurrency fell more than 4% on Friday to $68,500, wiping out gains built over the past three months and casting doubt on whether its bear market was ever really over.

The asset also faces weaker investor appetite, according to crypto analytics provider CryptoQuant. The firm’s demand indicator recorded its weakest reading since December 2023, while Bitcoin exchange-traded funds became net sellers again.

The recent downturn has also extended to other parts of the crypto market. That includes Tether’s USDT, the largest cryptocurrency pegged to the U.S. dollar, whose total value shrank by $7.7 billion over the past two months, according to CryptoQuant, a sign that less cash is available in crypto markets.

This time around, inflation has been the main culprit. Tuesday’s Consumer Price Index report showed prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists expected. Even stripping out food and energy, inflation ran hotter than forecast. Traders now overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point in December, with some betting on an even bigger increase.

“Because these are non-yielding assets, and we expect inflation to rise… people are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin to find… government bonds that are going up, providing you [with] income,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at financial technology company IG Group, told Fortune.

Bitcoin isn’t alone in its retreat. Gold traded near $3,900 an ounce on Friday, well below its January peak of about $5,600, according to financial data provider Trading Economics. Prices have fallen roughly 5% over the past month and nearly 5% from a year ago.

Friday’s drop dealt a fresh blow to Bitcoin investors, who had only recently found their footing after months of losses. After Bitcoin hit $58,000 in June, optimism returned in August when the U.S. Treasury announced plans to expand its bond buybacks. The announcement helped spark a rally that carried Bitcoin to $86,000 in September. Since then, though, it has been sliding again.

Recent political news has also made Bitcoin’s recovery an uphill battle, though it held its ground until Friday. The midterm elections handed Democrats control of Congress, a setback for a crypto industry that has leaned on Republican allies to advance favorable legislation. Still, Bitcoin initially took the results in stride.

That was largely because investors had seen the outcome coming, according to Stephen Coltman, head of macro at crypto asset manager 21Shares. “The midterm results weren’t a surprise, and they don’t change the regulatory interpretations as they stand today… We at least have some regulatory stability for two years,” he said.

Inflation and politics aren’t the only forces shaping Bitcoin’s outlook. Analysts say the cryptocurrency is also caught up in the AI boom, which is competing for investors’ money while helping keep the economy strong enough for interest rates to stay high.

Heavy borrowing and spending on AI have created what 21Shares calls an “AI black hole,” drawing money toward the sector and away from assets like Bitcoin and gold. But Bitcoin remains “joined at the hip” with tech stocks, according to Beauchamp. That leaves it in an awkward position: It faces competition for investment dollars when enthusiasm for AI runs high, yet can get dragged down when that enthusiasm fades.

The boom also complicates the outlook for interest rates. In Coltman’s view, AI spending is helping prop up an otherwise weak economy, giving the Fed room to keep fighting inflation with higher rates. If rising borrowing costs force AI companies to rein in spending, the economy could weaken enough to push the Fed to change course, potentially giving Bitcoin some breathing room.
